questions.title: Writing and Estimating User Stories for a BI Deliverable in Sprint Planning
questions.prompt: Your Scrum team is planning the next sprint. Product wants 'a dashboard showing customer lifetime value by region' as a single backlog item, estimated at 3 story points by a junior analyst who hasn't scoped the data sources yet. As the senior BI person on the team, you suspect this is actually multiple stories hiding inside one, with real uncertainty in the CLV calculation logic and an unvalidated data source. How do you handle this in backlog grooming?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer uses backlog grooming to decompose the vague item into independently valuable, estimable stories rather than accepting or silently re-estimating a single large story. The candidate should describe splitting it along natural seams: a story to validate and document the CLV calculation logic with the business stakeholder, a story to confirm and connect the required data sources, a story to build the underlying semantic model/measures, and a story for the dashboard visualization itself — each with its own acceptance criteria.

The candidate should explain why the junior analyst's 3-point estimate was likely too low without undermining them in front of the team: the estimate was made before the unknowns (calculation logic, data source validation) were surfaced, which is a common and correctable planning gap, not a competence failure. A senior team member re-estimates collaboratively, using planning poker or a similar team technique, once the stories are properly split, rather than overriding the estimate unilaterally.

The response should also note the broader behavior being modeled for the team: a senior person makes unknowns visible early in grooming rather than letting the team discover them mid-sprint, and treats precise, honestly-scoped story splitting as part of their responsibility to the sprint's predictability, not just a nice-to-have.
questions.professionalAnswer:
In grooming, I'd just say out loud, 'I don't think this is one story — I think there are at least three stories hiding inside it.' I'd split it: one story to pin down the actual CLV formula with Product, because 'lifetime value' means five different things depending on who you ask; one to confirm the data sources actually have what we need and are joinable; one for the underlying model and measures; and one for the dashboard itself.

I'd be careful not to make the junior analyst feel called out for the 3-point estimate — I'd frame it as, 'this was estimated before we knew about the unknowns in the calculation logic, which is totally normal, that's exactly what grooming is for.' Then I'd have the team re-estimate each piece together once it's split, rather than me just overriding his number myself. Honestly, the biggest thing I'm modeling here for the team is that surfacing unknowns in grooming, before the sprint starts, is a core part of the job — not something you only do when something breaks mid-sprint.
questions.example: Split: (1) Validate CLV calculation logic with Product, (2) Confirm/connect data sources, (3) Build semantic model & measures, (4) Build dashboard visualization — each separately estimated.
commonMistakes: Accepting a vague, oversized story as a single sprint item without decomposing it
Silently re-estimating the story unilaterally instead of involving the team
Publicly undermining the junior analyst's original estimate instead of framing it as a normal grooming gap
Not surfacing the calculation-logic ambiguity ('lifetime value' meaning) before committing to the sprint
Letting unknowns about data source validity go unaddressed until mid-sprint discovery
keyPoints: Decomposes a vague, oversized backlog item into independently valuable, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation and data-source unknowns during grooming, not mid-sprint
Reframes the original estimate's gap constructively rather than as a mistake by the junior analyst
Facilitates collaborative team re-estimation rather than overriding unilaterally
Models proactive unknown-surfacing as a senior responsibility within the Scrum process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and decomposes the oversized/ambiguous story into discrete, estimable stories
Surfaces calculation logic and data source unknowns proactively during grooming
Handles the junior analyst's original estimate constructively and respectfully
Uses collaborative, team-based re-estimation rather than unilateral override
Demonstrates understanding of how senior ownership operates within the Scrum process

questions.title: Pushing Back on Mid-Sprint Scope Creep on a Dashboard User Story
questions.prompt: Three days into a two-week sprint, the Product Owner messages you asking to add two new filter dimensions and a drill-through page to a dashboard user story your team already committed to and sized at the sprint's start. She frames it as 'small additions.' Your team is on track to meet the original commitment but adding this would jeopardize that. As the senior BI person others look to for how to handle this, what do you do?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats this as a textbook mid-sprint scope protection moment, and models the correct Scrum behavior for the rest of the team rather than just solving it quietly themselves. The candidate should first assess honestly whether the additions really are small or whether 'small additions' is underselling the actual work (new filter dimensions typically require model changes, not just visual tweaks, and a drill-through page is a materially new deliverable) — and should say so plainly rather than accepting the framing uncritically.

The response should describe declining to silently absorb the scope change into the current sprint, instead offering the Product Owner a clear choice: add the new items to the backlog for the next sprint with proper estimation, or, if there's a true urgent business reason it must happen now, negotiate explicitly what gets removed or deferred from the current sprint to make room — making the tradeoff visible rather than letting the team silently absorb unplanned work and risk the whole sprint's commitment.

A senior answer also addresses team dynamics: communicating this decision transparently to the team so junior members see that sprint commitments are protected deliberately, not just hoped for, and that saying 'let's scope this for next sprint' is a normal, healthy part of the process rather than a failure to be agile.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd push back right away, but not harshly — I'd say, 'Those aren't actually small. New filter dimensions usually mean model changes, not just UI tweaks, and a drill-through page is basically a new deliverable on its own. Let's not pretend this fits inside what we already committed to.' I wouldn't just quietly try to squeeze it in and hope the team absorbs it, because that's exactly how a sprint commitment turns into nobody trusting sprint commitments.

Then I'd give her the real choice: 'I can add both to the backlog for next sprint and we'll estimate them properly, or if this genuinely can't wait, tell me what you want to cut from the current sprint to make room — I'm not going to have the team just quietly work nights to fit it in.' Honestly, I think the most important part of handling this is doing it visibly, in front of the team, not just in a DM with the PO — because the newer folks on my team need to see that protecting the sprint commitment is a deliberate, normal thing a senior person does, not some rare act of defiance.
questions.example: Response to PO: 'Those two filters and the drill-through aren't small — they're more like a model change plus a new page. Backlog them for next sprint, or tell me what to cut from this one to make room.'
commonMistakes: Accepting the 'small additions' framing uncritically without assessing the real scope impact
Silently absorbing the extra work into the sprint without renegotiating the commitment
Not making the tradeoff (what gets cut or deferred) explicit and visible to the Product Owner
Handling the pushback privately instead of modeling the behavior transparently for the team
Treating 'no, let's backlog this' as a failure of agility rather than a normal part of sprint discipline
keyPoints: Accurately assesses whether 'small additions' genuinely are small before responding
Declines to silently absorb unplanned scope into an already-committed sprint
Offers a clear choice: backlog for next sprint, or explicit trade-off within current sprint
Makes the scope/trade-off conversation visible rather than handling it quietly alone
Models healthy sprint-commitment protection behavior for junior team members

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Accurately assesses the real scope impact rather than accepting the 'small' framing
Protects the sprint commitment rather than silently absorbing new scope
Offers the Product Owner a clear, explicit choice/trade-off
Handles the situation transparently in a way that models good practice for the team
Maintains a collaborative, non-adversarial tone with the Product Owner

questions.title: What a Senior BI Engineer Owns Differently in Release Management
questions.prompt: Your team follows a Dev/QA/UAT/Production promotion process with scheduled releases for dashboard and dataset changes. A junior analyst asks you, 'Why do you get involved in release planning meetings and change approval boards when I just push my changes through QA and wait for sign-off?' How do you explain what a senior BI person owns differently in this release process, and demonstrate it with a specific example?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer distinguishes individual-contributor responsibility (getting one's own change correctly through Dev, QA, and UAT) from senior ownership of the release as a whole system of interacting changes and business risk. The candidate should explain that a senior BI person in the change approval board is evaluating cross-change interactions a junior analyst focused on a single change wouldn't see — for example, catching that their own dataset refactor scheduled for this release will conflict with another analyst's report change going out the same day because both touch the same shared dimension table, and that conflict wouldn't surface in either person's individual UAT testing.

The response should also cover timing and business-risk judgment: a senior person weighs release timing against business calendar risk (e.g., not deploying model changes to executive dashboards the day before quarter-end close) in ways that require broader context than any single ticket carries, and owns the rollback plan and communication plan for a release, not just the change itself.

Finally, the answer should frame this as a growth path for the junior analyst, not a permanent gatekeeping distinction — explaining what experience and context (seeing more releases, more incidents, more cross-team dependencies) builds the judgment to eventually sit in those same rooms, and perhaps inviting the junior analyst to shadow the next change approval board meeting as a concrete next step.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell him the honest difference is scope, not status. 'When you push a change through QA, you're making sure your change is correct. When I sit on the change approval board, I'm checking whether your change and three other people's changes, all going out in the same release, interact badly with each other — which none of you would catch in your own individual UAT.' And I'd give him a real example: 'Last release, your dataset refactor and Priya's report change both touched the shared customer dimension table. Neither of your individual tests would've caught that, because you were each only looking at your own piece.'

I'd also point out the stuff that's easy to miss when you're focused on one ticket — like not scheduling a model change to the exec dashboard the day before quarter-end close, or making sure there's an actual rollback plan if something breaks, not just hoping it doesn't. And I'd end on, 'This isn't a permanent wall between us — it's exactly the kind of judgment you build by seeing more releases and more of what goes wrong. Come sit in on the next change approval board with me, you'll pick it up fast.'
questions.example: Example cited: a dataset refactor and a separate report change both modifying the same shared dimension table in the same release — invisible in either individual's UAT, caught only at the release-level review.
commonMistakes: Framing the difference as seniority/status rather than genuine difference in scope of responsibility
Not providing a concrete, specific example of a cross-change risk individual testing wouldn't catch
Omitting business-calendar timing judgment (e.g., avoiding risky releases near quarter-end) from the explanation
Failing to mention rollback/communication plan ownership as part of release-level responsibility
Presenting the distinction as a permanent gatekeeping barrier rather than a growth path for the junior analyst
keyPoints: Distinguishes individual change correctness from release-level, cross-change ownership
Gives a concrete example of a cross-change conflict invisible to individual UAT testing
Covers business-calendar timing judgment as part of senior release responsibility
Includes ownership of rollback and communication plans, not just the technical change
Frames the distinction as a growth path, inviting the junior analyst to build toward it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clearly distinguishes individual change ownership from release-level/cross-change ownership
Provides a concrete, specific example illustrating the difference
Covers business-risk/timing judgment and rollback/communication ownership
Frames the explanation as a growth path rather than permanent gatekeeping
Communicates respectfully in a way that supports the junior analyst's development

questions.title: Lookup vs. Master-Detail Relationship Tradeoffs
questions.prompt: You're designing a custom Project Management app with a Projects object and a Task object. The business wants a rolled-up total of Task hours displayed on each Project record, and wants Tasks to always be deleted automatically when their parent Project is deleted. A junior admin proposes a simple Lookup relationship from Task to Project because 'it's more flexible.' Walk through whether that choice actually satisfies both requirements, and explain the sharing and ownership consequences of whichever relationship type you'd actually recommend.
questions.modelAnswer:
A Lookup relationship fails both stated requirements. Roll-up summary fields are only available on the master side of a Master-Detail relationship, because the platform needs the tightly bound, lifecycle-linked relationship that Master-Detail provides to automatically maintain that aggregate. A Lookup is a loose reference with no lifecycle tie between the two records, so there is no roll-up option and no automatic cascade delete. Cascade delete itself is also exclusive to Master-Detail; a Lookup would require a Flow or Apex trigger to manually delete children, which adds maintenance risk the business almost certainly doesn't want for something this core to the data model.

The correct recommendation is Master-Detail from Task to Project. That immediately gives automatic cascade delete when the Project is removed, and it unlocks a roll-up summary field on Project that sums Task hours declaratively with no code. The tradeoff the junior admin should understand is what Master-Detail costs in flexibility: detail records on a Master-Detail relationship have no independent OwnerId and cannot have their own sharing rules or manual shares — their visibility is entirely inherited from the master record's sharing. That's usually fine for a Task that conceptually only exists in the context of its Project, but it would be the wrong call if Tasks ever needed to be shared independently of their Project.

One more architectural caution worth raising in this conversation: an object can have at most two Master-Detail relationships, and converting an existing Lookup to Master-Detail later requires every existing record to already have a non-null parent value before the conversion is allowed. If there's any chance this data model needs a second parent relationship down the line, that should be weighed now rather than after the Lookup is already live with real data in it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I've actually had this exact conversation with a junior admin before, and the way I explain it is: 'flexible' is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and it's flexibility we don't actually want here. I'd ask them two questions back — does this app need a rolled-up total, and does it need Tasks to disappear automatically with their Project? Both are yes, so Lookup is already off the table, because neither a native roll-up field nor automatic cascade delete exists on a Lookup relationship. You could fake both with a Flow, but that's extra automation to build, test, and maintain forever for something Master-Detail just gives you for free.

So I'd go with Master-Detail, Task as the detail, Project as the master. What I'd specifically flag to the team before we build it, though, is what we're giving up: once Task is a detail record, it loses its own Owner field and any independent sharing — if Sarah owns a Task but Bob owns the Project, visibility follows the Project's sharing, not Sarah's ownership. On a project-tracking app that's almost always the right behavior anyway, since nobody expects to see a task without being able to see its project. I'd also mention, almost as a footnote but an important one, that Salesforce caps you at two Master-Detail relationships per object — so if there's a future idea floating around about linking Tasks to, say, a Client Contract object directly, now's the time to raise it, not after we've already burned one of those two slots.

Honestly, in my experience the 'Lookup feels safer/more flexible' instinct usually comes from not yet having hit the wall where you need a roll-up and realize you can't get one without Master-Detail. Once you've been burned by that once, you start asking 'does this need an aggregate or a cascade?' before every relationship decision instead of after.
questions.example: If Task currently has 40 existing records with a blank Project lookup, Salesforce will block converting that Lookup to Master-Detail until every one of those 40 records has a Project value populated first.
commonMistakes: Believing roll-up summary fields work on any relationship type, not just Master-Detail
Not realizing Master-Detail detail records lose independent ownership and sharing
Forgetting that converting a Lookup to Master-Detail later requires populating every existing record's parent field first
Assuming cascade delete requires a trigger when it's inherent to Master-Detail
Ignoring the two-Master-Detail-relationships-per-object limit when planning future relationships
keyPoints: Roll-up summary fields only exist on the master side of a Master-Detail relationship
Cascade delete is automatic and built into Master-Detail, not available on a Lookup without custom automation
Detail records inherit ownership and sharing from the master and have no independent OwnerId
Master-Detail relationships are harder to change later due to conversion and reparenting constraints
Lookup is the right call when independent ownership, sharing, or an optional parent is actually needed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that a Lookup cannot support roll-up summaries
Correctly identifies Master-Detail is required for automatic cascade delete
Explains the ownership/sharing inheritance consequence of Master-Detail
Notes conversion limits or future-flexibility tradeoffs
Clarity and communication

questions.title: Dynamic Forms Migration Mechanics and Limits
questions.prompt: A legacy custom Service Request object has one Page Layout with about 60 fields across three record types, used heavily on both desktop and mobile. The business wants a field like Escalation Reason to appear only when Priority equals Critical, without maintaining three separate layouts per record type. Explain mechanically what changes when you move this to Dynamic Forms, and name one real limitation that still ties you back to the Page Layout.
questions.modelAnswer:
Dynamic Forms takes individual fields out of the static Page Layout and places them directly onto the Lightning Record Page as independent field sections, each carrying its own component visibility filter. Instead of needing three record-type-specific layouts to control which fields appear, you build one set of field sections and attach a filter condition directly to the Escalation Reason field's section — for example, Priority equals Critical — evaluated per record, in real time, regardless of record type. The migration itself is mechanical: in Lightning App Builder, the record page shows an 'Upgrade Now' prompt once Dynamic Forms is available for the object; clicking it converts the existing layout's field arrangement into an editable field section on the page, preserving the original field order as a starting point that you then reorganize and attach filters to.

The real limitation is that Dynamic Forms does not retire the Page Layout entirely. The Page Layout still governs the compact layout and highlights panel (the summary fields shown at the top of the record and in hover previews), the mini page layout used in lookup hover-overs, and in some cases the default field arrangement shown in quick-create or inline-edit contexts outside the full record page. So even after a full Dynamic Forms migration, an admin still has to maintain the Page Layout for those specific surfaces — it's demoted, not eliminated. It's also worth confirming object support before planning around this, since Dynamic Forms availability has expanded over releases but isn't universal across every standard object.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame this for the team is that Dynamic Forms doesn't remove the Page Layout, it just takes away most of its job. Before, if you wanted Escalation Reason to only show up for Critical priority tickets, you were stuck building three nearly-identical layouts and assigning them by record type — a maintenance headache every time a field changes. With Dynamic Forms, I just drag that field into its own section on the Lightning page and set a visibility rule right there: Priority equals Critical, done, no second layout needed. In practice I'd do this by hitting 'Upgrade Now' in App Builder, which pulls the existing layout's fields in as a starting section, and then I'd actually sit down with support reps to figure out which fields really need to be grouped together or hidden conditionally, because 60 fields is a lot to reorganize thoughtfully in one sitting.

What I always warn people about, though, is the highlights panel at the top of the record — that's still driven by the Page Layout's compact layout, Dynamic Forms doesn't touch it. So if someone asks 'can we just delete the old layout now,' the answer is no — it's still doing real work for the compact layout and for things like the hover preview on lookups. I usually tell teams to think of it as: Dynamic Forms owns the body of the record now, but the Page Layout still owns the header and a few background jobs. On a 60-field object with three record types, that's honestly a huge win even with that caveat, because you go from three layouts to maintain down to effectively one Dynamic Forms configuration.
questions.example: A field section containing Escalation Reason can carry a filter such as {Priority} equals 'Critical', so the field only renders for that specific record state rather than needing a Critical-only Page Layout.
commonMistakes: Thinking Dynamic Forms fully replaces Page Layouts so the object no longer needs one at all
Assuming field visibility rules in Dynamic Forms require a Flow or formula field instead of a built-in filter condition
Forgetting the compact layout/highlights panel is still controlled outside Dynamic Forms
Trying to use Dynamic Forms on an object or context where it isn't yet supported
Treating the Upgrade Now migration as fully automatic without reviewing record-type-specific layout differences first
keyPoints: Dynamic Forms moves individual fields/sections onto the Lightning page with independent visibility filters
Visibility rules can be based on field values, not just record type or profile
Migration uses Upgrade Now in Lightning App Builder, converting existing layout fields into an editable section
The Page Layout still governs the compact layout, mini page layout, and some quick-create/inline-edit surfaces
Object support for Dynamic Forms should be verified before planning a migration around it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the mechanic of fields moving into independent sections with visibility filters
Correctly describes the Upgrade Now migration process
Identifies at least one accurate remaining dependency on the Page Layout
Clarity and technical accuracy

questions.title: Building a Consultant-to-Project Junction Object
questions.prompt: Consultants work on multiple Projects at once, and Projects have multiple Consultants assigned, with hours logged per consultant per week. The business wants a total-hours figure visible on each Project and a total-hours figure visible on each Consultant. Walk through, step by step, exactly how you would build this declaratively — name the objects and fields you'd create and specify where each roll-up summary field would actually live.
questions.modelAnswer:
The many-to-many relationship between Consultant and Project requires a junction object in between — call it Project Assignment. That object needs two Master-Detail relationships, one to Project and one to Consultant, which is exactly the maximum of two Master-Detail relationships an object can carry, so this design uses that limit precisely as intended. On Project Assignment, add a Number field, Hours Logged, and a Date field, Week Ending, so each record represents one consultant's logged hours on one project for one week.

With both Master-Detail relationships in place, two roll-up summary fields become available: a Total Hours field on Project that sums Hours Logged across all related Project Assignment records, and a separate Total Hours field on Consultant that sums the same Hours Logged field across all of that consultant's Project Assignment records. Both roll-ups read from the same child field but live on different parent objects, which is the whole point of putting the junction object between them.

Two consequences are worth calling out before this ships. First, because Project Assignment has two Master-Detail relationships, a user generally needs access to both the related Project and the related Consultant to view or edit the Project Assignment record — sharing isn't just inherited from one side. Second, cascade delete applies from either master: deleting a Project deletes its Project Assignment records, and deleting a Consultant does the same, which also means the historical hours data disappears with them unless the business has a retention requirement that needs to be raised separately.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd do is sketch the relationship on paper before touching Setup, because the direction matters: Consultant and Project are the two parents, and I need a junction object in the middle, which I'd call Project Assignment. I'd create that as a new custom object, then add the first Master-Detail field pointing to Project, and the second Master-Detail field pointing to Consultant — that uses up both of the Master-Detail slots this object will ever get, so I'd double check with the team there's no third parent anyone's expecting later. Then I'd add the actual data fields: Hours Logged as a Number, and Week Ending as a Date, so every record is one consultant's hours on one project in one week.

Once both Master-Details exist, I'd go build the roll-ups — one on Project summing Hours Logged from its Project Assignment child records, and a second, separate roll-up on Consultant doing the same sum but scoped to that consultant's own assignments. I'd test this with a couple of sample consultants each assigned to two or three projects before calling it done, just to make sure the numbers land where I expect on both sides. The thing I always flag to stakeholders at this point is the sharing behavior — because this junction object has two Master-Details, someone needs visibility into both the Project and the Consultant to see the assignment record, which occasionally surprises people who assumed access to just the Project was enough. And I'd make sure whoever owns data retention policy knows that deleting a Project or a Consultant cascades down and wipes out the logged-hours history with it.
questions.example: A single Project Assignment record with Hours Logged = 12 contributes 12 to that Project's Total Hours roll-up and 12 to that same Consultant's Total Hours roll-up simultaneously, since both roll-ups read the identical child field from two different parent relationships.
commonMistakes: Using a single Master-Detail plus a Lookup for the second parent instead of two Master-Details, losing roll-up capability on one side
Forgetting the junction object can have at most two Master-Detail relationships, blocking any future third parent
Not realizing access to the junction record generally requires access to both parent records
Forgetting that deleting either parent cascades and removes the junction records, including historical hours data
Placing both roll-up summary fields on the same object instead of one on each parent
keyPoints: The junction object uses two Master-Detail relationships, one to each parent
The two-Master-Detail-relationship limit per object constrains any future third parent
Roll-up summary fields are placed on Project and on Consultant separately, both summing the same child field
Access to the junction record generally depends on access to both parent records
Cascade delete from either parent removes junction records and their historical hours data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the junction object with two Master-Detail relationships
Correctly places roll-up summary fields on both parent objects
Explains sharing/access implications of dual Master-Detail relationships
Explains the cascade delete consequence
Clear, logical build sequence

questions.title: Assembling a Lightning Record Page for Equipment Rentals
questions.prompt: You're building a custom Equipment Rental app on a Rental Agreement object. Finance needs to see financial fields that other roles shouldn't, warehouse staff need a quick action called Mark Returned that only appears when Status equals Checked Out, a related list of Equipment Items needs to be visible, and the whole thing has to work well on a phone for staff scanning equipment in a warehouse. Walk through how you'd configure this record page in Lightning App Builder.
questions.modelAnswer:
Start by creating or cloning the Lightning Record Page for Rental Agreement and upgrading its field layout to Dynamic Forms so individual sections can carry their own visibility rules. Group the financial fields — rate, deposit, late fees — into their own section and set a component visibility filter based on the user's Profile or, better for long-term scalability, a custom permission or permission-set-based condition, so only Finance sees that section regardless of how many profiles exist down the road. Keep the remaining operational fields — equipment, dates, status — in a separate, universally visible section.

The Mark Returned quick action's conditional visibility is not configured in Lightning App Builder itself — that's a common point of confusion. Conditional quick action visibility is set through Dynamic Actions on the object's Page Layout, where you add a filter such as Status equals Checked Out directly on that action in the action list. Add a Related List - Single component for Equipment Items, filtered and sorted so warehouse staff see exactly what's checked out without extra clicks.

For mobile, activate the page as the org default or assign it per app/profile/record type as needed, and separately verify or create a distinct activation for the Salesforce mobile app's phone form factor using the App Builder's mobile preview — desktop density rarely works well on a phone. Trim the number of visible fields and sections for the phone view specifically, prioritize the Mark Returned action and the Equipment Items list near the top, and confirm every component used is actually supported on mobile before relying on it in the field.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start in App Builder by cloning the existing Rental Agreement page so I'm not breaking anything live, then click into Dynamic Forms if it hasn't been upgraded yet. I'd pull the financial fields — rate, deposit, late fees — into their own section and lock that down with a visibility filter on the user's profile or permission set, so Finance sees it and nobody else does by default. Everything else — the operational stuff warehouse folks actually care about — I'd leave broadly visible in its own section above that.

For Mark Returned, I'd actually go to the object's Page Layout and look at the Actions area, because that's where Dynamic Actions live and where I can set the condition Status equals Checked Out on that specific action — this trips people up because they go hunting for it in App Builder and it's genuinely not there. I'd drop a Related List - Single component for Equipment Items on the page too, filtered so it's not showing noise.

The mobile piece is where I'd spend the most actual testing time, honestly. I'd use the phone preview inside App Builder constantly while building, and I'd probably end up with a genuinely different, trimmed-down activation for the phone form factor rather than assuming the desktop version just scales down fine — warehouse staff scanning equipment on a five-inch screen need Mark Returned and the Equipment Items list front and center, not buried under six field sections they have to scroll past first. I'd also double-check every component I used is actually mobile-supported before I called this done, because it's an easy thing to assume and be wrong about.
questions.example: A Dynamic Action filter of {Status} equals 'Checked Out' on the Mark Returned action means it simply won't render on the page at all for an Available or Reserved rental agreement, desktop or mobile.
commonMistakes: Trying to set conditional quick action visibility inside Lightning App Builder instead of via Dynamic Actions on the Page Layout
Assuming one Lightning page activation automatically applies to the Salesforce mobile app without a separate activation
Overloading the mobile layout with the same density as the desktop version, hurting warehouse staff usability
Using profile-based component visibility when a permission-set or custom-permission condition would scale better across future profiles
Forgetting that component visibility filters control what's shown, not field-level security or edit access
keyPoints: Dynamic Forms sections can be filtered by profile, permission set, or field-value conditions
Dynamic Actions, not Lightning App Builder, control conditional quick action visibility by record field values
Lightning pages can be activated differently for desktop versus the Salesforce mobile app's phone form factor
Related list components can be filtered and sorted independently of the object's default related list
Mobile-specific design requires trimming fields and sections, not reusing the desktop layout as-is

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly separates Dynamic Forms field visibility from Dynamic Actions for quick actions
Correctly describes activation across app/profile/record type and mobile form factor
Addresses related list component configuration
Addresses mobile-specific UX tradeoffs
Clear step-by-step structure

questions.title: Enforcing Discount Thresholds with Validation Rules and Formulas
questions.prompt: Sales reps apply discounts on a custom Quote Line object. Any discount over 20% must never save directly — it has to route to a manager for approval instead of being silently blocked. Walk through, field by field and rule by rule, how you'd build this without writing any Apex, and explain specifically why a validation rule by itself is the wrong tool for the 'route to approval' part.
questions.modelAnswer:
A validation rule can only do one of two things on save: allow it or block it with an error. It has no concept of 'submit this for review and let it through later' — that routing behavior belongs to an Approval Process, a separate declarative tool entirely. So the first design decision is that these two tools have to cooperate rather than one replacing the other, and the validation rule's job narrows to exactly one thing: preventing a discount over 20% from ever being saved outside of the approval workflow.

To make that cooperation work, add a text or picklist field, Approval Status, that the Approval Process itself updates at each stage — Pending on submission, Approved on final approval, Rejected on rejection. The validation rule then reads: block the save when Discount Percent is greater than 0.20 AND Approval Status is not Pending AND Approval Status is not Approved. That exclusion is the critical piece — without it, the validation rule would also block the Approval Process's own field updates as the record moves through Pending and Approved states, because those are saves too, and the rule would fire on them just like it fires on a rep's manual edit.

The Approval Process itself is built separately with entry criteria of Discount Percent greater than 0.20, routing to the rep's manager, with an initial submission action that sets Approval Status to Pending and a final approval action that sets it to Approved. One thing worth testing explicitly before this ships: editing an already-approved high-discount Quote Line should be considered, since a straightforward exclusion on Approved status would let a rep edit an already-approved record's discount further without triggering a new validation block — which the business may or may not want, and is worth raising rather than assuming.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain to the team up front that a validation rule is a yes/no gate, full stop — it can't hand a record off to someone else for a decision, it can only let it through or stop it cold. So if we want discounts over 20% to go to a manager instead of just failing, we need an Approval Process doing the actual routing, and the validation rule's job shrinks down to just keeping people from sneaking a high discount through outside that process.

The piece I'd build first, actually, is a tracking field — I'd call it Approval Status — because the validation rule needs some way to tell 'this record is legitimately moving through approval' apart from 'someone's just trying to save a high discount directly.' The Approval Process sets that field as it moves: Pending when submitted, Approved when a manager signs off. Then the validation rule formula is basically: block if the discount's over 20% and the status isn't Pending and isn't Approved. I've been burned before by skipping that exclusion and watching the approval process's own submission action get blocked by the very rule it was supposed to get past — that's a frustrating bug to debug because it looks like the approval button is broken when really it's the validation rule fighting the approval engine.

One thing I always test manually before calling this done: what happens if someone goes back and edits a Quote Line that's already sitting in Approved status with a 35% discount? Depending on how I wrote the exclusion, that edit might sail through without triggering a fresh approval, which usually isn't what the business actually wants once you ask them directly. I'd rather surface that edge case in a demo than have it discovered three months later by an auditor.
questions.example: A validation rule of AND(Discount_Percent__c > 0.20, NOT(ISPICKVAL(Approval_Status__c,'Pending')), NOT(ISPICKVAL(Approval_Status__c,'Approved'))) blocks a direct 25% discount save but lets the Approval Process's own submission and approval field updates through.
commonMistakes: Trying to make a validation rule itself 'send for approval' when it can only allow or block a save
Forgetting to exclude in-process or approved records from the validation rule, which blocks the approval process's own field updates
Not accounting for editing an already-approved high-discount record and whether it should re-trigger the block
Hardcoding the discount threshold in the validation rule formula instead of referencing a maintained field or custom setting
Assuming validation rules, approval processes, and other automation fire in a simple, fixed order without testing it
keyPoints: Validation rules can only block or allow a save; they cannot submit a record for approval
Routing to approval requires a separate Approval Process with its own entry criteria
The validation rule must explicitly exclude pending/approved records to avoid blocking the approval process's own updates
A tracking field like Approval Status is needed so the validation rule can distinguish record states
Editing an already-approved record is an edge case that needs explicit testing and a business decision

Designs a working validation rule that excludes in-process/approved records
Correctly describes the approval process and its interaction with the validation rule

questions.title: Roll-Up Summary Field Showing Zero Despite Child Records
questions.prompt: A Total Hours roll-up summary field on the Project object is showing zero even though the related Project Assignment records clearly have populated Hours Logged values. Walk through your troubleshooting sequence to find the root cause — list the specific things you'd check, in order, and what each one would tell you.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first and most common culprit is the roll-up field's own filter criteria, so that's where this check starts: open the roll-up summary field definition and look for a conditional filter — something like Status equals Closed — that may be silently excluding every Project Assignment record currently in an Open or In Progress state. This single misconfiguration accounts for the majority of 'roll-up shows zero' tickets in practice.

If the filter criteria looks correct, the next check is confirming the relationship is genuinely still Master-Detail and that the roll-up is summing the field actually intended — it's possible a duplicate or deprecated field with a similar label exists and the roll-up references the wrong one. After that, check whether the child records were created through a bulk data load; certain bulk operations can leave roll-up values stale until a manual recalculation is triggered, which would explain real data that simply hasn't been aggregated yet. Also check the Recycle Bin — roll-up summaries exclude soft-deleted records even before they're permanently purged, so if someone deleted and expected-to-restore records recently, the total would legitimately read lower.

Field-level security is worth ruling out explicitly, but only as a red herring: FLS controls whether a user can see the roll-up field's value, not whether the platform calculates it. If the admin troubleshooting this can't see the field at all due to their own profile's FLS, that's a visibility problem layered on top of, and separate from, the actual calculation — checking it rules out 'the number looks like zero because I can't actually see it' as a distinct, simpler explanation before digging further into the real calculation.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I always check, every time, is the roll-up's filter criteria — in my experience that's the cause behind the vast majority of these tickets. I'll open the roll-up field definition and look for a condition that's quietly excluding the exact records someone's asking about, like a Status filter that doesn't match what's actually on those child records right now. Nine times out of ten that's the whole answer.

If that comes back clean, I go check the relationship type next — has anything changed about Project Assignment being Master-Detail to Project, and am I even summing the field I think I am, versus some similarly-named field someone created later. Then I think about how the data actually got there: was this a recent data load? Because bulk-loaded records sometimes need a manual roll-up recalculation to actually populate the total, and that's an easy thing to forget exists as a step.

I'd also specifically check the Recycle Bin, because I've seen someone delete a batch of records, panic, and ask why the total dropped — the answer being those records are sitting in the bin, excluded from the roll-up, not actually gone yet. And I always explicitly rule out field-level security early on too, mostly to save myself time — if I can't see the field value at all because of my own profile's FLS, that's a completely different and much simpler problem than an actual broken calculation, and I don't want to spend twenty minutes debugging a calculation that was never actually wrong.
questions.example: A roll-up filtered to Status equals 'Completed' will correctly show zero for a brand-new Project whose Project Assignment records are all still 'In Progress', even though the underlying hours data is perfectly accurate.
commonMistakes: Assuming field-level security on the roll-up field blocks the calculation itself, rather than just the viewer's visibility
Not checking the roll-up's filter criteria first, even though it's the most common real-world cause
Forgetting that bulk data loads can require a manual mass recalculation to populate roll-ups retroactively
Not verifying the relationship is still Master-Detail rather than having drifted to a Lookup configuration
Overlooking that records in the Recycle Bin are excluded from roll-up totals
keyPoints: Roll-up filter criteria is the most common cause of unexpectedly low or zero totals
Roll-up summary fields require Master-Detail; confirm the relationship type hasn't drifted
Field-level security affects visibility, not calculation, so it's a red herring for the actual number
Bulk-loaded child records may need a manual roll-up recalculation
Deleted or Recycle-Bin records are excluded from the total

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Provides a logical, ordered troubleshooting sequence
Identifies filter criteria as a likely root cause
Correctly distinguishes field-level security visibility from calculation
Mentions recalculation and Recycle Bin edge cases
Clarity

questions.title: Users Missing Expected Visibility to Custom App Records
questions.prompt: After launching a custom Vendor Management app, several account managers report they can't see Vendor records that colleagues on their same team can see, even though all of them have identical profile and permission set assignments. Walk through how you'd isolate whether the cause is organization-wide defaults, role hierarchy, a sharing rule, manual sharing, or something else entirely — and what you'd check at each step.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first thing to confirm is the Organization-Wide Default for Vendor, because if it's Private, a profile's object permissions only grant the capability to read or edit records a user can already see — they don't grant visibility by themselves. That reframes the whole investigation: identical profiles and permission sets guarantee identical CRUD capability, not identical record access, so the actual cause has to be something at the record-sharing layer, not the profile layer.

The fastest diagnostic from there is opening one of the problem records and using the sharing detail view to see exactly why the users who can see it have access — owner, role, a named sharing rule, a team, or a manual share — and then comparing that directly against the user who can't. This almost always points straight at the gap instead of requiring guesswork. A very common finding at this point is that the two users sit in different branches of the role hierarchy, so a sharing rule based on role-and-subordinates grants access to one branch but not the other, even though both users' profiles and permission sets look identical on paper.

If the sharing detail doesn't immediately explain it, check whether any sharing rule is criteria-based on a field value — such as a Region or Business Unit field on the Vendor record — and whether the specific records in question actually meet that criteria; a rule can be correctly configured and still not apply to certain records. Finally, rule out that this is actually a list view or report filter problem rather than a true access problem, by having the affected user try to open the record directly by URL — if they can open it directly but it's missing from their list view, the fix is entirely different from a sharing fix.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The very first thing I do, before touching any configuration, is pull up one of the problem records and click into its sharing detail — on most orgs that's the 'Sharing' button or an equivalent view that tells you exactly why every current viewer has access: role, sharing rule name, team, manual share, whatever it is. I do the same comparison for the user who's missing access, and nine times out of ten the difference just jumps out at you instead of me having to guess at configuration.

In my experience, 'identical profile and permission set but different visibility' almost always comes down to role hierarchy. I've seen this exact scenario before, where two account managers had the literal same profile and permission sets assigned, but one reported up through a different regional role branch than the other, and a sharing rule granting access to 'Role and Subordinates' only covered one of those branches. It looks like a mystery until you actually compare their roles side by side instead of just their profiles.

If role hierarchy checks out fine, I go looking at sharing rule criteria next, specifically whether it's based on a field value on the record itself — because a rule can look completely correctly built and still just not apply to the specific records someone's asking about if those records don't match the criteria. And before I go any further down the security rabbit hole, I always have the affected user try opening the record directly by its URL — because more than once what looked like a sharing problem turned out to be a list view filter silently excluding records the person could actually open just fine.
questions.example: Two account managers with identical profiles but roles on opposite branches of the hierarchy — one under Northeast Sales Manager, one under Southeast Sales Manager — will see different Vendor records if a sharing rule is scoped to Role and Subordinates for only one of those branches.
commonMistakes: Assuming identical profiles and permission sets guarantee identical record access, ignoring role hierarchy and sharing rules
Forgetting that Organization-Wide Default being Private means profile object permissions alone never grant visibility
Not using the record's sharing detail view before guessing at configuration changes
Overlooking that a sharing rule's criteria may be based on a field value the specific records don't meet
Confusing a list view or report filter problem for an actual record access problem
keyPoints: Profile and permission set control object/field CRUD, not record visibility, when Organization-Wide Default is restrictive
The record's sharing detail view is the fastest way to isolate the actual access grant or lack of one
Role hierarchy branch differences between otherwise-identical users is a common silent cause
Sharing rule criteria based on field values can exclude specific records even for the right role or group
Distinguish a visibility problem from a list view/report filter problem before changing security configuration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes profile/permission set from record-level sharing
Describes using the sharing detail diagnostic approach
Covers role hierarchy and sharing rule criteria as likely causes
Rules out non-security explanations such as list view or report filters
Clear, methodical approach

questions.title: Approval Process Locking Conflicts with an Automated Flow Update
questions.prompt: Submitting an Expense Report into an approval process works fine, but a record-triggered Flow that's supposed to update a related Expense Line's status immediately after submission is failing silently and leaving stale data behind. Diagnose the likely root cause related to record locking and automation order of operations, and explain specifically how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
Submitting a record for approval places a system-level lock on it, and that lock blocks updates from automation just as much as it blocks manual edits — it isn't only a user-permission restriction. If a separate Flow fires after submission and tries to update the Expense Report, or an Expense Line whose lock is extended from the parent depending on how the approval process is configured, that update will be rejected by the platform. Because this often happens on an asynchronous path, the failure doesn't surface as a visible error to the user — it just fails quietly, which matches exactly what's being described.

The fix has two parts. First, move the field update that needs to happen at submission time into the Approval Process's own Initial Submission Action rather than a separate competing Flow — field updates configured as part of the approval process's own steps are exempt from the lock they themselves create, because they run as part of the approval engine. Second, for anything that genuinely can't live inside the approval process's own actions, use explicit Unlock Record and Lock Record Flow actions around the update, rather than assuming the update will simply go through.

It's also worth checking whether this specific approval process is configured to extend its lock to related detail records, since some approval process configurations lock only the submitted record while others optionally lock related children too — that configuration detail determines whether the Expense Line itself, not just the Expense Report, is the one actually blocked. Regardless of which fix is chosen, every Flow involved in this chain should have a fault path added so a locking conflict like this surfaces as a visible error in the future instead of failing silently again.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first instinct here is the record lock, because that's exactly the signature of this kind of bug — works fine on submission, then something downstream silently fails to update. When a record goes into an approval process, it gets locked at the platform level, and that lock doesn't care whether the thing trying to update it is a person clicking Save or a Flow running in the background — both get blocked the same way. If this Flow is asynchronous, which a lot of record-triggered Flows running after a submission action effectively are, the failure just disappears instead of throwing something the user would actually see.

So I'd go check two things in order: first, whether the approval process is set to lock only the submitted record or also its related children, because that tells me exactly which record the Flow is actually choking on. Then I'd look at whether this field update genuinely needs to be a separate Flow at all, or whether it should just be folded into the Approval Process's own Initial Submission field update action — those run inside the approval engine itself and don't fight the lock the way an outside Flow does. If there's a real reason it has to stay a separate Flow, I'd add explicit Unlock Record and Lock Record steps around the update rather than hoping it works.

Honestly, regardless of which fix I land on, the thing I'd insist on before closing this out is adding a fault path to that Flow. Silent failures on locked records are exactly the kind of bug that comes back three more times in slightly different forms if nobody can actually see when it happens — I'd rather get a visible error in a debug log next time than have to reverse-engineer 'stale data' reports again.
questions.example: An Initial Submission Action on the Approval Process setting Expense_Line_Status__c to 'Under Review' will succeed because it runs as part of the approval engine, while a separate record-triggered Flow trying to set that same field moments later on the now-locked record will fail.
commonMistakes: Assuming only the submitted record is ever locked, when approval processes can optionally lock related child records too
Not adding a fault or error path to Flows, letting locking conflicts fail silently instead of surfacing clearly
Trying to force a Flow update through a locked record instead of using the approval process's own step-level field updates
Confusing a user-permission edit restriction with the system-level record lock from an active approval process
Not testing automation order when submission and other automation fire from the same user action
keyPoints: Submitting for approval places a system-level record lock that blocks automation updates, not just manual edits
Approval processes can optionally extend the lock to related detail records depending on configuration
Field updates tied to the approval process's own steps are exempt from the lock and are the right place for this kind of update
Asynchronous Flow failures on locked records often fail silently without a fault path
Unlock/Lock Record actions exist but should be used deliberately, not as a workaround for poor sequencing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the record lock as the root cause
Proposes using approval process field updates instead of a competing Flow
Mentions fault path or silent failure diagnosis
Notes related-record lock extension as a configuration detail to check
Clarity
