questions.title: Selecting the Right Automation Stack for a Multi-Department Approval
questions.prompt: Expense reports under $500 should auto-approve, between $500 and $5,000 they should route to the direct manager, and over $5,000 to the manager and then a Finance director, with Slack and email notifications firing along the way and multiple related records updating at each stage. Propose the overall automation architecture — which tool handles which part and why — and justify why you would not build this entirely inside one single tool.
questions.modelAnswer:
The human approval chain itself — manager, then Finance director, with recall, delegation, and a built-in audit trail of who approved what and when — is exactly what an Approval Process is purpose-built for, and reimplementing that inside Flow means rebuilding approval history, recall, and delegated-approver behavior that Salesforce already gives for free. So the approval chain for the $500-to-$5,000 and over-$5,000 tiers belongs in native Approval Processes, potentially as two separate approval processes on the object distinguished by entry criteria on the amount, each with its own step sequence and approvers.

Everything else belongs in Flow. The under-$500 auto-approval case shouldn't go through a human approval step at all — a record-triggered Flow evaluating the amount at submission can bypass approval entirely and set the record's status directly, which is both faster and avoids burdening managers with approvals that were never really decisions. Flow is also the right place for the Slack and email notifications and the related-record updates, because Flow's invocable actions are considerably more flexible for integrations like Slack than an approval process's own limited email-alert and field-update actions per step.

The reason this isn't a single-tool build is that each tool is weak exactly where the other is strong: an Approval Process has no good answer for an external Slack callout or complex conditional bypass logic, while Flow alone can technically approximate a human approval chain but throws away the native approval engine's auditability, recall, and mobile/Chatter approve actions in the process — reinventing those adds ongoing maintenance for a benefit the platform already provides. Combining them — Flow as the orchestrator and bypass/notification layer, Approval Process as the actual human-decision engine — uses each tool where it's genuinely strongest.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd actually push back a little if someone proposed building this entirely in Flow, because I've seen that approach before and it always ends up reinventing things Salesforce already built for free — approval history, recall, delegated approvers, the mobile approve/reject actions people are used to. None of that comes free if you build the whole chain in Flow instead of the native Approval Process.

So here's how I'd split it: the actual manager-then-Finance-director approval chain for anything $500 and up goes into native Approval Processes — I'd probably build two of them, one for the $500-to-$5,000 tier and one for the over-$5,000 tier, each with its own entry criteria on amount so they don't compete with each other. For anything under $500, I wouldn't even route it through a human approval step — I'd have a Flow catch it at submission and auto-approve it directly, because making a manager rubber-stamp a $40 expense report isn't actually a decision, it's just friction.

The Slack notifications and the related-record updates, I'd put all of that in Flow too, triggered off status changes or the approval steps' own outcomes, because Flow's invocable actions give me a lot more room to do an actual Slack callout than an approval process's built-in email alert ever will. The way I'd explain the overall split to a stakeholder: Flow decides who should even go through approval and handles everything that happens around the approval, while the Approval Process itself is purely the human decision chain — I don't want those two jobs tangled together in one tool, because then every future change to notification logic risks breaking the approval chain and vice versa.
commonMistakes: Trying to build the entire conditional routing and notification logic inside a single Approval Process, which only supports limited field-update, email-alert, and outbound-message actions per step
Reinventing approval history, recall, and delegated-approver functionality inside Flow instead of using the native approval engine
Forgetting that an object can have multiple Approval Processes with entry criteria rather than cramming all amount tiers into one with internal branches
Using outdated Process Builder thinking instead of modern Flow for the orchestration and notification layer
Forcing the under-$500 case through a human approval step instead of bypassing approval entirely for efficiency
keyPoints: Approval Process is the right tool for the human approval chain itself: steps, approvers, recall, delegation, audit history
Flow is the right tool for conditional branching, bypass logic, and integrations or notifications like Slack
Multiple approval processes with entry criteria can exist on one object instead of cramming all logic into one
Combining tools avoids reinventing native approval engine features inside Flow
Auto-approval for low-dollar amounts should bypass the human approval step entirely for efficiency

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assigns the human-approval-chain responsibility to the Approval Process
Correctly assigns conditional routing/integration responsibility to Flow
Justifies why a single tool is insufficient for the full requirement
Addresses the under-$500 auto-approval bypass case
Clarity and architectural reasoning

questions.title: Layering Security for a Sensitive Multi-Business-Unit App
questions.prompt: A new custom Compensation Adjustment app stores sensitive salary change data across four business units. HR Business Partners should see only their own business unit's records, HR Directors should see all records, managers should see only their direct reports' records and only non-salary fields, and Finance needs read-only access to records with a status of Approved. Design the full security architecture across object, field, and record level, and explain how the pieces work together.
questions.modelAnswer:
Start with Organization-Wide Default, which should be set to Private, because that's the most restrictive persona's requirement — HR Business Partners need to see only their own business unit — and sharing should always be added on top of a restrictive baseline rather than carved away from a permissive one. HR Directors sit above HR Business Partners in the role hierarchy, which naturally grants them visibility into records owned within that branch, but role hierarchy alone doesn't reach Finance or the general manager population, since those personas sit outside the HR reporting structure entirely.

For Finance, the correct mechanism is a criteria-based sharing rule scoped to a Finance public group, with criteria of Status equals Approved — this is precisely the case criteria-based sharing exists for, since it isn't about who owns the record or where they sit in a hierarchy, it's about a condition on the record itself. For managers seeing only their direct reports, if ownership and role assignment are modeled correctly, standard role hierarchy visibility already covers 'manager sees subordinate's owned records' without an additional sharing rule, though a sharing rule can reinforce this where ownership doesn't map cleanly to the role hierarchy.

The manager's 'non-salary fields only' restriction is a completely separate, independent layer: field-level security, delivered through a dedicated Manager permission set that hides the salary amount field specifically. This is the point worth emphasizing — record-level access (Organization-Wide Default, role hierarchy, sharing rules) and field-level access (profiles and permission sets) are two independent gates, and a user needs to clear both to see a given field's value on a given record. Finance's permission set should grant Read Only object-level access with no edit or delete, paired with field-level security exposing exactly the fields Finance actually needs. Public groups should be used to target both the Finance sharing rule and any manager-related sharing rule cleanly, rather than sharing records manually one at a time.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd build this persona by persona, starting with the most restrictive one, because that tells me the Organization-Wide Default baseline. HR Business Partners only seeing their own business unit means Private is the right OWD — I'm not going to start permissive and try to claw access back later, because sharing tools only ever add access, they can't take it away once OWD or a broader permission set has already granted it.

For HR Directors, I'd lean on role hierarchy — put them above the Business Partners in the hierarchy and they naturally inherit visibility into everything their subordinates own, no extra sharing rule needed there. Managers seeing their direct reports' records is usually the same story, assuming ownership and role assignment line up the way they should; if it doesn't cleanly map, I'd add a sharing rule to cover the gap rather than assume hierarchy alone handles it perfectly.

Finance is the persona that needs its own sharing rule, because 'read-only on Approved records across all business units' doesn't come from anywhere in the hierarchy — I'd build a criteria-based sharing rule off a Finance public group with the condition Status equals Approved, and pair it with a permission set that's explicitly Read Only at the object level so nobody on that team can accidentally edit compensation data. And the manager's 'no salary fields' requirement — I'd stop anyone from trying to solve that with a sharing rule, because that's not a record-visibility problem at all, it's field-level security, full stop. I'd build a Manager permission set that just hides the salary field outright, completely separate from whatever sharing rules control which records they can even open. I'd test every persona with Login As before calling this done, because security bugs here are the kind nobody notices until payroll finds out the hard way.
questions.example: A manager with record access to a direct report's Compensation Adjustment but without the Manager permission set's field-level security restriction would still see the hidden Salary Amount field, because record access and field-level security are evaluated independently.
commonMistakes: Trying to solve the 'managers see non-salary fields only' requirement with a sharing rule instead of field-level security
Setting Organization-Wide Default to Public Read/Write for convenience and trying to claw back access with restrictive permission sets
Forgetting that record-level access and field-level security are independent layers that both must permit access
Using role hierarchy alone for Finance's cross-business-unit, status-filtered access instead of a criteria-based sharing rule
Sharing records manually one at a time instead of using public groups to target sharing rules cleanly
keyPoints: Organization-Wide Default should be set to the most restrictive persona's needs, with access added on top via roles and sharing
Role hierarchy alone doesn't cover personas outside the natural reporting structure, such as Finance
Criteria-based sharing rules handle status-filtered, cross-hierarchy access like Finance's Approved-only view
Field-level security via permission sets is independent of, and necessary alongside, record-level access
Sharing rules and permission sets only add access on top of a restrictive baseline; they cannot remove access granted elsewhere

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sets the Organization-Wide Default baseline and explains why
Correctly addresses record-level access per persona via role hierarchy and sharing rules
Correctly addresses field-level security independently for the manager persona
Correctly addresses Finance's criteria-based, status-filtered access
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: Cascading Delete Risk in an Invoice-to-Payment Data Model
questions.prompt: A stakeholder proposes a Master-Detail relationship from Invoice, as master, to Payment, as detail, specifically so a roll-up summary of Total Paid can appear on the Invoice. Before approving that design, what risk would you raise about deleting an Invoice, and what alternative data model would you propose given a compliance requirement that payment records must never disappear, even if the related invoice is deleted?
questions.modelAnswer:
The risk is cascade delete, and it's not optional or configurable per field — any Master-Detail relationship automatically deletes all detail records when the master is deleted. For financial and audit data specifically, that's a serious compliance problem: deleting an Invoice, whether intentionally or by mistake during cleanup, would take every related Payment record down with it, and while the Recycle Bin provides a short recovery window, a permanently purged Invoice or a mass-delete operation across many invoices multiplies the real risk of permanently losing payment history that regulators or auditors may need later.

The alternative is a Lookup relationship from Payment to Invoice instead of Master-Detail. That avoids cascade delete entirely, but it costs the native roll-up summary field, since roll-ups require Master-Detail. The declarative replacement is a record-triggered Flow on Payment, firing on create, edit, and delete, that recalculates and writes Total Paid back onto the related Invoice — a bit more to build and maintain than a roll-up, but it keeps the compliance-critical relationship type safe.

The piece that completes this design, and is the actual declarative safeguard for the compliance concern, is the Lookup field's own deletion constraint setting: it can be set to 'Don't allow deletion of the lookup record that's part of a lookup relationship,' which blocks anyone from deleting an Invoice while Payment records still reference it. That's a native, no-code setting on the Lookup field itself, not something that requires an Apex trigger, and combined with the Flow-based Total Paid recalculation, it fully replaces what the Master-Detail design was trying to achieve without the cascade delete exposure.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I've actually seen this exact proposal come up before, and I always flag the same thing immediately: Master-Detail cascade delete isn't something you can dial back or turn off selectively, it's just how the relationship behaves. If someone deletes that Invoice, intentionally or by a cleanup script gone wrong, every Payment tied to it goes with it. For a compliance requirement that says payment records can never disappear, that's basically the opposite of what we need the data model to guarantee.

My pushback would be: let's get the Total Paid roll-up a different way and keep Payment as a Lookup to Invoice instead. Yes, that means no native roll-up summary field, but a record-triggered Flow on Payment that recalculates Total Paid on the Invoice whenever a payment is created, edited, or deleted covers that completely — it's a bit more setup than clicking through the roll-up wizard, but it's not exotic.

The part people usually don't know exists, and the part that actually solves the compliance concern directly, is that the Lookup field itself has a deletion constraint option — you can set it so Salesforce simply won't allow someone to delete an Invoice while Payments still point to it. That's declarative, no Apex trigger required, and it's exactly the guardrail a compliance team would want to hear exists. I'd present it as: same end-user experience, same Total Paid number on the Invoice, but the data model can't silently wipe out payment history the way the Master-Detail version could.
questions.example: With the Lookup field's deletion constraint set to disallow deletion when referenced, an attempt to delete an Invoice that still has three related Payment records would be blocked outright, rather than silently cascading those Payments into the Recycle Bin.
commonMistakes: Not realizing Master-Detail cascade delete is automatic and unavoidable, not something that can be turned off per field
Assuming a roll-up summary is only achievable via Master-Detail, unaware of the Flow-based recalculation alternative for Lookups
Forgetting the Lookup field has a native deletion constraint option that directly solves this compliance concern
Believing cascade-deleted records are just as recoverable as any other deleted record within the Recycle Bin window
Proposing a custom Apex trigger as the only way to prevent deletion when a declarative Lookup constraint already covers it
keyPoints: Master-Detail cascade delete is automatic and would delete all Payment records if the Invoice is deleted
A Lookup relationship avoids cascade delete but loses the native roll-up summary capability
The Lookup field's deletion constraint can block deleting an Invoice that still has referenced Payments
A record-triggered Flow can recalculate Total Paid on the Invoice to replace the lost roll-up
Compliance-sensitive financial data should default to the relationship type that cannot silently cascade-delete

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and explains the cascade delete risk
Proposes a Lookup relationship as the compliant alternative
Identifies the Lookup field's deletion constraint as the safeguard
Proposes a Flow-based roll-up replacement
Clarity

questions.title: Environment Strategy for Parallel Teams Building One App
questions.prompt: Two admin teams are simultaneously building different feature sets on the same custom app — one team is adding new objects and fields, the other is building Flow automation and page layouts — and both are targeting the same production release date. With only declarative tools available, no CI/CD pipeline and no version control yet, design the sandbox and deployment strategy you'd use to avoid the teams overwriting each other's work, and explain specifically why change sets make this harder than it looks.
questions.modelAnswer:
Give each team its own isolated sandbox to build in, branched from a recent copy of production, and introduce a shared integration sandbox that both teams deploy into before anything goes near production. The integration sandbox's job is to be the place where conflicts between the two teams' work surface first, in a low-stakes environment, rather than during a production deployment. Only after both teams' changes have been merged and tested together in that shared sandbox should a combined change set, or a carefully sequenced pair of change sets, go to production.

The reason change sets specifically make concurrent work harder than it looks is that a change set is not a diff or a merge tool — it's a snapshot bundle of whichever metadata components the admin selects, and deploying it overwrites the destination's entire definition of each selected component with the version in the change set. If both teams independently modify the same metadata component, such as the same Page Layout or the same object's field set, in their separate sandboxes, whichever change set deploys second completely overwrites the first team's changes to that component — there's no merge, no conflict warning beyond a possible dependency validation error, just a silent full overwrite.

Two additional constraints matter in planning this: change sets require the sandboxes involved to be connected through an explicit deployment connection configured in Deployment Settings before a sandbox-to-sandbox deployment is even possible, and sandboxes have different refresh intervals (Developer, Partial Copy, Full) that affect how current the metadata and data in each environment actually is. The most durable mitigation beyond the integration-sandbox step is defining clear component ownership boundaries between the two teams wherever the feature sets allow it, so the number of components both teams are independently touching is minimized in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Given no CI/CD and no version control yet, I'd set up each team in their own sandbox — probably Developer sandboxes if the feature sets are mostly metadata-only, Partial Copy if either team genuinely needs representative data to build against — and then I'd insist on a shared integration sandbox that both teams deploy into before either team even thinks about production. That integration sandbox is where I want any conflict between the two teams to blow up first, not on release day.

The thing I'd specifically walk both teams through up front is why change sets are riskier here than people assume: a change set doesn't merge anything, it just ships the whole definition of whatever component you picked and overwrites the destination's version of it. So if Team A and Team B both end up touching the same Page Layout — which happens more than people expect, because 'new fields' and 'automation and layouts' overlap exactly on layouts — whichever one deploys second to the integration sandbox just wipes out the other team's layout changes with no warning beyond maybe a validation error if something's missing a dependency.

Before we even get that far, I'd also confirm the deployment connections between these sandboxes are actually configured in Deployment Settings, because you can't just change-set from one sandbox to another without that link existing first — I've watched people assume that part just works and lose a day figuring out why it doesn't. And honestly, the highest-leverage thing I'd push for isn't technical at all — it's getting the two team leads to agree on who owns which specific layouts and components before building even starts, so we're minimizing how often they're stepping on the exact same metadata in the first place.
questions.example: If both teams independently edit the Rental Agreement Page Layout in their own sandboxes and each includes it in their change set, deploying Team B's change set second will fully overwrite Team A's layout changes with no merge and no automatic warning.

Deploying straight from each team's isolated sandbox to production without an integration or testing step
Not configuring deployment connections between sandboxes before assuming a change set can be sent sandbox-to-sandbox
Ignoring sandbox refresh intervals (Developer, Partial Copy, Full) when planning how current test data and metadata will be
Failing to define component ownership boundaries, leading both teams to edit the same layout or Flow independently

Two teams editing the same component in parallel risk a silent overwrite when the second change set deploys
A shared integration sandbox as a merge point surfaces conflicts before they reach production
Sandbox-to-sandbox change set deployment requires an explicit deployment connection configured first
Clear component ownership boundaries between teams reduce the chance of an overwrite conflict

questions.title: Declarative Limits vs. Custom Lightning Components for Scheduling UI
questions.prompt: The business wants a drag-and-drop weekly scheduling grid on a custom Resource object's record page, letting dispatchers drag technicians onto time slots with conflicts highlighted in real time. Evaluate whether this is realistically achievable with declarative tools alone, and lay out the architecture tradeoffs between pushing Flow and Dynamic Forms further versus investing in a custom Lightning Web Component.
questions.modelAnswer:
This specific requirement sits genuinely outside declarative reach, and it's worth being precise about why rather than just asserting it. Flow screens are step-based rather than a persistent live canvas, and neither Flow nor Dynamic Forms provides a native drag-and-drop interaction model or real-time, in-place visual updates like conflict highlighting without a screen refresh. No amount of clever Flow screen design produces a genuinely interactive grid with live feedback — this is a case where the honest answer to a stakeholder is that declarative tools have a real ceiling, and this request is above it.

The right architecture is a custom Lightning Web Component embedded as one component on the existing Lightning Record Page, sitting alongside Dynamic Forms sections handling the Resource's ordinary fields — not a wholesale replacement of the record page with code. The component should prefer Lightning Data Service or UI API wire adapters for straightforward data access, reserving custom Apex specifically for the conflict-detection logic itself if that logic is too complex for declarative data retrieval alone.

The tradeoff to present honestly to stakeholders is cost and governance, not just capability: a custom component brings ongoing maintenance, the need for a developer, test coverage for any Apex involved, and a release process that moves through the Metadata API or packages rather than simple admin change sets. That's a real cost, and the admin's actual job in this conversation is correctly identifying that this particular requirement crosses the declarative ceiling — not reaching for code by default, and not forcing declarative tools past their honest limits just to avoid that conversation.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell the business directly: this one's past what clicks-not-code can do, and I'd rather say that clearly now than spend three sprints trying to fake drag-and-drop inside a Flow screen and still end up with something clunky. Flow screens run step by step, they're not a living canvas, and nothing in Dynamic Forms gives you a grid that redraws itself and highlights conflicts the instant you drop something onto it. That's just not the tool for this job.

What I'd propose instead is bringing in a developer to build a single Lightning Web Component just for the scheduling grid itself, and dropping that onto the existing Resource record page next to the regular Dynamic Forms fields — I wouldn't let anyone talk me into rebuilding the whole record page in code just because one piece of it needs to be. For the data behind the component, I'd push the developer toward Lightning Data Service or the UI API wire adapters first, and only reach for custom Apex if the actual conflict-detection logic turns out to be too complicated for that.

The conversation I'd have with stakeholders up front is about what this actually costs going forward — once there's Apex and a custom component involved, we're not just change-setting this anymore, we need real test coverage, a different deployment process, and ongoing developer time whenever it needs tweaking. I think the value is there for a genuinely interactive scheduling tool dispatchers will use every day, but I want that tradeoff on the table honestly instead of discovering it six months later when nobody wants to touch the component because nobody remembers how it works.
questions.example: A Flow screen could show a static list of today's assignments with a picklist to reassign a technician, but it cannot render a live grid where dragging a technician's card between two time slots instantly recomputes and visually flags a scheduling conflict.
commonMistakes: Trying to force a genuinely interactive drag-and-drop UI into Flow screens, producing a clunky result instead of recognizing the declarative ceiling
Reaching for a custom Lightning Web Component by default instead of first confirming the requirement truly exceeds declarative capability
Replacing the entire record page with custom code instead of embedding the custom component alongside existing declarative sections
Underestimating the ongoing maintenance, testing, and release-process cost a custom component introduces compared to clicks-not-code
Defaulting straight to custom Apex for data access instead of considering Lightning Data Service or UI API wire adapters first
keyPoints: Flow screens and Dynamic Forms lack a persistent, real-time drag-and-drop canvas, placing this requirement genuinely beyond declarative tools
The right architecture embeds a custom Lightning Web Component alongside, not instead of, the rest of the declarative Lightning page
Lightning Data Service and UI API wire adapters can reduce how much custom Apex the component actually needs
Custom components bring real ongoing costs: source control, testing, and a different release/deployment process
The admin's judgment call is identifying genuinely declarative-exceeding requirements rather than defaulting to code or clicks out of habit

questions.title: Defending a Data Model Decision to a Skeptical Steering Committee
questions.prompt: You've designed a junction-object data model with two Master-Detail relationships and three roll-up summaries to support a new multi-department resource allocation app. A steering committee of mixed technical and business leaders is reviewing it before build sign-off, and one business VP says it looks 'needlessly complicated' compared to just adding a few fields directly onto the existing Project object. Describe how you'd present and defend your design decision in that meeting while staying genuinely open to their pushback.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by acknowledging that the VP's instinct is reasonable rather than treating it as something to overcome — fewer objects genuinely does look simpler on a diagram, and dismissing that observation outright would read as defensive rather than collaborative. The candidate should then translate the technical tradeoff into business consequences instead of platform terminology: explain concretely that adding resource-assignment fields directly onto Project would mean either duplicating Project records per resource assignment, which breaks every report the committee has asked for, or hard-capping how many resources a single project can have, which is a real operational constraint the business almost certainly doesn't want. The three roll-up summaries should be framed as the thing that makes the committee's own requested dashboards possible without someone manually reconciling a spreadsheet every week.

The second half of a strong answer is demonstrating genuine openness rather than pure defense. That means asking a real clarifying question back to the room — for instance, confirming whether there's actually a hard constraint on how many resources a project can ever have — because the answer to that question could legitimately change the recommendation. If the true constraint is one resource per project today, a simpler Lookup-based model is honestly viable, and the candidate should say so, while flagging the migration cost of introducing the junction object later if that assumption turns out to be wrong. Ending the meeting with a documented decision and a clear point to revisit if requirements shift shows the committee this isn't a one-way defense but a decision made with them, not just presented to them.

What distinguishes a senior-level answer here is not winning the argument but correctly calibrating confidence: defending the junction object firmly where the business case for it is real and specific, while being visibly willing to simplify where the committee surfaces a constraint that actually changes the calculus.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I don't start by defending the diagram. I start by agreeing with the part of what the VP said that's actually true — yes, three objects and three roll-ups looks more complicated than four new fields on Project, and if I pretended that observation wasn't fair, I'd lose the room immediately. So I'd say something like, 'You're right that this looks like more moving parts, let me show you why the simpler version breaks down once you add a second resource to a project.'

Then I'd walk through a concrete before-and-after rather than talking in platform terms — I'd say, 'if we put resource fields directly on Project, the day you need to assign a second consultant to that project, you either duplicate the Project record, which breaks every report you've asked me to build, or we tell you projects can only ever have one resource, forever.' I've found that landing one specific, visualizable consequence does more than any amount of explaining what a junction object or a roll-up summary technically is.

And then I'd actually ask them something, not just wait for pushback — I'd ask directly whether there's a real ceiling on how many resources a project can have, because if the answer is genuinely 'always exactly one,' I'd tell them straight up that the simpler model is fine and I'd rather build that than defend complexity nobody needs. I've had that happen before, where asking the question out loud actually changed my own recommendation. What I wouldn't do is let the meeting end without a clear next step — I'd want everyone to leave knowing what we decided and why, and knowing exactly what would make us revisit it, so it doesn't feel like I bulldozed the room or that the decision just evaporates the moment someone forgets the reasoning.
questions.example: If the committee reveals that resource-to-project assignment is genuinely always one-to-one today with no roadmap plans otherwise, a simpler Lookup field directly on Project may be the right call even though it sacrifices future flexibility — and saying so builds more trust than defending the junction object on principle.
commonMistakes: Defending the design purely in platform terminology, such as Master-Detail and roll-up summary, without translating to business impact
Treating committee skepticism as something to overcome rather than a legitimate input that might change the design
Failing to offer the real simpler alternative and its honest tradeoff, making the defense look like stonewalling
Not anticipating the 'why not just add fields' question in advance with a concrete business consequence ready
Ending the conversation without a clear next step or a way to revisit the decision if requirements change
keyPoints: Translate the technical tradeoff (junction object and roll-ups) into concrete business consequences, not jargon
Acknowledge the committee's simpler-looking alternative honestly before explaining why it breaks down
Ask a real clarifying question back to surface the actual constraint driving the skepticism
Offer the genuine simpler alternative and its cost, letting the committee make an informed choice
Close with a documented decision and a clear point to revisit if requirements change

Shows genuine openness to pushback rather than pure defense

questions.title: Choosing Before-Save vs After-Save Record-Triggered Flows
questions.prompt: Your team needs a flow on Opportunity that recalculates a custom 'Weighted Amount' field (Amount times a probability multiplier) every time Amount or StageName changes, and a second flow that creates a related Task record and posts a Chatter update whenever an Opportunity is marked Closed Won. A junior admin built both as after-save flows and is wondering why the Weighted Amount one feels slower than it should. Explain which trigger type each requirement actually calls for and why.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by distinguishing what each trigger context is actually for. A before-save (fast field update) record-triggered flow runs in the same database transaction before the record is committed, and it can only update fields on the triggering record itself -- it cannot create, update, or delete other records, send emails, or post to Chatter. Because it skips a second commit/save operation that an after-save update would require, it's measurably faster and is the recommended pattern specifically for same-record field calculations like the Weighted Amount field. The candidate should recommend converting that flow to before-save: it reads Amount and StageName off the record already in context, calculates the weighted value, and sets it directly on the record, with no extra DML round-trip.

The Closed Won automation is a different shape of problem: it needs to create a new Task record and interact with Chatter, both of which require touching objects other than the triggering record, which before-save flows cannot do. That one correctly belongs in an after-save flow, which runs after the Opportunity is committed and can perform DML against related objects and call actions like posting to Chatter.

The performance complaint is explained by the mismatch: running the Weighted Amount calculation as an after-save flow forces a second, separate update transaction on the Opportunity record purely to set one field, which is unnecessary overhead and also increases the risk of recursive triggering if other automation reacts to Opportunity updates. The fix isn't to add bypass logic or recursion guards -- it's to move that specific flow to the correct trigger context, which eliminates the extra save cycle entirely.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk through this by asking what each flow is actually touching. For the Weighted Amount field, the flow only ever needs to read and write fields on the same Opportunity record that fired it -- that's the textbook case for a before-save flow. Before-save flows run inline as part of the initial save, so there's no second update statement hitting the database afterward; it just sets the field value before the record is written once. I've seen teams build these as after-save out of habit because that's the pattern they're used to from Process Builder, and the cost is real -- you're forcing a second DML operation on every single Opportunity edit just to populate one formula-like field, which is exactly the slowness this junior admin is noticing.

The Closed Won flow is different because it's not just updating the Opportunity -- it's creating a Task and posting to Chatter, both of which are actions against other objects or features that a before-save flow simply isn't allowed to do. So that one has to stay after-save, and that's fine, because the extra transaction there is actually buying you something (new related records), not just re-saving the same record redundantly.

If I were coaching that junior admin, I'd tell them the rule of thumb I use: if the flow's job is 'calculate and set a field on the record that triggered it, and nothing else,' default to before-save every time. The moment the flow needs to touch a different object, send an email, post to Chatter, or call a subflow that does DML elsewhere, it has to move to after-save. I'd also flag that converting the Weighted Amount flow will immediately cut out one of the two save cycles happening on every Opportunity update, which is the actual root cause here, not something to patch around with bypass flags.
questions.example: A before-save flow setting Weighted_Amount__c = Amount * 0.5 when StageName = 'Negotiation' commits that value in the same write as the user's edit; an after-save version would instead save the user's edit first, then issue a second UPDATE statement just to patch that one field.

Assuming before-save flows can create related records or send notifications if you just add the right element
Not recognizing that an unnecessary after-save update adds a full extra save cycle and recursion risk
Believing before-save and after-save are interchangeable performance-wise with no real cost difference
Trying to fix the slowness with recursion-prevention flags instead of moving the logic to the correct trigger context
keyPoints: Before-save flows run inline pre-commit and can only modify the triggering record's own fields
After-save flows run post-commit and are required for DML on related records, Chatter, email, or other actions
Before-save eliminates a redundant second save cycle, which is the real performance win for field calculations
Misassigning a same-record calculation to after-save is a common root cause of 'slow' automation
The decision rule is based on scope of effect: same record only vs. cross-object/side-effect actions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies Weighted Amount as a before-save candidate and why
Correctly identifies Closed Won automation as requiring after-save

questions.title: Designing Fault Paths Instead of Letting Flows Fail Silently
questions.prompt: A record-triggered flow on Case updates a related Account's 'Open Case Count' field and also calls an external callout through an autolaunched subflow. Right now, if either step fails, the end user just sees a generic 'An error occurred' banner and support leadership has no visibility into how often this happens. Explain how you would redesign this flow's fault handling so failures are recoverable or at least visible, and what the actual Fault connector does versus what people assume it does.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer first clarifies what a Fault connector actually is: it's a separate path that fires only off a specific element (a Create Records, Update Records, Get Records, or Action element) when that particular element throws an error, and it lets the flow branch into custom logic instead of immediately halting. It does not automatically retry the failed operation, does not roll back or undo anything already committed earlier in the flow, and does not apply globally across the whole flow -- each DML or action element needs its own fault connector wired explicitly, or it falls through to Salesforce's default behavior, which is exactly the generic error banner and an email to the running user (or flow admin) that leadership never sees.

For this scenario, the candidate should recommend adding a fault path off the Account update element that catches the failure, writes a lightweight log record (a custom object like Flow_Error_Log__c, or at minimum a Chatter post or task assigned to an admin queue) capturing the record ID, error message, and timestamp, so the failure is visible to leadership without relying on someone noticing the banner. For the callout inside the subflow, the fault path should similarly catch the failure and, depending on the business requirement, either queue the Case for retry via a flag field and scheduled flow, or notify a support team queue -- the key point is that the subflow's own fault handling should bubble up cleanly rather than assuming the parent flow will somehow catch it, since fault connectors are local to the element that failed, not inherited across subflow boundaries without being explicitly built.

The broader principle is that fault connectors turn an unhandled exception into a handled branch of business logic, but they require deliberate design per element -- treating 'add fault paths' as a checkbox rather than designing what each specific failure should actually do (log, retry, notify, degrade gracefully) is why many flows still fail silently even after someone added fault connectors to them.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd correct is the assumption that a fault connector is some kind of safety net that automatically protects the whole flow -- it's not. It only exists on individual elements like a Create or Update Records step or an Action call, and it only fires if that specific element errors. If you don't explicitly drag a fault path off an element, Salesforce falls back to its default error behavior, which is the vague banner the user sees and an email buried in someone's inbox that leadership will never check. So step one here is going through both risky elements -- the Account update and the callout action -- and giving each one its own fault path, not assuming one fault connector somewhere covers everything downstream.

For the Account update failing, I'd have the fault path write to a simple error-logging object -- just Case ID, error message, element name, and a timestamp -- so support leadership can actually query 'how many times did this fail this month' instead of guessing. That's a small data model addition but it's the difference between an invisible problem and a trackable one. For the callout, since external systems are inherently less reliable, I'd want the fault path to do more than log -- probably flip a 'Callout_Failed__c' checkbox and timestamp on the Case, which a separate scheduled flow can pick up later to retry, rather than just recording the failure and leaving the Case in a broken state forever.

And I'd flag one more thing from experience: if the callout lives inside a subflow, don't assume its internal fault handling automatically protects the parent flow too -- I've seen teams build a fault path inside the subflow, feel like they covered it, and then the parent flow still blows up on an unrelated issue because the subflow's fault path only handled what was local to it. You really do have to think through each element individually and decide: should this log, retry, notify, or stop the whole transaction, because 'let the default behavior handle it' is functionally the same as having no fault handling at all.
commonMistakes: Believing one fault connector anywhere in the flow protects every element downstream
Assuming a fault path automatically retries the failed operation rather than just branching to custom logic
Leaving DML or callout elements with no fault connector at all, relying on the default error email nobody reads
Thinking a fault path inside a subflow automatically covers errors in the calling parent flow
Logging the failure without giving leadership any way to query or report on it, defeating the purpose of logging
keyPoints: Fault connectors are element-specific, not flow-wide, and must be added deliberately per risky element
Default (no fault path) behavior is a generic user-facing error plus an email most people never see
A fault path branches into custom logic -- it does not automatically retry or roll back prior steps
Logging failures to a queryable record (not just Chatter) gives leadership real visibility
Subflow fault handling is local to the subflow and does not automatically protect the calling flow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that fault connectors are per-element, not global
Corrects the misconception that fault paths auto-retry or roll back
Proposes a concrete, queryable logging/visibility mechanism for leadership
Addresses subflow fault handling boundaries correctly
Clarity and completeness of the redesign

questions.title: Bulkifying a Flow That Updates Related Contacts
questions.prompt: You inherit a record-triggered flow on Account that, for each updated Account, runs a Get Records to find its Contacts, then uses a loop containing an Update Records element inside the loop to set a 'Parent Account Status' field on every Contact one at a time. It works fine in testing with a single record but times out during a data load that updates 5,000 Accounts at once. Walk through exactly what's wrong and how you would rebuild it to be bulk-safe.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer identifies the core defect immediately: placing a DML element (Update Records) inside a loop means that for every single Contact, the flow issues a separate DML statement. Flow enforces the same per-transaction governor limits as Apex -- 150 total DML statements per transaction -- and when 5,000 Accounts each trigger this flow and each Account might have multiple Contacts, the cumulative DML operations across the batched trigger context blow past that limit almost immediately, which is exactly why it works for one record and fails at scale.

The fix is to rebuild the loop so it only collects changes in memory and performs a single bulk DML operation after the loop completes. Concretely: use the Get Records element to retrieve the related Contacts (ideally already scoped efficiently, not one Get Records call per Account if this can be collapsed), then loop through that collection, and inside the loop use an Assignment element to set Parent_Account_Status__c on each loop variable and add that record to a separate collection variable (e.g., 'ContactsToUpdate') using 'Add' -- critically, do not call Update Records inside the loop. After the loop exits, place a single Update Records element outside the loop that updates the entire 'ContactsToUpdate' collection in one bulk DML operation, which collapses what could have been thousands of individual DML statements into one.

The candidate should also flag that Get Records inside a loop has the same problem as DML inside a loop and should be checked for and removed if present, and that because this flow is record-triggered, Salesforce already processes it in batches of up to 200 triggering records per transaction, so the 'collect then bulk-update once' pattern needs to hold even within a single batch of up to 200 Accounts, not just conceptually for the whole 5,000-record load.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The symptom -- works for one record, falls over at volume -- is the single clearest signature of a non-bulkified flow, so that's where I'd start looking, and sure enough the Update Records element sitting inside the loop is the problem. Every pass through that loop fires its own separate DML statement against Salesforce, and Flow is bound by the exact same 150-DML-statements-per-transaction limit Apex is. One Account with a handful of Contacts might sneak under that limit; a batch of 200 Accounts each with several Contacts absolutely will not.

The way I'd rebuild it: keep the Get Records and the loop, but change what happens inside the loop. Instead of updating each Contact as I go, I'd use an Assignment element inside the loop to set the Parent_Account_Status__c value on the current loop variable, and then add that record into a collection variable I set up beforehand -- basically building up a list in memory while the loop runs, not touching the database at all. Once the loop finishes, I put exactly one Update Records element outside the loop, pointed at that whole collection, so Salesforce does one bulk DML call covering every Contact across every Account in that transaction instead of one call per Contact.

I'd also double check the Get Records element isn't doing the same thing in reverse -- if it's inside a loop somewhere making a query per Account instead of one query that returns everything needed up front, that's the SOQL version of the same mistake and would hit the 100-SOQL-queries-per-transaction limit just as fast. And I'd specifically test this fix against a bulk scenario -- updating 200+ Accounts in one data load -- before calling it done, because the whole reason this bug shipped in the first place is that it was only ever tested against a single record.
questions.example: Inside the loop: Assignment sets loopContact.Parent_Account_Status__c and adds loopContact to collection var contactsToUpdate using 'Add'; after the loop ends, one Update Records element updates contactsToUpdate in a single bulk DML call.
commonMistakes: Placing a DML (Create/Update/Delete Records) element inside a loop instead of collecting and updating once after
Placing a Get Records element inside a loop, causing repeated SOQL queries per iteration
Testing only with a single record and assuming that validates bulk behavior
Not realizing record-triggered flows batch up to 200 triggering records per transaction, compounding the per-record DML cost
Building the collection variable incorrectly (overwriting instead of using 'Add') so only the last record ends up queued for update
keyPoints: DML or SOQL inside a loop is the classic non-bulkified flow pattern and the root cause here
Flow enforces the same 150 DML / 100 SOQL per-transaction limits as Apex
Correct pattern: collect records into a collection variable inside the loop, perform one DML call after the loop
Record-triggered flows process in batches up to 200 records, so bulk-safety matters even within one batch
Testing must include a bulk scenario, not just a single-record test, to catch this class of bug

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses DML-inside-loop as the root cause
Correctly cites the relevant governor limit(s)
Describes the collect-then-bulk-update rebuild pattern accurately
Checks for the parallel Get Records/SOQL-in-loop issue
Notes the need to test with bulk/batch scenarios going forward

questions.title: Refactoring Duplicated Logic Into a Reusable Subflow
questions.prompt: You notice the same block of logic -- look up a Territory record based on a Region and Postal Code combination, then set three fields on the current record from that Territory -- has been copy-pasted into four different flows across Lead, Opportunity, Case, and Account automation, each built by a different admin at slightly different times. Describe how you would consolidate this into a subflow, including what the subflow needs to expose as inputs and outputs, and what you'd watch out for during the migration so you don't break the four flows currently using the duplicated logic.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats this as both a design task and a migration-risk task. On the design side, the candidate should build a single autolaunched flow -- the subflow -- that takes the Region and Postal Code as input variables (marked 'Available for input'), performs the Get Records lookup against Territory internally, and exposes the three resulting field values as output variables (marked 'Available for output'). Keeping the subflow's interface narrow and explicit -- only the inputs it truly needs, only the outputs callers actually use -- is what makes it safely reusable across four very differently-shaped parent flows without forcing those parent flows to share unrelated context.

On the migration side, the key risk is that the four existing flows were each built independently and may have subtly diverged -- one admin might have added a null-check on Postal Code, another might default to a 'Default Territory' record when no match is found, and those differences would silently disappear if the candidate just deletes the duplicated logic and drops in a bare subflow call without first reconciling what each of the four actually does today. The candidate should audit each of the four implementations side by side before building the subflow, decide deliberately whether to standardize behavior (likely desirable, since divergence was probably unintentional drift rather than an intentional business rule) or to parameterize the difference as an additional subflow input, and only then swap each parent flow's inline logic for a Subflow element.

Finally, the candidate should flag that this change touches four flows across four different objects, so it needs phased testing and deactivation of old versions rather than a single mass edit -- deactivate and replace one flow at a time, confirm via debug runs that the subflow's output values match what the old inline logic produced for representative records, and keep the prior flow versions available (not deleted) so there's an immediate rollback path if the consolidated subflow behaves differently than expected for an edge case none of the four original admins had tested against.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move wouldn't be building the subflow -- it'd be pulling up all four flows side by side and actually diffing the logic, because 'the same block of logic copy-pasted by four different admins over time' almost always means it's not actually identical anymore. I'd bet at least one of them handles a blank Postal Code differently, or falls back to a default Territory, or has an extra condition the others don't. Finding and reconciling those differences before I touch anything is the part people skip, and it's exactly how a 'simple refactor' quietly changes business behavior on one of the four objects without anyone noticing until weeks later.

Once I know what the real, unified logic should be, I'd build it as an autolaunched flow with a clean, minimal interface -- Region and Postal Code in as input variables, and the three Territory-derived fields out as output variables. I'd keep it deliberately narrow; I wouldn't pass the whole record in or try to make it 'smart' about which object called it, because that's how subflows turn into unmaintainable Swiss-army-knife flows. If one of the four callers genuinely needs different fallback behavior, I'd add that as its own input parameter rather than hardcoding a one-off branch inside the subflow for 'just the Case version.'

For the rollout, I'd do it one flow at a time, not all four in one sitting. For each one: swap the inline Get Records and Assignment logic for a single Subflow element wired to the new subflow, run it against a handful of real test records I already know the expected output for from the old version, and only then deactivate the old version -- I'd keep the prior version sitting there inactive rather than deleting it, specifically so if something surfaces on, say, the Case flow a week later that nobody tested for, I can reactivate the old version immediately while I fix the subflow, instead of being stuck debugging live.
questions.example: Subflow 'Get_Territory_Assignment' takes inputRegion and inputPostalCode, internally runs Get Records on Territory__c, and outputs outputTerritoryName, outputTerritoryManager, and outputSupportTier as three output variables consumed identically by the Lead, Opportunity, Case, and Account flows.

Designing the subflow's inputs/outputs too broadly (passing whole records) instead of only what's needed
Migrating all four parent flows simultaneously instead of one at a time with verification between each
Deleting the old flow versions immediately instead of deactivating and retaining them as a rollback path
Hardcoding one caller's edge-case behavior into the shared subflow instead of exposing it as a parameter

Design the subflow with a narrow, explicit set of input and output variables
Parameterize genuine behavioral differences rather than hardcoding one caller's special case
Migrate and verify one parent flow at a time rather than all at once
Retain deactivated prior flow versions as an immediate rollback path during migration

questions.title: Migrating a Legacy Process Builder Off Deprecated Automation
questions.prompt: A legacy Process Builder process on Opportunity has three criteria nodes, each calling a different Workflow Rule-era field update plus one immediate email alert, and it has been quietly running in production for years. You've been asked to retire it and rebuild the equivalent logic as a single record-triggered flow before Process Builder support fully winds down. Walk through your actual migration approach, not just the end state.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats migration as a documentation-first task before it's a building task. The candidate should start by fully reverse-engineering the existing Process Builder process: documenting each of the three criteria nodes' exact entry conditions, what each associated field update actually sets, the recipients and template of the email alert, and critically, the evaluation criteria setting ('only when a record is updated to meet criteria' vs 'every time a record is updated and meets criteria') because that setting materially changes behavior and is easy to overlook when translating to a flow's entry conditions.

Next, the candidate should design the replacement as a single after-save (or before-save, if none of the three branches require cross-object DML or the email alert can be isolated) record-triggered flow with one Decision element containing branches that mirror the three criteria nodes, using the same field-level logic. Each branch should perform the equivalent Update Records or Send Email action. The candidate should flag that Process Builder's 'every action in every criteria node that matches runs' behavior needs to be replicated carefully -- if a record could satisfy more than one of the three original criteria simultaneously, a Decision element's default top-to-bottom evaluation (which stops at the first matching outcome unless explicitly built otherwise) could silently change which actions fire compared to the original process, so this needs to be tested against real historical data, not just assumed to translate one-to-one.

For rollout, the candidate should build and fully test the new flow in a sandbox against a representative sample of real Opportunity records (ideally replaying recent production scenarios), deactivate the Process Builder process and activate the flow in the same deployment window to avoid a gap or an overlap where both run simultaneously and double-fire the email alert or field updates, and keep the deactivated Process Builder process in the org (not deleted) for a defined rollback window in case the flow's behavior diverges from production reality in a way sandbox testing didn't catch.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Before I build anything, I spend real time just understanding what this Process Builder has actually been doing in production, because 'three criteria nodes plus a Workflow-era field update and an email alert' built up over years is exactly the kind of automation where the documented intent and the actual behavior have drifted apart. I'd pull up each criteria node, write down its exact filter logic, what each field update sets, who the email alert goes to and with which template, and I'd specifically check the evaluation criteria setting on the process -- whether it only fires on records newly meeting the criteria or every time a matching record is edited -- because that's a subtle setting that's easy to misread and completely changes how often this thing has actually been firing.

Once I've got that fully mapped out, I'd build one new record-triggered flow with a single Decision element that has a branch for each of the three original criteria nodes, doing the equivalent field update or email send in each branch. The part I'd be most careful about is overlap -- if an Opportunity could technically satisfy more than one of those three original criteria at once, Process Builder would have run every matching node's actions, but a Decision element by default only takes the first branch that matches. I wouldn't assume that doesn't matter here; I'd actually test it against a handful of real records that I know satisfy multiple conditions and confirm the new flow does the same thing the old process did, or deliberately decide it shouldn't and document why.

For the actual cutover, I treat deactivating the old and activating the new as one atomic step, not two separate deploys with a gap in between -- I don't want a window where neither one is running, and I especially don't want a window where both are running and someone gets the same email alert twice. And I don't delete the Process Builder process afterward; I leave it sitting there deactivated for a couple of weeks as a safety net, because if the new flow misses an edge case that only shows up with real production data, I want a fast way back rather than having to rebuild the old logic from memory under pressure.
commonMistakes: Skipping the reverse-engineering step and assuming the process's current behavior matches its original documented intent
Overlooking the 'evaluate every time vs only when newly meeting criteria' setting during translation
Assuming a Decision element's branches behave identically to Process Builder's independent criteria-node evaluation when overlap is possible
Cutting over with a gap or an overlap window between deactivating the old process and activating the new flow
Deleting the legacy Process Builder process immediately instead of retaining it deactivated as a rollback option
keyPoints: Fully document the legacy process's actual behavior, including the evaluation criteria setting, before building anything
Translate each criteria node into an equivalent Decision branch with matching field-update/email logic
Explicitly test for overlap cases where multiple original criteria could match the same record simultaneously
Cut over in a single deployment window to avoid a gap or double-firing overlap
Retain the deactivated legacy process temporarily as a rollback path rather than deleting it immediately

questions.title: Debugging a Flow That Passes in Debug Mode but Fails for Real Users
questions.prompt: A screen flow that creates a new Case and attaches it to the current logged-in user's Account passes every time you run it yourself using 'Run' and the Debug tool in Flow Builder, but several end users report it failing with a permissions-style error in production. Explain how you would actually investigate this, including why the Debug tool passing doesn't prove the flow works for those users.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by naming the actual gap: running a flow via Flow Builder's Debug tool executes in the context of the admin building it (or whatever user is clicked into the builder), with that user's full permission set, record access, and field-level security -- it does not automatically simulate a different user's profile, permission set, or sharing rules. So 'it works when I debug it' only proves the logic is sound for someone with the admin's access, not that it works for the actual end users hitting the permissions error, which is a completely different question.

The candidate should describe the correct next step: in Flow Builder's Debug panel, there's an option to run the debug session 'as a different user' (or, if unavailable/insufficient, actually log in as one of the affected users via 'Login As' from Setup, assuming that's permitted) so the flow executes under that user's actual profile, permission set assignments, and sharing model. This surfaces the real discrepancy -- commonly, the affected users' profile or permission set lacks Create access on Case, lacks field-level security on a field the flow is trying to set, or the flow's Create Records element is trying to set the Case's AccountId to an Account the running user doesn't have at least Read access to under the org's sharing rules, which an admin's typically broader access would never expose.

The candidate should also mention checking whether the flow runs in 'System Context with Sharing' versus 'User Context' (an autolaunched/screen flow setting), since a flow explicitly set to run in system context would bypass the user's object and field permissions entirely and mask exactly this class of bug during admin testing -- if that's the case, the real question becomes whether running in system context was an intentional security decision or an oversight, because reverting to user context (or enforcing sharing) is often the right fix once the actual permission gap is identified and granted properly rather than papered over by elevating the flow's run context.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing I'd point out right away is that clicking 'Run' or using the Debug tool in Flow Builder runs the flow as me, the admin building it, and admins almost always have way more access than the end users this flow is actually built for. So the fact that it passes for me doesn't tell me anything about whether a regular user's profile actually has Create access on Case, or field-level security on whatever fields the flow is setting, or sharing access to the Account it's attaching the Case to. I'd stop treating 'it works for me' as evidence of anything here.

What I'd actually do is use the 'run as a different user' option in the Debug panel and point it at one of the affected users, or if that's not giving me enough signal, use Login As to literally become that user and run the flow live. That almost always reproduces the exact error immediately, and usually it's one of a short list of things: the user's permission set is missing Create on Case, there's a field on the Case the flow sets that their profile can't edit, or -- and this is the one I'd check first given it's attaching to an Account -- the user doesn't actually have read access to that specific Account under our sharing rules, even though the flow logic itself is completely fine.

One more thing I always check on screen flows specifically: whether it's set to run in system context with sharing, system context without sharing, or user context. If someone set this to run in system context, it would completely bypass the user's actual object and field permissions while I'm testing as an admin and while it runs for regular users too -- which actually means the permissions error they're hitting might be coming from somewhere other than object/field security, more likely sharing-rule access on the Account specifically, since system context without sharing would skip CRUD/FLS checks but sharing rules can still be a separate layer depending on configuration. Either way, I wouldn't just crank up the flow's run context to 'fix' it -- I'd rather find out exactly which permission is missing and grant it properly, because silently running everything in system context just hides the next permissions gap instead of solving this one.
commonMistakes: Treating a passing Debug tool run as proof the flow works for all end users
Not knowing the Debug panel has a 'run as a different user' option to actually test under the real user's access
Assuming a permissions error is always a Case object permission issue without checking Account-level sharing access
Not checking the flow's run-context setting (system context with/without sharing vs user context)
'Fixing' the issue by elevating the flow to system context instead of identifying and granting the specific missing permission
keyPoints: Debug tool runs execute under the builder's own access, not the end user's profile/permission set/sharing
Use 'run as a different user' in the Debug panel or Login As to reproduce the real user's actual error
Common root causes: missing object CRUD, missing field-level security, or insufficient sharing access on a related record
Check the flow's run-context setting since system context bypasses user permissions entirely
The fix should be granting the correct specific permission, not broadly elevating the flow's run context

questions.title: Diagnosing a Record-Triggered Flow Stuck in Recursive Updates
questions.prompt: After deploying a new after-save flow on Opportunity that updates a 'Last Automation Run' timestamp field whenever Amount changes, users start reporting that saving an Opportunity sometimes takes noticeably longer than before, and the field history shows the timestamp updating multiple times in rapid succession from a single user edit. Diagnose what's happening and how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer names this immediately as flow recursion: the after-save flow updates the Opportunity (setting Last Automation Run), that update is itself a save on Opportunity, and because the flow's entry condition is 'Amount changes' or broadly 'record is updated' without excluding its own update, the flow's own write can re-trigger itself, or re-trigger evaluation of its criteria against the newly-saved record. Record-triggered flows do have built-in recursion protection against infinite loops in many cases, but a flow can still legitimately re-fire multiple times within the same transaction if each update meets the entry criteria again and the field being checked (or a related field) changes with each pass, and even bounded recursion that stops after a few iterations still causes the slowdown and multiple timestamp writes users are seeing.

The root cause is almost certainly that the entry condition is evaluating on 'record updated' generally, or on Amount changing, without also checking that Last Automation Run isn't already current -- so after the flow sets Last Automation Run, if that update is evaluated against the same entry criteria (which it can be, depending on exactly how the flow is built and whether the field update happens before-save or after-save), the flow fires again. The fix is to tighten the entry condition so the flow only fires when the condition that should trigger it is true AND the automation hasn't already run for that state -- commonly by adding a filter condition comparing Last Automation Run against the current save, or better, by moving the timestamp-setting logic to a before-save flow if it only needs to set a field on the same record, since before-save flows update the record as part of the single initial save and don't trigger a second after-save evaluation cycle for that same change.

The candidate should also mention using Flow's debug/execution logs or the 'Flow Interview' details (or Apex debug logs showing nested flow interview executions) to confirm exactly how many times the flow actually fired per save, rather than assuming the cause -- confirming the mechanism before changing the entry conditions avoids masking a different underlying bug with a superficial condition tweak.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This smells like classic recursion the moment I hear 'multiple rapid-fire updates to the same field from one user edit,' so that's where I'd start. What's almost certainly happening: the flow updates Last Automation Run whenever Amount changes, but that update is itself a write to the Opportunity, and if the entry condition is just 'Amount changed' or 'record updated' without anything excluding the flow's own resulting save, that write can satisfy the entry criteria all over again and the flow fires a second, maybe third time in the same transaction before anything stops it.

Before I touch the flow, though, I'd actually confirm this rather than guess -- I'd look at the flow's execution details, or Apex debug logs if needed, to see literally how many times the Flow Interview ran for a single save. I want to know it's really firing 3 times, not assume it and then 'fix' the wrong thing.

Once confirmed, my fix would be one of two things depending on what this flow actually needs to do. If setting that timestamp is genuinely the only job of this flow -- just stamping a value on the same record -- I'd move it to a before-save flow entirely, because before-save updates happen as part of the one initial save and don't create a second after-save transaction that can re-trigger evaluation. If there's a real reason it has to be after-save, I'd tighten the entry condition instead -- add a check that Last Automation Run doesn't already reflect this save, so the second pass through sees nothing new to act on and the flow's criteria simply doesn't match anymore. Either way, I wouldn't leave it as 'it fires a few extra times but eventually stops' -- even bounded recursion is doing real, measurable, unnecessary work on every single save, which is exactly the slowdown users are reporting.
commonMistakes: Assuming record-triggered flows can never recurse because Salesforce 'handles that automatically'
Fixing the symptom by adding a formula/workaround field instead of addressing the entry condition causing re-evaluation
Not confirming the actual number of flow executions via debug/execution logs before changing anything
Not considering moving the logic to before-save as the cleaner structural fix
Tightening the entry condition so aggressively it also blocks legitimate re-runs the business actually needs
keyPoints: Diagnoses the issue as flow recursion caused by the flow's own update re-satisfying its entry criteria
Confirms the mechanism via execution/debug logs before changing the flow
Considers moving same-record field updates to before-save to eliminate the recursive after-save cycle
Alternatively tightens the entry condition to exclude saves where the automation already ran
Recognizes that even bounded recursion causes real performance cost, not just a cosmetic issue

Recommends confirming via execution/debug logs before changing the flow
