questions.title: Resolving an Intermittent 'Too Many SOQL Queries' Error
questions.prompt: A flow on Case that was working fine for months suddenly starts throwing 'System.LimitException: Too many SOQL queries: 101' errors, but only during the busiest hour of the support team's shift, never during quiet periods. The flow itself hasn't been changed recently. Explain your troubleshooting approach and the most likely explanations.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer leads with the key insight: the 101-SOQL-query limit is a per-transaction limit, and a transaction in Salesforce can include far more than just this one flow -- it can include other triggers, other flows, validation rule formulas referencing related objects, and Apex running in the same context, all stacking their SOQL usage together. The fact that this only happens during the busiest hour, with no recent change to the flow itself, points strongly toward volume-driven contention rather than a logic bug in this specific flow: during peak hours, Cases are likely being updated via bulk operations (API integrations, bulk reassignment tools, list views with mass edit, or an integration syncing records), and when many Case records are processed in a single transaction, any inefficiency in this flow -- even something that was 'fine' at low volume, like a Get Records call that isn't a problem for 1 record but adds up when the same flow executes for 150 Cases in one batch -- gets multiplied across the whole batch.

The candidate should describe checking Setup's Flow error emails and debug logs captured specifically during a peak-hour failure (not reproducing in isolation, which likely won't show the issue, exactly as described) to see the actual count and source of SOQL queries in that transaction, and should also check what other automation runs on Case -- other flows, Apex triggers, validation rules with cross-object formula fields -- because the 101st query might not even come from this flow; this flow could simply be the one that happens to push the transaction over the edge that some other piece of automation was already close to.

The most likely root cause to investigate first is a Get Records (or other SOQL-issuing element) that sits inside a loop in this flow, or in another flow/trigger on the same object, because that's the one pattern whose SOQL cost scales directly with how many Case records are touched in a single transaction -- which lines up exactly with a failure that only appears under peak-hour bulk volume and never during quiet single-record edits.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The detail that jumps out at me immediately is 'only during the busiest hour' with no recent change to the flow -- that's a strong signal this isn't a bug in the flow's logic, it's a volume problem, and the 101-query limit is scoped to the whole transaction, not just to this one flow. During a quiet period, maybe one Case gets updated at a time and whatever SOQL this flow runs stays well under the limit. During the busy hour, if Cases are coming in through a bulk path -- an API integration, a bulk status-update tool, a list view mass edit -- this flow (and anything else that runs on Case) could be executing for 150 or 200 records in a single transaction, and anything in this flow that issues a query per record instead of once per transaction gets multiplied by however many Cases are in that batch.

So my first move is pulling actual debug logs from during a real failure at peak time, not trying to reproduce it myself with a single test record, because a single-record test is exactly the scenario that won't show this. I want to see the real query count and, ideally, which element or which piece of automation issued the 101st query. And I wouldn't assume it's necessarily this flow's fault just because this flow's name is on the error -- I'd check what else runs on Case in the same transaction, other flows, any Apex triggers, cross-object formula fields in validation rules, because this flow might just be the thing that happens to tip an already-strained transaction over the limit.

Given the pattern though, my top suspect going in is a Get Records element sitting inside a loop somewhere in this flow's structure -- that's the one thing whose query cost scales directly with batch size, stays invisible at low volume, and suddenly becomes a real problem exactly when a lot of Cases get processed together, which matches this symptom almost perfectly. I'd confirm it in the logs before changing anything, but that's where I'd look first.
commonMistakes: Trying to reproduce the error with a single test record and concluding there's no problem when it doesn't reproduce
Assuming the 101st query necessarily comes from this flow rather than other automation sharing the same transaction
Not recognizing governor limits are per-transaction, so bulk operations multiply any per-record inefficiency
Overlooking Get Records (or other SOQL) inside a loop as the most likely scalable-with-volume root cause
Fixing it by requesting a governor limit increase instead of finding and fixing the actual inefficient query pattern
keyPoints: The SOQL limit is per-transaction and shared across all automation (flows, triggers, formulas) in that transaction
Peak-hour-only failures point to bulk/volume-driven causes, not a logic change in this specific flow
Pull debug logs from an actual peak-time failure rather than trying to reproduce with a single record
Check other automation on the same object, since this flow may not be the sole source of the 101st query
Get Records (or other SOQL) inside a loop is the prime suspect because its cost scales with batch size

questions.title: Fixing Conflicting Automation Order Between Two Flows on the Same Object
questions.prompt: Two after-save record-triggered flows both run on Lead: one assigns the Lead to a sales rep based on territory rules, and another sends a welcome email referencing the 'Assigned Rep' field. Support reports that the welcome email sometimes goes out with the Assigned Rep field blank, but only sometimes, and the two flows have never had an explicit order set between them. Diagnose the issue and describe the fix.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer explains that when multiple record-triggered flows exist on the same object and event, and no explicit trigger order has been set on each flow, Salesforce does not guarantee which one runs first -- without an explicit order value, execution order among same-context flows is effectively unpredictable from the admin's perspective (historically based on creation order or internal tie-breaking that shouldn't be relied upon). That exactly explains the intermittent symptom: when the territory-assignment flow happens to execute first, Assigned Rep is already populated by the time the welcome-email flow reads it and the email is correct; when the welcome-email flow executes first (or the two race in a way influenced by other factors like bulk processing order), it reads Assigned Rep before the other flow has set it, and the email goes out blank.

The fix is to use the Trigger Order field (available on record-triggered flows in Flow Builder's flow properties) to explicitly set the territory-assignment flow to a lower order number than the welcome-email flow, guaranteeing the assignment always completes first within the same trigger context. The candidate should note this only works within the same before-save or after-save context -- if the two flows are both after-save, explicit ordering resolves it cleanly; if they were split across before-save and after-save, that itself resolves the ordering (before-save always completes before after-save flows run), so the real fix depends on confirming which context each flow runs in before deciding whether to use Trigger Order, consolidate them into one flow with Decision logic, or restructure which context each piece of logic belongs in.

The candidate should also flag the longer-term architectural point: relying on two independent flows with an implicit dependency between them (one needs to read a field the other sets) is fragile by design, and consolidating them into a single flow with the assignment logic followed by the email logic in sequence, or at minimum documenting and enforcing the Trigger Order explicitly, removes the ambiguity entirely rather than just making it 'usually' work.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The word 'sometimes' is the whole clue here -- if this were a logic bug, it'd fail consistently. Intermittent failure across two flows on the same object screams race condition, and sure enough, if nobody ever explicitly set a trigger order on either of these two after-save flows, Salesforce doesn't promise you a specific order between them. So depending on whatever internal tie-breaking happens that day, sometimes the territory-assignment flow finishes first and the welcome email flow reads a populated Assigned Rep field, and sometimes it's the other way around and the email goes out blank.

The actual fix is pretty mechanical once you know that: each record-triggered flow has a Trigger Order field in its properties, and I'd explicitly set the assignment flow to run before the email flow -- give assignment something like order 1 and the email flow order 2. That removes the guessing entirely; assignment is now guaranteed to finish before the email flow even starts, every single time, not just most of the time.

But honestly, if I found this in an org, I'd flag it as a bigger pattern problem, not just fix the ordering and move on. Having two separate flows where one silently depends on data the other one sets is fragile -- the next admin who touches either flow has no way of knowing that dependency exists unless they go digging, and 'sometimes blank' bugs like this are exactly what that fragility produces. I'd seriously consider just merging this into one flow -- do the territory assignment first, then the email send, right in sequence in a single flow -- so the dependency is explicit and visible in the flow's own structure instead of being an invisible assumption living in the Trigger Order field that someone could change later without realizing what breaks.
questions.example: Setting the territory-assignment flow's Trigger Order to 1 and the welcome-email flow's to 2 guarantees Assigned Rep is always populated before the email flow evaluates, eliminating the intermittent blank-field bug entirely.
commonMistakes: Assuming Salesforce automatically runs flows on the same object in creation order or a predictable sequence by default
Not knowing the Trigger Order property exists on record-triggered flows and can be set explicitly
Treating the intermittent symptom as a data issue or email template bug instead of an execution-order race condition
Fixing the order without recognizing the underlying architectural fragility of two flows with a hidden cross-flow dependency
Not checking whether the two flows are even in the same trigger context (before-save vs after-save) before assuming ordering alone explains it
keyPoints: Flows on the same object/event with no explicit order have unpredictable relative execution order
The intermittent blank field is explained by a race condition between the two flows
Trigger Order on record-triggered flows can explicitly force assignment to run before the email flow
Ordering only resolves contention within the same trigger context (before-save vs after-save matters)
The deeper fix is reducing hidden cross-flow dependencies, ideally by consolidating into one sequenced flow

questions.title: Scheduled Flow Running on the Wrong Set of Records
questions.prompt: A scheduled flow is supposed to run nightly and flag any Opportunity that has been in the same stage for more than 30 days by setting a 'Stalled' checkbox. After a few weeks in production, you discover it's been flagging Opportunities that moved stages just yesterday, and missing some that have genuinely been stalled for months. Diagnose the likely design flaw and describe how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer suspects the flow's entry/filter logic is checking the wrong date field or comparing against the wrong baseline. The most common root cause for this exact symptom is that the scheduled flow's Get Records filter (or a Decision element) is comparing today's date against the Opportunity's generic LastModifiedDate rather than a field that specifically tracks when the stage last changed -- LastModifiedDate updates on any edit to the record at all, including unrelated field changes, owner changes, or even system updates, so an Opportunity edited yesterday for a completely unrelated reason (updating a description, for instance) would show a very recent LastModifiedDate even though its stage has been unchanged for months, causing it to be incorrectly skipped; conversely, if the comparison logic has an off-by-one error or is checking 'modified within the last 30 days' instead of 'not modified in the last 30 days,' it would flag recently-touched records instead of stale ones, explaining both halves of the reported symptom.

The correct fix requires a dedicated 'Stage Last Changed Date' field that is only updated by automation specifically when StageName changes -- typically set via a small before-save or after-save record-triggered flow on Opportunity that checks whether StageName has changed (using the ISCHANGED-equivalent entry condition on the trigger) and, only then, stamps a Stage_Last_Changed_Date__c field with today's date. The nightly scheduled flow should then filter Opportunities where Stage_Last_Changed_Date__c is more than 30 days in the past, which correctly isolates records that have genuinely sat in the same stage, independent of unrelated edits to the record.

The candidate should also note the importance of validating this with real data before trusting it again: pulling a sample of Opportunities that were incorrectly flagged and incorrectly skipped, checking their actual LastModifiedDate and StageName history (via field history tracking, if enabled) against what the flow used, confirms the diagnosis rather than assuming it, since a scheduled flow with a logic bug like this can run silently wrong for a long time with no error thrown -- it executes successfully every night, it's just evaluating the wrong condition.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first guess, before I even open the flow, is that it's checking LastModifiedDate instead of a field that actually tracks when the stage specifically changed -- and that one bug would explain both halves of what's being reported. LastModifiedDate updates on literally any edit to the record, so an Opportunity that's been stuck in the same stage for four months but had someone fix a typo in the description yesterday would show a LastModifiedDate of yesterday, even though nothing about its stage actually changed -- that's your 'genuinely stalled ones get missed' case. And depending on exactly how the comparison is written, if there's a sign error or the condition is backwards, you could also get records that were just touched flagged as stalled instead of skipped -- that's the other half.

I'd open the flow and go straight to whatever Get Records filter or Decision condition defines 'stalled' and check exactly which date field it's using and which direction the comparison runs. If it's LastModifiedDate, that confirms it, and the real fix isn't a tweak to this scheduled flow at all -- it's adding a dedicated field, something like Stage_Last_Changed_Date__c, that only gets stamped by its own small record-triggered flow specifically when StageName changes, nothing else. Then this nightly scheduled flow gets pointed at that new field instead, and now 'more than 30 days since the stage changed' actually means what it says, independent of unrelated edits to the record.

Before I trust it again, though, I'd pull a handful of the actual Opportunities people reported as wrong -- the ones flagged after moving stages yesterday, and the ones that should've been flagged months ago and weren't -- and manually check their real stage history against what the old logic would have evaluated. I want to see the bug reproduce on real records, not just assume my theory is right and ship a fix without confirming it, because a scheduled flow like this runs successfully every single night with zero errors even while it's silently evaluating the wrong thing -- nobody gets an error email pointing them at the bug.

questions.title: One Flow Per Object vs. Many Small Flows: Making the Architectural Call
questions.prompt: Your org currently has seven separate record-triggered flows on the Case object, each built by a different person over two years for a different requirement, with no documented strategy. You've been asked to set the standard going forward. Explain the trade-offs between consolidating into one large flow per object and event versus keeping many small single-purpose flows, and what you would actually recommend for this org.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer frames this as a real trade-off, not a universal right answer. Consolidating into one flow per object and trigger context (e.g., one before-save and one after-save flow on Case) gives explicit, visible control over execution order within that single flow's own Decision/branch structure, avoids the implicit-ordering risk that comes from having seven independently-authored flows with no coordinated Trigger Order values, and reduces the per-transaction overhead of initializing multiple separate flow interviews. It also makes governor-limit budgeting easier to reason about, since all the DML and SOQL usage for that object's automation lives in one place that can be reviewed holistically for bulkification.

The cost of consolidation is that one large flow becomes a single point of complexity and risk: a change by one admin for one business requirement now requires understanding (or at least not breaking) six other unrelated pieces of logic living in the same flow, testing becomes harder because any change has a larger blast radius, and version control/rollback becomes coarser -- you can't cleanly deactivate just one business rule without potentially affecting others if they share elements or variables. Many small single-purpose flows are easier to understand, test, and roll back in isolation, and they're easier to attribute to a specific business owner or requirement, but they reintroduce the exact implicit-ordering and redundant-overhead problems the consolidated approach solves, especially as the count grows unmanaged like it has here.

For this specific org, the candidate should recommend a middle path: consolidate down to one flow per object per trigger context (so, likely two flows total for Case -- one before-save, one after-save) using a single Decision element with clearly-labeled, well-documented branches for each of the seven original requirements, which gets the ordering and overhead benefits of consolidation while using subflows to keep each branch's actual business logic modular, readable, and independently testable rather than becoming an unreadable monolith. This should be paired with a written naming/documentation standard (clear flow and branch names, a description field on each flow explaining its purpose and owner) so the next person inheriting this doesn't recreate the same seven-flows-with-no-strategy problem.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd tell this org there isn't a universally 'correct' number of flows per object -- both extremes have real costs, and seven undocumented flows built by seven different people over two years is actually a symptom of neither extreme being chosen on purpose, which is the real problem.

The case for consolidating toward one flow per object per context -- say, one before-save and one after-save flow on Case -- is that it gives you direct control over execution order, since right now these seven flows have some kind of implicit, probably undocumented relative order, and that's exactly the kind of thing that produces the intermittent race-condition bugs I've debugged before. It also cuts down the overhead of spinning up seven separate flow interviews on every single Case transaction, and it makes it much easier to look at everything running on Case in one place and sanity-check it for bulkification and governor-limit usage together instead of guessing how seven independent flows interact.

The honest downside of going all the way to one giant flow is that it becomes intimidating and risky to touch -- if I'm the eighth admin who needs to add one more business rule, I now have to understand a sprawling flow built by seven different people before I can safely add my piece, and testing any single change means being careful about everything else living in that same flow. So what I'd actually recommend here is consolidating to one before-save and one after-save flow on Case, but inside each one, using a clean Decision element with a clearly labeled branch per original requirement, and pushing the actual business logic for each branch into its own well-named subflow. That gets me the ordering and overhead benefits without turning the whole thing into unreadable spaghetti, and each subflow stays testable and ownable on its own. Just as important, I'd write down a naming and documentation standard right now -- flow descriptions, branch labels, who owns what -- because the actual root cause of today's mess wasn't 'too many flows,' it was nobody deciding on a strategy at all.
commonMistakes: Treating 'one flow per object' or 'many small flows' as a universally correct rule rather than a trade-off decision
Consolidating into one flow without using subflows, producing an unreadable, high-risk monolith
Ignoring the implicit ordering risk that unmanaged multiple flows on the same object/context create
Not addressing documentation/naming standards as the actual root cause of the current mess
Overlooking that consolidation should be scoped per trigger context (before-save vs after-save), not forced into a single flow regardless of context
keyPoints: Both extremes (one giant flow vs. many small flows) have genuine, specific trade-offs, not a universally correct answer
Consolidation improves execution-order control and reduces per-transaction overhead
Consolidation without subflows risks creating an unmanageable, high-blast-radius monolith
A middle path -- one flow per object per trigger context, using subflows per branch -- balances both concerns
A written naming/documentation standard addresses the actual root cause of the current seven-flow sprawl

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Articulates genuine trade-offs on both sides rather than declaring one approach universally correct
Correctly explains the ordering/overhead benefits of consolidation
Correctly explains the complexity/blast-radius risk of over-consolidation
Recommends a concrete, well-reasoned middle-path architecture using subflows
Addresses documentation/naming standards as part of the fix

questions.title: Orchestration vs. Chained Autolaunched Flows for a Multi-Step Onboarding Process
questions.prompt: A new customer onboarding process spans several business days: it needs a sales rep to complete a handoff form, then waits for a manager approval step, then triggers provisioning tasks for two different internal teams who each need their own screen flow to mark their piece done, and finally sends a completion notification. Explain whether you'd build this with Flow Orchestration or with a chain of autolaunched and screen flows connected by record updates, and justify the choice.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer recognizes the defining characteristics of this requirement that point toward Flow Orchestration: the process has multiple distinct stages spanning real elapsed time (business days, not seconds), it involves multiple different people/roles each responsible for a discrete step (sales rep, manager, two separate internal teams), and the overall process needs visible, trackable status as a whole, not just as independent disconnected automations. Orchestration was built specifically for this shape of problem -- it models a multi-stage, multi-actor process as a single Orchestration Work Guide, assigns steps to specific users or queues, tracks the status of each stage explicitly, and supports both flow-driven background steps and interactive steps presented to the right person at the right time.

A chain of independent autolaunched and screen flows connected only by record-field updates (e.g., a 'Stage' picklist that each flow checks and advances) can technically replicate parts of this, but it recreates, by hand, the coordination problem Orchestration already solves: tracking which stage a given onboarding is in requires building and maintaining that status field and the entry-condition logic on every flow in the chain, there's no built-in work-assignment or task-surfacing mechanism for the two internal teams (each would need separate, hand-built notification/task logic), and visibility into 'where is this specific onboarding stuck right now' requires custom reporting rather than Orchestration's native stage-tracking.

The candidate should recommend Flow Orchestration here, with each major stage (handoff form, manager approval, each team's provisioning step, final notification) built as its own flow (screen flows for the interactive steps, autolaunched for the background notification step) and assembled into an Orchestration's stages and steps, which gives the process owner a single place to see status across all active onboardings and assigns each interactive step directly to the right person or queue without hand-rolled task-creation logic. The candidate should be honest that Orchestration adds its own learning curve and is a relatively newer, more specialized tool than plain flows, so it's the right call specifically because this process has the multi-actor, multi-stage, time-spanning shape Orchestration targets -- not every multi-step process justifies it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The details that tell me this is an Orchestration problem, not a chain-of-flows problem, are the time span and the number of different people involved. This isn't one flow handing off to the next flow in the same transaction -- it's a process that lives for multiple business days, touches a sales rep, a manager, and two separate internal teams, and somebody is going to want to know 'where is this specific onboarding right now' at any point in that timeline. That's exactly the problem Orchestration was built to solve, and building it as a chain of autolaunched flows connected by a status field would mean me hand-building everything Orchestration already gives for free -- a status field and entry-condition checks on every flow to simulate stage tracking, and separate notification or task-creation logic for each of the two internal teams so they actually know it's their turn.

So my actual recommendation is to build each real step as its own flow -- the sales rep's handoff as a screen flow, manager approval as a screen flow (or an approval process feeding into the orchestration), each team's provisioning step as its own screen flow so they can mark their piece done, and the final notification as a simple autolaunched flow -- and then assemble all of those into an Orchestration, with each one becoming a stage or step that gets assigned to the right person or queue automatically. That gives whoever owns this process a single screen where they can see every onboarding currently in flight and exactly which stage each one is sitting in, instead of someone having to go dig through records guessing.

I'd be upfront that Orchestration is a less commonly used tool than a regular flow and has its own learning curve, so I wouldn't reach for it on every multi-step process -- if this were just two autolaunched flows running back to back in the same transaction with no human waiting in between, I'd just chain them. But the moment you've got multiple different humans each responsible for a piece of a process that spans days, Orchestration is doing real work for you that you'd otherwise be reinventing badly by hand.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to a chain of flows connected by a status field without recognizing the multi-day, multi-actor shape that calls for Orchestration
Reaching for Orchestration on every multi-step process regardless of whether multiple people/time-spanning stages are actually involved
Underestimating how much hand-built logic (status tracking, task/notification creation) is needed to replicate Orchestration with plain flows
Assuming Orchestration replaces screen/autolaunched flows rather than assembling them as its underlying steps
Not acknowledging Orchestration's own learning curve and relative novelty as a real trade-off to weigh
keyPoints: Multi-day, multi-actor processes needing visible stage tracking are the signature use case for Flow Orchestration
Orchestration assembles existing screen/autolaunched flows as steps rather than replacing them
A hand-built chain of flows would have to recreate status tracking and task/notification assignment manually
Orchestration provides native visibility into where any given process instance currently stands
The choice should be justified by the specific shape of the problem, not applied as a default for every multi-step process

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the multi-actor, multi-day shape as the reason Orchestration fits
Correctly explains Orchestration assembles existing flows as steps, not a replacement for them
Articulates what a hand-built chain-of-flows alternative would be missing
Gives a balanced, non-default justification (acknowledges when Orchestration would be overkill)
Clarity and technical accuracy

questions.title: Deciding Between Flow, Validation Rule, and Apex for a Discount Approval Rule
questions.prompt: Sales leadership wants a rule enforced on Opportunity: any line item discount over 20 percent must be blocked from saving unless the Opportunity owner's role is Sales Director or above, and the logic needs to check the user's role hierarchy position, not just a hardcoded list of names. Walk through how you'd decide between a validation rule, a record-triggered flow, and an Apex trigger for this, and what you'd actually choose.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by identifying the real complexity driver: the requirement isn't just 'check a field value,' it's 'determine the running user's position in the role hierarchy relative to a named role,' which is not something a standard validation rule formula can evaluate directly -- validation rules can reference $Profile and some user fields, but there's no native formula function that walks the role hierarchy to answer 'is this user's role at or above Sales Director.' That rules out a pure validation rule as a complete solution on its own, though it doesn't rule out validation rules from playing a supporting role.

Between record-triggered flow and Apex trigger, the candidate should note that a before-save record-triggered flow can absolutely do this: it can use a Get Records element to query the running user's Role (via UserRole, checking RollupDescription or a custom hierarchy-level field) or, more robustly, query the role hierarchy for whether the user's RoleId is the Sales Director role or a role that rolls up to/above it, and then use a Decision element to add a validation-style error (using the Add Error action available in before-save flows, or by preventing save via a custom error message) when the discount exceeds 20 percent and the role check fails. Since this is pure declarative logic with no need for complex recursive hierarchy traversal beyond what Get Records plus a Decision can express (especially if the org maintains a simple 'Role Level' custom field for quick comparison), Apex is not required to achieve the business requirement, and the team should prefer the before-save flow precisely because it keeps the logic visible and maintainable by admins rather than locked in code only developers can change.

The candidate should recommend: a before-save record-triggered flow that checks the discount condition and the role-hierarchy condition via a Get Records on UserRole (possibly against a helper 'Role Level' field maintained for this exact purpose, since deep recursive hierarchy walking is awkward in pure flow), using Add Error to block the save with a clear message when both conditions are true. Apex would only become the better choice if the hierarchy logic needed genuine recursive traversal of arbitrary depth that a flat helper field couldn't represent, or if this rule needed to be tightly bundled with other complex Opportunity logic already living in Apex for maintainability reasons -- neither of which applies here.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The part of this that rules out a plain validation rule right away is the role hierarchy check -- validation rule formulas just don't have a function that walks up the role hierarchy and tells you 'is this user's role Sales Director or above.' A validation rule can check a flat field easily, but it can't natively answer a hierarchy-relative question like this one, so I know this needs something with more logic behind it, even if parts of the final solution still end up using validation-rule-style error messages.

From there it's really a flow-versus-Apex decision, and I'd lean flow first and ask whether Apex is actually necessary, not the other way around. A before-save record-triggered flow can use a Get Records element to look up the running user's role, and if the org has a simple helper field like 'Role Level' maintained on the Role or User object specifically for comparisons like this, the flow's Decision element can check 'discount over 20 percent AND role level below Sales Director' and use Add Error to block the save with a clear message, right there in before-save, no Apex needed. That's a completely reasonable, maintainable way to express this rule, and it means the next admin, not just a developer, can see and adjust this logic later.

I'd only reach for Apex if the hierarchy logic turned out to need real recursive traversal that a flat helper field couldn't represent cleanly -- say, if 'Sales Director or above' had to be computed dynamically across an arbitrarily deep, frequently-restructured hierarchy rather than something a maintained Role Level field could capture. Even then, I'd push back a little and ask whether maintaining that helper field via a small periodic flow or a one-time setup is actually simpler than writing and maintaining Apex for this. For the actual scenario as described, I'd build it in a before-save flow and treat Apex as the fallback only if the hierarchy complexity turns out to be worse than it sounds.

Defaulting to Apex immediately because 'role hierarchy' sounds complex, without checking whether a flow plus a helper field can express it
Not knowing before-save flows can use Add Error to block a save with a custom validation-style message
Overlooking that deep, frequently-changing role hierarchies may genuinely need Apex-level recursive traversal
Failing to justify the tool choice against the actual complexity driver (hierarchy lookup), not the discount-percentage check, which is trivial in any of the three tools
keyPoints: A plain validation rule cannot natively evaluate the user's role hierarchy position
A before-save record-triggered flow can use Get Records plus Add Error to express this declaratively
A maintained 'Role Level' helper field is a practical way to make hierarchy comparison flow-friendly
Apex should be the fallback, justified only if hierarchy traversal complexity genuinely exceeds what a helper field and Decision element can express
The architectural decision should be driven by the specific complexity (hierarchy lookup), not the discount threshold check itself

Proposes a concrete before-save flow design using Get Records/Decision/Add Error

questions.title: Justifying Flow Automation to a Skeptical Developer
questions.prompt: A developer on your team is pushing to rebuild a moderately complex lead-routing requirement in Apex, telling leadership that Flow is 'not robust or scalable enough for real business logic' and that your flow-based proposal will just create technical debt. You believe the requirement is well within Flow's capabilities and that rebuilding it in Apex would be slower to ship and harder for the admin team to maintain. Describe how you would make your case in that conversation, including being honest about where the developer might actually have a point.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer avoids a defensive, tool-loyalty framing and instead reframes the conversation around the actual requirement's characteristics rather than abstract claims about which tool is 'better.' The candidate should describe opening by asking the developer to be specific about which part of the lead-routing logic they believe exceeds Flow's capabilities -- record volume, callout complexity, recursive/transactional subtlety, or something else -- because 'not robust enough' is frequently a holdover impression from Workflow Rules/Process Builder-era limitations that modern record-triggered flows with proper bulkification, fault handling, and governor-limit-aware design have substantially closed. If the actual requirement is bulkified correctly (collections, no DML/SOQL in loops, appropriate before-save/after-save split, explicit fault paths), Flow genuinely does scale to standard transaction volumes and is not inherently 'less robust' for logic of this complexity.

The candidate should then make the maintainability case concretely: Apex requires a developer to review, test, and deploy every future change to this routing logic, including likely business-driven tweaks (new territory, new exception rule) that are common for lead routing specifically, while a well-built flow lets the admin team iterate directly, with full audit trail and rollback via flow versioning, without a developer deployment cycle for each change. This is a genuine, quantifiable cost difference in time-to-change, not just a philosophical preference.

Critically, the candidate should concede real ground where it exists: if the routing logic genuinely needs complex external callout orchestration with retries and complex response parsing, truly intricate recursive data structures, or has to be tightly integrated with substantial existing Apex already governing Lead on this org, Apex may legitimately be the better tool for that slice of the problem, and a strong answer says so plainly rather than defending Flow as always correct. The honest position is that the right call depends on the requirement's actual shape, and the candidate's job is to evaluate it on those specific technical merits with the developer, point to the specific governor-limit and bulkification evidence for why this particular requirement fits comfortably within Flow's capabilities, and be willing to agree Apex is right if the evidence actually pointed that way.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't come into that conversation trying to defend Flow as a tool -- I'd ask the developer to get specific with me about what part of this lead-routing requirement they think Flow can't handle, because 'not robust enough' on its own isn't really an argument I can respond to. A lot of the time when I've heard that phrase, it's someone's leftover impression from Process Builder or Workflow Rules days, and modern record-triggered flows with proper bulkification and fault handling have moved a long way past that. If they can point to something concrete -- a specific callout pattern, a volume concern, a recursive edge case -- great, now we're actually evaluating the requirement instead of arguing about reputations.

Then I'd make the maintainability argument really concrete, because that's usually the strongest card I have. Lead routing rules change constantly -- new territories, new exception carve-outs, a VP who wants one specific account routed differently. If that logic lives in Apex, every one of those changes needs a developer's time, a deployment, and test coverage, even for something as small as adding one more routing exception. If it's built as a well-structured flow, our admin team can make that change directly, see exactly what changed via flow versioning, and roll back instantly if something's wrong. That's not a small difference over the life of this automation -- it's probably the single biggest cost difference between the two options.

But I'd also tell the developer flat out where I think they might actually be right, because I don't want this to come across as me just defending my own tool. If this routing logic ends up needing to call an external system with retry logic and complicated response parsing, or if it really needs to be woven tightly into existing Apex that already governs a bunch of other Lead behavior in this org, I'd say Apex is probably the better call for that piece, and I'd rather say that upfront than pretend Flow can do everything. I think that honesty is actually what gets a skeptical developer to take the rest of my argument seriously -- if I only ever say 'Flow can do it,' no matter what, I've got no credibility left for the cases where I say it clearly can.

Failing to make a concrete, quantifiable maintainability argument (who can change this logic, how fast, with what risk)
Refusing to concede any case where Apex is genuinely the better tool, undermining credibility in the rest of the argument
keyPoints: Reframes the debate around the specific requirement's technical characteristics, not abstract tool loyalty
Distinguishes legacy Process Builder/Workflow Rules limitations from modern record-triggered flow capabilities
Makes a concrete maintainability/iteration-speed argument for declarative automation

questions.title: Why a Validation Rule Didn't Catch a Workflow-Driven Update
questions.prompt: An Opportunity has a validation rule requiring Primary_Competitor__c to be populated whenever StageName equals 'Closed Won.' If a rep manually clears that field on a closed-won deal, the rule correctly blocks the save. But your team discovers dozens of closed-won Opportunities where Primary_Competitor__c is blank, and the audit trail shows an old workflow rule's field update cleared it as a side effect of recalculating a related field, with no validation error ever logged. Your director wants to know how a system field update produced the exact invalid state the validation rule exists to prevent, with zero error thrown. Walk through where a workflow field update's forced re-save falls in Salesforce's order of execution, and explain precisely why validation rules don't stop it the way they stop a manual edit.
questions.modelAnswer:
A standard save runs through a well-defined sequence: system validation, then before-save flows and before triggers, then custom validation rules, then duplicate rules, then the record commits to the database, then after triggers run, then assignment and auto-response rules, and only after all of that does Salesforce evaluate workflow rules. If a workflow rule includes a field update, Salesforce performs a second, forced DML operation on the already-committed record to apply that update. That forced re-save re-runs before/after triggers and any record-triggered flows tied to the update, but it does not re-run custom validation rules. This is documented platform behavior, not a bug, and it exists largely to avoid cascading validation loops on system-initiated updates. The practical consequence is exactly what the director is seeing: a workflow field update can push a record into a state a validation rule was written to prevent, and no error ever surfaces, because validation rules simply are not in that specific code path.

The fix is not to expect validation rules to catch this. Since the gap is structural, the correct response is to rebuild the logic so the field update itself can never produce an invalid combination. That usually means moving the recalculation off the legacy workflow rule entirely and into a before-save record-triggered flow, where the logic executes before the record commits and therefore before validation rules run against the final values, or by adding explicit guard logic inside the automation itself so it only clears or sets Primary_Competitor__c when doing so would still satisfy the rule's condition, rather than relying on a safety net that was never actually watching that update.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by walking the director through the save sequence in plain terms: think of a record save as having two separate 'checkpoints' moments, with validation rules only present at the first one. Everything that happens before the record first commits -- field updates from a before-save flow, triggers, and then the custom validation rules -- gets checked. But workflow rules only run after that commit has already happened, in a later phase, and if they include a field update, Salesforce quietly does a second save behind the scenes to apply it. That second save re-fires triggers, but it skips validation rules entirely. So the workflow rule's field update isn't breaking any rule, it's just operating in a phase where that rule was never going to see it.

Once that's clear, I'd pivot straight to the fix rather than dwelling on the explanation, because this is a known, structural gap rather than something worth arguing with Salesforce about. My move would be to retire that legacy workflow rule's field update and reimplement the same recalculation as a before-save flow, since before-save logic finishes before validation rules evaluate, which closes the gap completely instead of relying on a validation layer that was never actually in that path. I'd also flag this as a pattern to go audit for -- anywhere else in the org a workflow or process field update touches a field that a validation rule also governs is a candidate for the exact same silent gap.

Confusing before-save flow timing with the later, post-commit timing of workflow rules
Not realizing a workflow field update performs a second, separate save operation on the record
Believing validation rules are universally 'always on' regardless of what process initiated the change
Treating this as a bug to report rather than documented order-of-execution behavior to design around
keyPoints: Salesforce's save order places validation rules before the initial commit, and workflow rules after it
A workflow (or legacy process) field update triggers a forced second save pass on the record
That forced re-save does not re-run custom validation rules
This is exactly why a system-initiated update can create a state a manual edit would be blocked from creating
The fix is architectural: move the logic earlier (before-save) rather than expecting validation to catch it later

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sequences the order-of-execution steps relevant to this scenario
Identifies that workflow field updates trigger a forced re-save that skips validation rules
Explains why this allows an otherwise-blocked invalid state through
Proposes a sound remediation such as moving logic to before-save or adding guard conditions
Clarity and technical precision

questions.title: Where a Real-Time Approval Workflow Hits Flow's Ceiling
questions.prompt: Legal wants an approval submission that, the instant a contract's discount exceeds 20%, calls an external credit-risk API and uses the live response to decide whether the deal can even be submitted for approval -- if the API says 'high risk,' the submission must be blocked outright, not just flagged for a human later. A stakeholder suggests building this entirely in Flow since 'Flow can do callouts now.' Explain why a synchronous, blocking external callout tied to a record save is exactly the kind of requirement that pushes past what declarative automation can safely do, and how you would actually architect the solution.
questions.modelAnswer:
The stakeholder's assumption glosses over timing, not capability. Record-triggered flows that run before the record saves (fast field updates) cannot perform callouts at all -- callouts are disallowed in that context because the transaction hasn't committed and the platform can't leave an HTTP call hanging mid-save. Callouts are only available in after-save flow contexts, which by definition run after the record has already been committed to the database. That means an after-save flow callout can never block the save itself; by the time it runs, the save already happened, so there is no transaction left to reject based on the API's answer.

Moving the logic to an Apex trigger doesn't solve it either: Salesforce does not allow synchronous callouts from a trigger context at all, because triggers execute inside DML operations, and mixing a live synchronous HTTP callout with pending DML is blocked by the platform specifically to avoid locking resources on an external network call. So neither Flow nor an Apex trigger can synchronously block a save on a live external response -- that ceiling exists at the platform level, independent of which tool you reach for.

The actual architecture has to move the blocking decision earlier, before the record transaction even begins. That means a Screen Flow, Lightning Web Component, or Quick Action that invokes an Apex class making a synchronous callout to the credit-risk API as part of the user's submission action -- before 'Submit for Approval' is even pressed. The Apex callout result determines whether the UI even allows the submission to proceed. This keeps the business rule enforceable and real-time, but it correctly places the blocking logic outside the record save transaction, which is the only place a synchronous external decision can actually gate anything.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I've run into this exact wall before, and I'd tell the stakeholder directly: it's not that Flow can't do callouts anymore, it's that the callout has to happen in a part of the process that's too late to stop anything. If I build it as a before-save flow, the platform won't even let a callout run there. If I build it as an after-save flow, the record has already been written to the database by the time that callout fires -- there's nothing left to block. And an Apex trigger has the same problem from the other direction: Salesforce flat-out doesn't allow a synchronous callout to run inside a trigger, because you can't have DML and a live network call pending at the same time.

So my actual recommendation is to move the decision point in front of the save entirely. I'd build a Screen Flow or a Lightning component tied to the submission button itself, which calls an Apex class that does the synchronous callout to the credit-risk API right then, before anything gets written or submitted for approval. If the API comes back 'high risk,' the screen simply doesn't let the user proceed to Submit for Approval. That gives Legal exactly the real-time blocking behavior they want, it just lives in the submission UI instead of inside the record-save mechanics, which is the only place in the platform where a synchronous external answer can actually stop something from happening.

questions.title: Building a Parallel Finance-and-Legal Quote Approval
questions.prompt: Walk through, step by step, how you would configure a Salesforce approval process so that when a Quote's discount exceeds 25%, it requires both the Finance approver and the Legal approver to sign off independently and in parallel, not one after the other. The deal is only approved once both approve, a rejection from either one immediately rejects the whole request, and the original submitter must be able to recall the request at any point while it's pending. What specific configuration choices actually produce that parallel, unanimous behavior?
questions.modelAnswer:
The entry criteria would be Discount__c greater than 25 on Quote. Initial submission actions would lock the record and set Approval_Status__c to 'Pending' so the record can't be edited mid-review. The parallel behavior comes from a single approval step, not two sequential steps: that one step is assigned to both the Finance approver and the Legal approver together, with the step's response behavior set to 'Require unanimous approval from all selected approvers' rather than 'first response.' With unanimous selected, Salesforce sends both approval requests out simultaneously, and the step only resolves as approved once both responses come back Approve; a single Reject from either approver resolves the step as rejected immediately, without needing to wait for the other approver's response.

Final approval actions unlock the record and set Approval_Status__c to 'Approved.' Final rejection actions unlock the record, set Approval_Status__c to 'Rejected,' and notify the submitter. To support recall, the process settings must explicitly enable 'Allow submitters to recall approval requests,' which surfaces a Recall button to the submitter while the request is pending; recall needs to run the same unlocking logic as the initial submission actions' reverse, and it's worth testing explicitly, since fields set by any individual approver's step-level action do not automatically revert on recall or rejection unless the rejection/recall actions are built to reset them. Testing should cover both response orderings -- Legal approves then Finance rejects, and the reverse -- since a unanimous step can resolve on the first rejection before the second approver ever responds.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start simple: entry criteria on discount percentage, then one approval step, not two, with both Finance and Legal added as approvers to that same step. The detail that actually makes it 'parallel' is the response behavior setting on that step -- I'd set it to require unanimous approval from all assigned approvers, which is what makes both requests go out at the same time instead of Finance approving and then it moving on to Legal next. I've seen admins build 'parallel' approvals wrong by creating two sequential steps instead, which just looks parallel on a diagram but actually routes to Finance first, then Legal second, which isn't what was asked for here.

For the rest, I'd lock the record on submission so nobody can quietly edit the discount while it's under review, and build out final approval and final rejection actions to set the status field and unlock the record appropriately. I'd turn on recall in the process settings so the submitter isn't stuck waiting, and then I'd specifically test what happens to any field a step action set if the record gets recalled or rejected after only one approver responded -- that's the part I'd never assume works automatically, because step actions fire independently of the step's eventual overall outcome.
questions.example: Submitting a Quote at 30% discount sends simultaneous approval requests to both the Finance queue and the Legal approver; if Legal approves first and Finance rejects two days later, the step resolves as rejected, and the final rejection actions -- not Legal's earlier response -- determine the record's final state.

Not selecting unanimous approval response, so the first response resolves the whole step incorrectly
Forgetting to lock the record during the pending approval, allowing edits mid-review
Not configuring recall availability, leaving submitters unable to withdraw a mistaken submission
Assuming rejection or approval step actions automatically revert on recall without explicit configuration

Unanimous response behavior vs first-response behavior changes how the step resolves
Record locking during pending approval protects data integrity
Recall must be explicitly enabled, and its effect on earlier step actions should be tested, not assumed
Both approval orderings should be tested since a unanimous step can resolve on the first rejection

questions.title: Designing a Validation Rule That Still Lets the Nightly Integration Through
questions.prompt: You need a validation rule on Contact requiring Phone or Email whenever the related Account's Industry is 'Healthcare' -- but a nightly middleware job running as an Integration User creates and updates thousands of Healthcare contacts in bulk from a system that doesn't always carry phone or email at creation, with those records legitimately getting enriched later. Describe specifically how you'd write this rule so it enforces fully in the UI but doesn't break the nightly integration, including the exact bypass mechanism you'd use and why you wouldn't just hard-code a check against the Integration User's profile.
questions.modelAnswer:
The core formula needs a cross-object reference to the parent Account's Industry field, something like AND(ISPICKVAL(Account.Industry, 'Healthcare'), ISBLANK(Phone), ISBLANK(Email)), which correctly targets the business condition regardless of who or what is saving the record. The bypass should not be a hard-coded $User.Profile or $User.Username check wrapped around that logic. Those checks are brittle: a profile gets renamed or consolidated during a later reorg, a sandbox refresh changes a username, or a second integration needs the identical bypass under a different user, and in every case the rule's formula has to be edited and redeployed just to keep working. The correct mechanism is a custom permission -- create one, assign it through a dedicated permission set to the integration user, and wrap the rule with NOT($Permission.Bypass_Contact_Validation) so the full formula reads AND(NOT($Permission.Bypass_Contact_Validation), ISPICKVAL(Account.Industry, 'Healthcare'), ISBLANK(Phone), ISBLANK(Email)).

A custom permission is metadata, not a data record or a profile name string, so it's discoverable directly in Setup, reusable across any number of rules that need the same bypass, and extensible to future integration users by simply adding them to the permission set -- no formula change required. This also keeps the bypass scoped precisely to this one validation concern rather than exempting the integration user's entire profile from anything else that profile might otherwise be subject to.
questions.professionalAnswer:
In my last org we had almost this exact situation with a middleware job loading partner contacts overnight. What I built was a custom permission called something like Bypass_Validation_Rules, put it on a dedicated permission set named for the integration, and assigned that permission set only to the integration user -- never touched their profile directly. Then every validation rule that needed to respect that bypass got the same pattern wrapped around its real business logic: check the permission first, and only evaluate the actual Healthcare/Phone/Email condition if the permission isn't present.

The reason I wouldn't hard-code a profile or username check is pretty practical -- those break in ways that are hard to notice, like a profile getting renamed during a license cleanup, and nobody remembers to go find every validation rule formula that silently referenced the old name. A custom permission sitting on its own permission set is visible in Setup, it's the same mechanism every time, and if a second system ever needs this exact bypass, I just add a user to the permission set instead of editing a formula. The one thing I'd flag as a real governance risk: that permission is powerful since it fully disables the rule for anyone who holds it, so I'd keep a short list of exactly which rules it touches and periodically check who's been granted it.

questions.title: Tracking Down an Infinite Flow Loop on Case Status Updates
questions.prompt: Support agents report that certain Case saves take ten or more seconds and occasionally throw a CPU time limit exceeded error. You find two separate record-triggered flows on Case: one sets Status to 'Escalated' whenever Priority changes to 'Critical,' and another sets Priority to 'Critical' whenever Status is 'Escalated' and the case is unassigned. Both are active and both run on create and update. Diagnose what's happening and describe exactly how you'd confirm it and fix it without simply disabling one of the flows outright.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is a classic cross-automation collision: Flow A reacts to Priority becoming Critical by setting Status to Escalated, and Flow B reacts to Status being Escalated on an unassigned case by setting Priority to Critical. If either flow's entry criteria only checks the current value of the field it's reacting to -- rather than specifically checking that the field just transitioned into that value -- the two flows can keep re-firing each other's updates within the same transaction until the platform's own recursion and governor limits step in, which is exactly why the symptom shows up as a CPU time limit error rather than a true infinite loop.

To confirm it, check Setup > Process Automation > Flow error history and debug logs for the affected records, looking specifically for repeated flow interview entries chained together within a single transaction, and reproduce it in a sandbox by manually toggling Priority on a test case. The fix is not to disable either flow, since both represent real business logic; it's to make each flow's entry criteria fire only on an actual transition rather than on any save where the condition happens to already be true. Record-triggered flow supports an entry condition option that evaluates against the record's prior values specifically for this purpose -- Flow A should require that Priority's prior value was not Critical, and Flow B should require that Status's prior value was not Escalated. That change lets each flow fire exactly once per real transition instead of re-triggering every time the other flow's update happens to still satisfy a current-value-only condition. Longer term, having two separate flows independently manage the same pair of fields on one object is itself worth revisiting -- consolidating this logic into a single flow with explicit decision branches removes the collision risk at its source rather than just guarding against it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
First thing I'd do is pull the Flow error history and debug logs for a few of the slow records, specifically looking for multiple flow interview entries firing back to back on the same transaction -- that pattern is the tell. I'd also just reproduce it myself in a sandbox by flipping Priority to Critical on a test case and watching what happens, rather than theorizing from the flow definitions alone.

Once I've confirmed the two flows are actually re-triggering each other, I wouldn't touch either one's core logic -- I'd fix the entry criteria. Record-triggered flow has a built-in option to only run when a record is updated to meet condition requirements, which under the hood compares against the record's prior value rather than just its current one, so I'd use that option on both flows instead of writing my own prior-value formula from scratch. That stops each flow from re-firing just because the other flow's update happened to leave the condition still true. Longer term, I'd flag to the team that having two flows independently manage Status and Priority on the same object is the real root cause here, and recommend merging them into one flow for Case so there's a single, sequenced place these two fields get resolved instead of two automations racing each other every time either field changes.

Consolidating same-object flows reduces collision risk going forward

questions.title: Diagnosing Inconsistent Data After a Parallel Approval Rejection
questions.prompt: Your unanimous, two-approver parallel approval step on Quote has Legal approve first, which fires a step-level action setting Legal_Reviewed__c to true. Finance then rejects, which correctly sets the Quote's overall Approval_Status__c to 'Rejected' through the final rejection actions. But Legal_Reviewed__c is still true on the rejected Quote, and a report built on that field is now showing rejected quotes as legally reviewed. Explain why this happened and how you'd fix both the immediate data and the process design.
questions.modelAnswer:
Approval step-level actions execute the moment that individual approver responds, independently of whatever the step's overall outcome eventually turns out to be. Legal's response fired its 'approve' step action and set Legal_Reviewed__c immediately -- that action already ran and completed before Finance ever responded. Final approval actions and final rejection actions only run once, when the process reaches its terminal state, and they do not automatically undo field changes that individual step actions already made along the way. So when Finance's rejection resolved the unanimous step as rejected overall, the final rejection actions correctly set Approval_Status__c to Rejected, but nothing in that rejection logic was built to also reset Legal_Reviewed__c, so it simply stayed true.

The immediate fix needs two parts. First, a data remediation -- a bulk update identifying every currently rejected Quote where a step-level action field like Legal_Reviewed__c is still set to true, resetting it to reflect reality. Second, and more importantly, a process design fix: the final rejection actions, and the recall action for completeness, need to explicitly reset every field that any step-level action in the process could have set, since nothing resets automatically. That also means auditing every other step action across the full approval process for the same gap, since this is almost certainly not the only field affected, and deciding whether Legal_Reviewed__c should even be set at the step level at all versus being set only once, in final approval actions, when the outcome is actually known.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I've been bitten by this exact thing before, and the mental model that fixed it for me is: each approver's response is basically its own little automation that fires immediately, and the only thing that 'wraps up' the whole process is whatever you explicitly built into the final approval and final rejection actions -- nothing rolls back on its own. So Legal approving set that field the moment they clicked approve, completely independent of what Finance was going to do three days later.

My actual fix would start with building a quick matrix across the whole approval process: every field any step action touches, and whether there's a matching reset for that field in the final rejection actions and in the recall action. Anywhere that matrix has a gap is a latent version of this exact bug waiting to surface on a different field. Then I'd run the data cleanup on currently affected Quotes, but I'd treat that as the smaller half of the fix -- the real fix is adding the missing resets so rejection handling gets the same deliberate design attention as approval handling, since right now it clearly didn't.

Not building explicit field resets into final rejection and recall actions
Treating approval step actions and final actions as equivalent in scope and timing
Fixing only the report or the bad data instead of the underlying process gap
Not auditing other step actions across the process for the same unresolved-reset risk after finding one instance

A unanimous step's rejection does not automatically undo actions already taken by other approvers

questions.title: Nightly Integration Suddenly Failing on a Validation Rule It Never Should Hit
questions.prompt: A validation rule on Case requires Root_Cause__c to be populated before Status can be set to 'Closed,' intended only for the manually-handled 'Enterprise Support' record type. Overnight, your integration user's bulk API job closing thousands of 'Self-Service' record type cases starts failing on that exact validation error, even though nobody touched the rule recently. Walk through how you'd investigate this, what you suspect happened, and how you'd fix the rule correctly rather than just exempting the integration user.
questions.modelAnswer:
The investigation should start by not taking 'nobody touched the rule' at face value -- check the Setup Audit Trail and the field's history for recent changes to the validation rule, any record type, or any page layout assignment, since even an unrelated record type consolidation elsewhere in the org can shift which cases now match a rule's criteria. In parallel, pull a handful of the actual failing Case IDs from the integration's error log and try to reproduce the failure by opening one directly in the UI and attempting the same save manually, confirming it really is this validation rule and not a different error with a similar message.

The most likely root cause is that the rule's formula never actually constrained by RecordType.DeveloperName in the first place -- a very common authoring mistake is naming or labeling a rule as scoped to 'Enterprise Support' while writing the formula as something like AND(ISPICKVAL(Status,'Closed'), ISBLANK(Root_Cause__c)), with no record type condition at all. In that case, the rule was always capable of blocking Self-Service cases too; it just happened not to, until some other change (a record type reassignment, a new automation path, or simply the integration starting to close cases it hadn't closed in bulk before) caused Self-Service cases to actually hit the closing condition at scale for the first time. The correct fix is adding the missing guard directly into the rule's formula, such as AND($RecordType.DeveloperName = 'Enterprise_Support', ISPICKVAL(Status,'Closed'), ISBLANK(Root_Cause__c)), not exempting the integration user, because the defect is in the rule's scope and would eventually affect manually-created Self-Service cases through the UI as well.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move would be practical, not theoretical: pull two or three of the actual failing record IDs out of the integration's error payload, open them directly in Salesforce, and try to reproduce the exact same save by hand. That confirms it's genuinely this validation rule and not, say, an API version mismatch or a different error that happens to look similar in a log.

Then I'd open the rule itself and read the formula literally, specifically looking for whether record type is actually part of the condition -- in my experience, 'it's scoped to one record type' almost always turns out to mean someone just named the rule that way without the formula actually constraining on RecordType.DeveloperName. I'd also check the Setup Audit Trail, because 'nobody touched it' is usually someone's assumption rather than a confirmed fact, and something nearby -- a record type merge, a new automation, a changed default record type -- is a much more likely trigger than the rule spontaneously starting to misbehave. Whatever I find, I would not just add the integration user to a bypass permission for this one, because that papers over a real logic defect that would eventually hit manually-created Self-Service cases through the UI too, just less visibly than a bulk overnight failure.

questions.title: Commission Field Calculating Off the Wrong Amount
questions.prompt: A legacy workflow rule recalculates Commission__c on Opportunity using Amount whenever Amount changes. A newer record-triggered flow applies a volume discount, reducing Amount, whenever Discount_Tier__c changes. Reps complain that Commission__c is being calculated on the pre-discount Amount, not the final discounted number, even though both automations fire on the same save. Diagnose why this is happening based on execution order, and describe how you'd fix it.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first thing to determine is whether the discount flow runs before-save or after-save, because that single fact explains the whole bug. Before-save automations finish before the record ever commits, so any field they change is part of the values validation rules and workflow rules ultimately see. After-save automations act on a record that has already been committed, and any field update they make triggers a separate, later DML pass. If the discount flow is an after-save flow, then on the initial save the record commits with its original, pre-discount Amount; the legacy workflow rule evaluates against that committed state and calculates Commission__c correctly against the number it saw, which is the wrong, pre-discount number. The after-save flow's later update to Amount happens in a subsequent pass that the already-completed workflow evaluation never revisits, unless the workflow rule's own criteria and evaluation setting ('created, and every time it's edited' versus a stricter transition-only criteria) happen to cause it to re-fire on that second update -- and in many orgs it won't, especially with stricter evaluation criteria options.

The fix is to stop the two calculations from racing across different phases of the save. The cleanest correction is converting the discount logic to a before-save flow so Amount is finalized before the record first commits, meaning the committed value workflow rules evaluate against is already correct. Longer term, the legacy workflow rule should be retired and Commission__c recalculated inside the same flow, sequenced explicitly after the discount decision, so there is exactly one automation making both decisions in the right order instead of two automations in different execution phases that can only coincidentally end up consistent.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd check is the discount flow's trigger type in Setup -- before-save or after-save -- because that's almost always where this exact symptom comes from. If it's after-save, the record already committed with the original Amount by the time that flow even runs, which means the legacy workflow rule evaluated Commission against the wrong number before the discount was ever applied. I'd also check the workflow rule's evaluation criteria, since 'created, and every time it's edited to subsequently meet criteria' behaves differently from the broader 'any time it's edited' option, and that difference affects whether the workflow even re-fires once the flow's later update happens.

In terms of the actual fix, my default move is to get rid of the legacy workflow rule entirely rather than try to patch the timing around it. I'd rebuild the discount logic as a before-save flow so Amount is correct before the record first commits, and move the commission calculation into that same flow, sequenced right after the discount decision, so one automation handles both in the right order. In my experience two separate automations racing across different save phases is never something you want to keep tuning around -- it's much more reliable to consolidate them so there's only one place making the decision.

questions.title: Architecting a Multi-Object Renewal Process: Flow, Approval, or Apex
questions.prompt: You're designing automation for a contract renewal process spanning Opportunity, Contract, Quote, and a related Asset object. It includes multiple conditional approval paths, needs to recalculate pricing from usage data pulled from an external billing system, and must scale to thousands of renewals processed in nightly batches without hitting governor limits. Walk through how you'd decide which parts belong in Flow, which belong in an approval process, and which genuinely need Apex, and how those pieces fit together architecturally.
questions.modelAnswer:
The decision should be made per component rather than as one all-or-nothing choice, starting declarative-first for maintainability but moving to Apex at specific, identifiable ceilings. Nightly batch volume at thousands of records is the first ceiling: Batch Apex gives explicit control over scope size, checkpointing, and retry behavior in a way that processing the same volume through Flow interviews does not, so the nightly orchestration layer belongs in Apex. The external billing system usage pull is the second ceiling: a dedicated Apex service class with proper pagination, retry, and error handling is considerably more robust than Flow's native HTTP callout action, which lacks that level of control. Human sign-off, by contrast, is exactly what native approval processes already solve well, with built-in approval history, email actions, and mobile approve or reject support that would be expensive to rebuild from scratch, so the review step itself stays a standard approval process.

The remaining piece -- conditional record creation and field population across Opportunity, Contract, Quote, and Asset -- is where business rules live that change often and should stay inspectable and editable by admins, which argues for Flow. The way these fit together architecturally is a thin Apex orchestration and integration layer (Batch Apex driving the nightly run, calling the billing API through its own service class) that invokes an autolaunched Flow per record for the actual conditional business logic, with the human-review portion handled by a standard approval process triggered from within that same flow. This pattern -- Apex for scale and integration, Flow for business rules, approval process for human sign-off -- avoids both a brittle 'everything in Flow' build that won't survive the batch volume, and an opaque 'big ball of Apex' build that admins can't maintain going forward.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd actually run this as a short project rather than deciding it alone at a desk. First step is whiteboarding the process end to end with the business and marking each piece as one of three things: needs human judgment, which goes to a native approval process; needs conditional record logic that's likely to change as the business changes its mind, which goes to Flow; or needs raw scale or external integration with real error handling, which goes to Apex. In this case the nightly batch volume and the billing system callouts both land clearly in the Apex bucket for me -- I've tried pushing that kind of volume and retry logic through Flow before and it gets fragile fast, especially the retry and backoff behavior Flow's native HTTP action just doesn't give you.

Concretely, I'd build a Batch Apex class as the nightly orchestrator, with its own service class handling the billing system callouts, and have that batch call an invocable Flow for each record to apply the actual business rules -- discount tiers, which fields update, which path a given renewal takes -- since that's the part that's going to keep changing and I want the team to be able to edit it without a deployment. The approval step itself stays a standard approval process invoked from inside that flow. I'd present this mixed architecture to the team explicitly up front, specifically calling out which parts are safely admin-editable and which parts require a developer, so nobody's caught off guard later that 'an admin automation project' quietly includes real code.
