questions.title: Scaling One Approval Process Across Five Business Units Without Forking It
questions.prompt: Your company has five business units, each with its own discount approval thresholds and its own approver hierarchy -- some route to a Regional Manager, some route to both a Regional Manager and Finance in parallel. Leadership wants one consistent approval experience, but a junior admin's instinct is to clone the approval process five times, once per business unit, and hand-maintain each copy. Explain the architectural problems with that approach as the company adds more business units, and describe how you'd design this to scale.
questions.modelAnswer:
Cloning the approval process five times turns every future policy change into five separate edits that have to be applied identically, and in practice at least one clone eventually drifts because the change gets missed on it, often not discovered until an audit or a complaint surfaces the inconsistency. Admins reach for cloning specifically because native approval processes resolve approvers through fairly rigid mechanisms -- specific users, queues, or a record's related-user lookup field -- with no native way to branch that lookup by a business unit value within a single process, so cloning feels like the only way to vary the approver per business unit.

The architectural fix is to externalize the variable logic -- thresholds and approver hierarchy -- into data rather than into structure. A custom metadata type keyed by Business_Unit__c can hold each unit's threshold and whether Finance review is required in parallel. A before-save flow run at submission time looks up the record's business unit against that metadata and writes the resolved approver into a relationship field on the record (for example Routing_Approver__c) along with a boolean such as Requires_Finance_Review__c. A single approval process then points its approver step at that relationship field using the standard dynamic 'related user' option, and its entry criteria or step branching reads the Requires_Finance_Review__c flag to decide whether the parallel Finance step applies. From the approval process's perspective it behaves identically every time; all of the business-unit-specific intelligence lives in the custom metadata and the flow, which means adding a sixth business unit is a metadata record and a flow update, not a sixth cloned process.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd flag to leadership isn't really technical, it's a maintenance-debt argument: every future policy change now has to be applied five times, and I'd ask them point blank what happens the first time someone updates four of the five clones and forgets the fifth, because that's not hypothetical, that's the default outcome of cloning. I'd also be honest that the junior admin's instinct makes sense given how Salesforce approval processes resolve approvers -- there's no native way to say 'look up the approver differently depending on business unit' inside one process, so cloning feels like the obvious workaround.

What I'd actually build is a before-save flow that runs right at submission and resolves 'who's the approver for this business unit at this threshold' into a couple of hidden fields on the record, driven by a custom metadata type that holds each business unit's threshold and approver logic. The one approval process just reads those resolved fields, so from its perspective every submission looks the same regardless of business unit. The real benefit is who can maintain it afterward -- adding a sixth business unit, or changing unit three's threshold, becomes a metadata record update that a business analyst could even do themselves, instead of a Salesforce release touching a cloned approval process.
questions.example: Adding a sixth business unit under this design means creating one new custom metadata record with its threshold and approver settings; under the cloned-process design it would mean building and testing an entire sixth approval process from scratch.
commonMistakes: Cloning the approval process per business unit instead of externalizing the variable logic into data
Not recognizing that policy changes must now be replicated across every clone, creating drift risk
Hard-coding specific users as approvers instead of resolving a dynamic approver field at submission time
Assuming Salesforce approval processes can natively branch routing by a field like business unit without a routing layer
Underestimating the documentation burden a data-driven routing layer introduces for future admins
keyPoints: Cloned approval processes multiply maintenance cost with every future policy change
Custom metadata can externalize threshold and approver logic per business unit
A before-save flow can resolve the correct dynamic approver into a field the approval process reads
One approval process reading computed fields scales better than structurally duplicated processes
The trade-off is added indirection that must be documented for future maintainers

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Clearly explains the maintenance-drift problem with cloning
Proposes a concrete data-driven routing architecture combining metadata, flow, and a single process
Explains how dynamic approver resolution actually works mechanically
Acknowledges trade-offs and documentation needs
Clarity

questions.title: Untangling 15 Years of Overlapping Automation on One Object
questions.prompt: You inherit an org where the Opportunity object has six workflow rules, four Process Builder processes, and nine flows, all active, built by different admins over 15 years, with no documentation and visible symptoms of recursion and inconsistent field states. Leadership wants this stabilized without a 'big bang' rewrite that risks breaking live deals. Describe your architecture and governance plan for bringing this under control.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first phase has to be a full inventory before anything is touched: export every automation on Opportunity and document its trigger type, entry criteria, field updates or actions, and apparent purpose in one place, since 15 years of undocumented sprawl almost always includes automations nobody realizes are dead or redundant once they're actually read side by side. The second phase classifies each entry by risk, specifically flagging any two automations writing to the same field on the same object, since that overlap is the highest-probability source of the recursion and inconsistent-state symptoms already being observed.

The third phase stabilizes before consolidating anything structurally: add monitoring through Flow error emails and debug log review, and where a collision risk is clearly identified, add a recursion guard such as a prior-value entry condition without removing any functionality, specifically to stop active bleeding without yet touching the broader architecture. The fourth phase migrates incrementally rather than all at once -- since both Process Builder and workflow rules are being retired by Salesforce in favor of Flow, the long-term target architecture consolidates toward a bounded number of flows per object per trigger context, but each legacy automation should move one at a time, in a sandbox, with before-and-after regression testing against real sampled records, never as a single bulk migration against a business-critical object. The final phase establishes governance going forward: a lightweight design review or change-log entry required before any new automation is added to a heavily-automated object, and a standing, kept-current inventory, so the same undocumented sprawl doesn't simply regrow over the next 15 years.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is never to touch anything -- it's to go get a full inventory, because I'd bet real money that some of those nineteen automations are dead weight nobody remembers the purpose of anymore. I'd set that expectation with leadership directly too: this is a quarter of disciplined work, not a sprint, if the goal is genuinely to do it without breaking live deals, and I'd rather say that up front than discover it halfway through.

Once the inventory's done, I'd add safety nets before touching anything structurally -- recursion guards and error monitoring on the clearest same-field collision risks I found, just to stop the bleeding. Then I'd sequence the actual migration starting with the safest, clearest wins first, like a Process Builder process nobody can explain the purpose of that turns out on inspection to be dead, because knocking those out first builds trust and gives the team a tested regression process before tackling the riskiest, most tangled pieces last. The last piece I'd push hard on is governance going forward -- nothing new gets added to this object's automation without an entry in the inventory and a sign-off, because undocumented sprawl with no review process is exactly how we ended up with nineteen overlapping automations in the first place.
commonMistakes: Attempting a full rewrite or big-bang migration on a live, business-critical object
Deleting or disabling automations without first confirming via inventory whether they're actually in use
Migrating Process Builder or workflow rules to Flow without regression-testing against real sampled records
Fixing recursion symptoms without first producing a full inventory, missing other collision risks
Not establishing forward-looking governance, allowing the same sprawl to recur
keyPoints: Full inventory and documentation must come before any structural change
Same-field, same-object write overlaps are the highest-risk candidates to flag first
Safety nets such as recursion guards and monitoring should stabilize risk before consolidation begins
Migration should be incremental and regression-tested, consolidating toward fewer flows per object and context
Forward governance such as a change log or design review prevents the sprawl from recurring

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes inventory and documentation as the necessary first step
Correctly identifies and prioritizes same-field or same-object collision risks
Describes a safe, incremental migration and consolidation approach
Proposes concrete forward-looking governance
Clarity and realism of the plan

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Admin Through a Validation Rule Blocking the Data Load
questions.prompt: A junior admin on your team built a validation rule on Lead a few weeks ago, and it's now blocking a legitimate monthly data load of partner leads from an external list broker, failing the whole batch. The junior admin is defensive, insists their rule logic is correct, and doesn't understand why 'a rule that obviously works for normal lead creation' is suddenly a problem. Walk through how you'd handle this conversation and the technical teaching moment, not just the fix itself.
questions.modelAnswer:
Before the conversation happens, the issue should be verified technically -- reproduce the failure and read the exact rule formula against a couple of the actual failing records -- so the mentoring moment is grounded in specifics rather than becoming a debate about assertions. In the conversation itself, the better opening is curiosity rather than correction: ask the junior admin to walk through the case they designed the rule for, which usually surfaces that they built and tested it only against manual, UI-driven lead creation and never considered bulk or API-created records, a very common blind spot for someone newer to the platform. Using one of the actual failing partner leads as the teaching artifact, walking the rule's formula against that record's real field values, lets the gap become self-evident rather than something the senior admin simply asserts is true.

The underlying concept to teach explicitly is that validation rules apply uniformly across every save path -- UI, Data Loader, API, integration -- unless the formula itself accounts for that, and that bulk-sourced records often legitimately lack fields a manually-entered record would always have. The fix itself should be co-designed rather than handed down: deciding together whether the right answer is a bypass permission for the integration path, a loosened criteria, or a Lead Source-based exclusion, and having the junior admin implement it with review, so they leave having updated their own mental model rather than just watching someone else patch their mistake. Closing by normalizing the mistake while being explicit about the new standard -- any new validation rule gets considered against all three creation paths before it ships -- turns a single incident into a durable team practice.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't open with 'your rule is wrong,' because that just gets someone more defensive -- I'd open with 'let's look at what actually happened on these specific records.' I'd pull two or three of the actual failed partner leads, sit down with the junior admin, and read the rule's formula line by line against those specific field values, letting them spot the gap themselves wherever possible rather than me pointing it out first.

I'd also tell them upfront that I've shipped the exact same kind of rule before without thinking about Data Loader or API-created records, because that framing makes it a universal admin lesson rather than something that singles them out, and it tends to lower the defensiveness fast. For the actual resolution, I'd lay out two or three real options -- a bypass permission for the integration path, a criteria change, or excluding based on Lead Source -- and let the junior admin pick one and implement it with my review, because the whole point of the mentoring is that they can catch this category of bug on their own next time, not that I quietly fixed it while they watched.
commonMistakes: Fixing the rule yourself without involving the junior admin in diagnosing it
Leading the conversation with blame or 'your logic is wrong' instead of grounding it in specific failing records
Not generalizing the lesson about UI versus API versus integration save paths beyond this one rule
Assuming the junior admin already knows validation rules apply uniformly across all save paths
Treating this as a one-time fix rather than an update to the team's rule-review and testing standard going forward
keyPoints: Verify and reproduce the technical issue with real failing records before the conversation
Lead with questions about design intent rather than immediate correction
Teach that validation rules apply to every save path unless explicitly scoped
Use the junior admin's own failing records as the teaching artifact rather than abstract explanation
Co-design and have the junior admin implement the fix so the learning sticks

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a grounded, specific diagnostic approach before the conversation
Demonstrates a non-defensive, curiosity-led mentoring approach
Correctly teaches the underlying concept of validation rules applying across all save paths
Involves the junior admin in designing and implementing the fix
Communication and empathy

questions.title: Scoping Down a Vague 'Automate the Whole Renewal Process' Request
questions.prompt: A VP of Sales emails you: 'We need you to automate our entire renewal process -- reminders, approvals, pricing, everything -- and we need it live in a week for next quarter.' There's no written requirements, the VP is only available for a 30-minute call, and 'everything' clearly isn't buildable or testable safely in a week. Walk through exactly how you'd handle that first conversation and get to a scope you can actually commit to, without damaging the relationship or just saying no.
questions.modelAnswer:
The limited 30-minute call should be used deliberately for triage, not for attempting full requirements gathering. The right questions are aimed at separating what's actually painful today from the broad word 'everything' -- something like 'walk me through what happens today when a contract is 60 days from renewal, what's the very first manual step someone does, and where does it usually go wrong or get missed.' This kind of question typically surfaces the single highest-value, narrowest slice, often something as specific as renewal reminders not going out reliably, or nobody knowing which renewals need manager approval before a rep can reprice.

Before the call ends, a proposed phase-one scope should be reflected back in plain business language rather than technical terms -- for example, committing to automatic reminders at 90, 60, and 30 days before renewal routed to the right rep, plus a simple approval step for any renewal with more than a 10% price change, framed as addressing the biggest pain point the VP just described, with full pricing and quote automation explicitly named as a larger build needing two to three additional weeks done properly. A written follow-up sent immediately after the call should restate that scope, explicitly list what's out of scope for week one, and give a rough timeline for the rest, so there's a documented agreement rather than a verbal impression that can drift. The pushback on the full one-week scope should be framed as a risk trade-off rather than a flat refusal -- rushing an untested approval or pricing automation at renewal time risks real revenue, so shipping the highest-impact piece solid in week one and layering in the rest protects the business outcome the VP actually cares about.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Honestly my first instinct with a request like this is to resist the urge to just say yes to be agreeable, because a rushed 'everything' build is the thing most likely to actually hurt renewals. On the call, I'd open by acknowledging the urgency is real, then ask two or three sharp questions to find the one thing that's actually costing them money or deals today -- in a case like this it often turns out to be something narrow, like nobody tracking renewal dates reliably and reps finding out too late to act.

I'd propose a phased plan live on the call rather than leaving the VP with a vague 'I'll look into it,' and I'd send a short written recap the same day, because verbal scope agreements with an executive evaporate fast -- I've been burned before by someone remembering a conversation differently a month later. I'd close the conversation by framing the whole thing around wanting this to actually work when it matters, which is why I'm not going to pretend 'everything' fits cleanly in a week -- in my experience that framing lands much better with executives than either hedging around the ask or over-promising just to avoid an uncomfortable moment.
commonMistakes: Trying to gather full detailed requirements in a single 30-minute call instead of triaging for the highest-value slice
Saying yes to the full one-week scope to avoid conflict, setting up a guaranteed failure
Giving a flat 'no' or 'that's not possible' without offering a concrete alternative scope
Not following up in writing, leaving scope as a verbal impression that can drift or be disputed later
Scoping based on what's technically easiest to build rather than what's actually most painful for the business today
keyPoints: Use limited stakeholder time to triage for the highest-impact narrow slice, not full requirements gathering
Ask specific process questions that surface where the real pain is today
Propose a concrete phased scope in plain business language before the call ends
Document the agreed scope and explicit out-of-scope items in writing immediately after
Frame scope limits around protecting the business outcome, not around admin workload or technical difficulty

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Demonstrates a concrete triage approach for a time-limited stakeholder conversation
Proposes a realistic phased scope rather than a flat yes or no
Addresses written follow-up and documentation of the agreed scope
Frames the negotiation around business risk and outcome while preserving the relationship
Communication clarity

questions.title: How OWDs, Role Hierarchy, and Sharing Rules Stack Together
questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: 'Walk me through, in order, how Salesforce actually determines whether a specific user can see a specific Account record, when org-wide defaults are Private, there's a role hierarchy, two sharing rules, and a manual share all potentially in play.' Explain the evaluation logic, using a concrete example of a user who ends up with access through more than one mechanism at once.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by establishing that organization-wide defaults set the floor, not the ceiling: Private OWD means nobody sees a record by default except the owner, and every other mechanism in play only ever adds access on top of that floor. From there, the candidate should describe each layer as additive: the record owner has access, then anyone above the owner in the role hierarchy inherits that access automatically (assuming the object isn't configured to skip hierarchy-based access), then any active owner-based or criteria-based sharing rule that matches the record extends access to whatever role, public group, or territory it targets, and finally manual shares or teams add one-off grants on top of all of that. The critical point is that Salesforce never evaluates these layers as competing or overriding one another — a user's final access to a record is the union of every grant that applies to them, and the system takes the most permissive level found across all of those grants.

A concrete example makes this click: imagine Account OWD is Private, a rep named Dana owns the account, and Dana's regional manager automatically has Read/Write access purely through the role hierarchy. Separately, a criteria-based sharing rule grants the 'National Accounts' public group Read-only access to any account tagged with a specific industry code, and Dana's manager happens to also be a member of that public group. The manager therefore ends up with access through two independent mechanisms — hierarchy and the sharing rule — but the final access level is simply Read/Write, because hierarchy already granted the higher level and the sharing rule's lower-level grant does nothing to reduce it. A candidate should be able to state plainly that no mechanism in this stack can ever take access away that another mechanism already granted.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk through it the way I actually troubleshoot it, as a checklist in my head. First question: what's the OWD floor — here it's Private, so nothing is visible by default except to the owner. Second: who owns the record, because ownership is always the first real grant. Third: I climb the role hierarchy from the owner upward, since anyone above the owner's role picks up whatever access level the hierarchy setting allows. Fourth: I check active sharing rules — both owner-based ones tied to a role or group, and criteria-based ones tied to field values — because any rule that matches this record extends access to its target group. Fifth: I check for manual shares or team membership, since those are one-off grants layered on everything else.

The part I always emphasize to someone newer is that this is strictly an 'OR,' never an 'AND' — none of these layers can cancel out another. So if I take a loan officer who's a member of a public group targeted by a sharing rule, and that same loan officer's manager also happens to sit above them in the role hierarchy, the manager isn't weighing two conflicting rules — they just end up with whichever access level is higher across both grants. I've actually seen admins get confused troubleshooting a 'why can this person see too much' ticket because they only looked at the sharing rule and missed that the person was also getting access through the hierarchy, or vice versa — you really have to check every layer, because the answer is always the max of all of them, not the last rule evaluated.
questions.example: Account OWD Private; Dana owns the account and has full access; Dana's manager gets Read/Write automatically via role hierarchy; a separate criteria-based rule grants the 'National Accounts' group Read-only on that same account, and Dana's manager also belongs to that group — the manager's final access stays Read/Write, the higher of the two grants, not a downgrade or a conflict.
commonMistakes: Assuming a sharing rule can restrict access tighter than the org-wide default
Thinking role hierarchy grants access downward to subordinates instead of upward to superiors
Believing a manual share and an active sharing rule conflict when both apply to the same user
Treating sharing evaluation as sequential/first-match instead of additive across every applicable grant
Forgetting that View All Data or object-level View All bypasses this whole stack entirely
keyPoints: OWD establishes the baseline/floor access for every record of that object
Record ownership plus role hierarchy climb grants visibility upward automatically
Sharing rules are additive, never reduce access, and can be owner-based or criteria-based
Manual sharing and teams add further one-off or team-based grants on top
Final access equals the most permissive level found across every applicable mechanism

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly states OWD as the restrictive floor, not a ceiling
Explains role hierarchy and sharing rules as additive layers
Correctly concludes access is the union/most-permissive grant, never a conflict
Uses a concrete, internally consistent example
Clarity and completeness of explanation

questions.title: Controlled by Parent vs. Independent Sharing on Child Objects
questions.prompt: Your org has a custom object 'Project' that is master-detail to Account, and a child custom object 'Project Task' that is master-detail to Project. A stakeholder asks why Project Task can't have its own, stricter org-wide default than Project. Explain how 'Controlled by Parent' sharing actually works, and separately explain what the 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' checkbox controls and why it only appears for custom objects.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer explains that 'Controlled by Parent' means the child record carries no independent sharing model at all — a user's access to the Project Task record is entirely derived from whatever access that same user has to its parent Project record, and this isn't optional when the relationship is a true master-detail: Salesforce enforces Controlled by Parent as the only available sharing setting for any master-detail child, precisely because master-detail implies the child has no independent existence, ownership, or lifecycle apart from the parent (it's deleted when the parent is deleted, it inherits the parent's owner in many cases, and so on). So the stakeholder's request — a stricter OWD on Project Task than on Project — is structurally impossible while the relationship stays master-detail; the only way to get independent sharing is to convert the relationship to a lookup, which comes with real trade-offs around roll-up summary fields, cascade delete behavior, and reparenting rules that need to be weighed before making that change.

The 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' checkbox is a separate concept entirely, and it only matters once an object does have its own org-wide default (so it's irrelevant to a Controlled-by-Parent child like Project Task, but very relevant to the Project object itself if Project's OWD were Private). For standard objects, this setting is always on and can't be turned off — a manager always inherits access to a Private record owned by a subordinate. For custom objects, Salesforce exposes a checkbox that lets an admin turn that inheritance off, which is used deliberately when a company wants to silo sensitive custom data — compensation plans, HR case records, disciplinary notes — so that a manager does not automatically see a subordinate's record just by virtue of sitting above them in the role hierarchy, even though they still could be granted access explicitly through a sharing rule or manual share if that's genuinely needed.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start by telling the stakeholder the honest answer: as long as Project Task is a true master-detail child of Project, it can't have its own org-wide default — Controlled by Parent isn't a setting you choose for a master-detail relationship, it's the only option, because the child record is treated as an extension of the parent, not a standalone record with its own ownership story. If they genuinely need Project Task to be more restrictive than Project, the real conversation is about converting that relationship to a lookup instead, and I'd walk them through what that actually costs — any roll-up summary fields on Project that reference Project Task would break and need Flow-based replacements, cascade delete behavior changes, and reparenting rules change — so it's not a free switch, it's an architecture decision.

On the hierarchy checkbox, I've used it in a past role on a custom 'Compensation Plan' object specifically so that a manager wouldn't automatically see a direct report's compensation record just because they're above them in the role hierarchy — we unchecked Grant Access Using Hierarchies on that object's sharing settings and then built an explicit sharing rule for the one HR-business-partner group that actually needed visibility. The thing I always point out is that this checkbox only shows up for custom objects at all — standard objects like Account and Opportunity always grant hierarchy-based access, you can't turn it off — so if someone's trying to silo sensitive data, it has to live on a custom object from the start, or you're stuck building workarounds like splitting the sensitive fields into a related custom object instead.
questions.example: A 'Compensation Plan' custom object with Private OWD and 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' unchecked means a sales manager does not automatically see a rep's compensation record despite being above them in the role hierarchy; only an explicit sharing rule targeting HR can grant that visibility.
commonMistakes: Assuming you can set an independent OWD on a true master-detail child object
Not realizing standard objects always grant hierarchy-based access, with no way to disable it
Confusing 'Controlled by Parent' sharing with the role hierarchy concept entirely
Underestimating the roll-up summary and cascade-delete fallout of converting master-detail to lookup
Assuming unchecking Grant Access Using Hierarchies also blocks access granted through other means like View All or an explicit sharing rule
keyPoints: Master-detail relationships enforce Controlled by Parent with no independent OWD possible
Converting to a lookup relationship is the only path to independent child sharing, with real trade-offs
Grant Access Using Hierarchies controls whether role hierarchy automatically grants access on that object
The checkbox is only exposed for custom objects; standard objects always have it effectively on
Unchecking it is the standard technique for siloing sensitive custom data from the management chain

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Controlled by Parent and why master-detail forces it
Correctly explains the lookup-conversion alternative and its trade-offs
Correctly explains what Grant Access Using Hierarchies controls
Correctly explains why the checkbox is custom-object-only
Clarity and technical precision

questions.title: Building a Regional Sales Sharing Model Step by Step
questions.prompt: The VP of Sales wants a new Opportunity sharing model: reps should see only their own opportunities, regional managers should see every opportunity owned by reps in their region, and a cross-functional 'Deal Desk' group needs Read/Write access to any opportunity over $250,000 regardless of region. Walk through exactly how you would configure this in Setup, step by step, and in what order.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer sequences the work rather than listing steps randomly, because order matters once there's existing data. First, set the Opportunity organization-wide default to Private under Setup > Sharing Settings — this must happen deliberately, ideally before reps start complaining about seeing everyone's deals, since narrowing an OWD on an org with existing data triggers a potentially long recalculation job. Second, verify the role hierarchy actually mirrors the region structure needed — regional managers' roles need to sit directly above their reps' roles, because that hierarchy relationship is what automatically grants the manager Read/Write access to every report's opportunities without any extra rule. Third, create a public group, something like 'Deal Desk,' and add its members. Fourth, build a criteria-based sharing rule on Opportunity: criteria Amount greater than $250,000, shared with the Deal Desk public group, access level Read/Write. Fifth, before telling anyone the rollout is done, use Login As (or Permission Set/Profile-based Run As testing in a sandbox) against a sample rep, a sample regional manager, and a Deal Desk member to confirm each persona sees exactly what's intended and nothing more.

The candidate should flag two things an interviewer is listening for: that an owner-based sharing rule would be the wrong tool for the Deal Desk requirement (it keys off who owns the record or what group/role the owner belongs to, not the Amount field, so it can't express a dollar threshold), and that the role hierarchy alone will never give Deal Desk visibility since they're not anywhere in the reporting chain — that's exactly why the criteria-based rule is necessary as a separate, additive mechanism.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd walk this one the way I'd actually click through it. I start in Setup, go to Sharing Settings, and set Opportunities to Private — and I'd flag to the team up front that doing this on an org with real production data kicks off a recalculation job that can take a while depending on volume, so I'd want to do it off-hours or during a maintenance window, not live during business hours. Next I go check the role hierarchy under Setup > Roles and make sure every regional manager's role is actually positioned above their reps — if the org chart says someone's a manager but their role in Salesforce doesn't reflect that, the hierarchy piece of this whole plan just silently doesn't work, so I always verify this visually in the role tree rather than trust what I'm told.

For the Deal Desk piece, I'd create a public group under Setup > Public Groups, add the Deal Desk folks as members, then go to Sharing Settings > Opportunity Sharing Rules > New, and build a criteria-based rule — Amount greater than 250000, share with that public group, Read/Write. The thing I always do before calling this 'done' is Login As a rep, a regional manager, and someone from Deal Desk, one at a time, and just look at what opportunities show up for each of them. I've been burned before by assuming a rule was right and finding out in production that a picklist value didn't match what I thought, so testing each persona before announcing the rollout isn't optional for me — it's the step that actually catches the mistakes.
questions.example: A criteria-based Opportunity sharing rule with filter 'Amount greater than 250000,' shared with the Deal Desk public group at Read/Write, runs independently of the role hierarchy and grants Deal Desk visibility into large deals in every region at once.
commonMistakes: Building an owner-based sharing rule when a criteria-based rule is needed to key off the Amount field
Assuming role hierarchy alone will surface records to Deal Desk even though they're outside the reporting chain
Setting OWD to something more open than Private and then trying to restrict visibility with sharing rules, which can't reduce access
Skipping Login As / persona testing before announcing the new model is live
Underestimating the sharing recalculation time when switching OWD on an org with substantial existing Opportunity data
keyPoints: Opportunity OWD must be set to Private first as the restrictive baseline
Role hierarchy must actually mirror the regional reporting structure for manager visibility to work
A criteria-based sharing rule, not an owner-based one, is required for the dollar-threshold exception
A public group organizes the Deal Desk membership that the rule targets
Login As / persona testing before go-live validates the model catches configuration mistakes early

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly sequences OWD, role hierarchy, group, and rule creation
Correctly identifies criteria-based (not owner-based) sharing rule as the right tool
Explains why role hierarchy alone doesn't cover the Deal Desk requirement
Includes persona-based testing before rollout
Clarity and practical, step-by-step accuracy

questions.title: Limiting Lead List Views with a Restriction Rule
questions.prompt: Leads org-wide default is Public Read/Write to support cross-territory collaboration, but reps complain that every list view and global search shows thousands of leads across all territories, making it hard to find their own. Leadership wants reps to default to seeing only their own territory's leads, without changing the underlying sharing model. Walk through implementing a restriction rule to solve this, and explain how it differs from a scoping rule.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer first reframes the problem correctly: this is a visibility-overload complaint, not an access-control problem, so the right tool narrows what's displayed without touching CRUD or the sharing model at all — Leads stay Public Read/Write for the collaboration the business genuinely needs. A restriction rule accomplishes exactly this: it's a record-level filter that applies on top of the existing sharing model, limiting what a targeted set of users can see in list views, related lists, search, and reports, without granting or revoking any actual record access. The implementation path is Setup > Restriction Rules, selecting Lead as the object, defining the filter logic — for example, Territory equals the user's own Territory, which can reference a formula or a field on the User record — activating the rule, and then assigning it to a permission set group rather than a profile, since restriction rules are only ever applied through permission set groups.

The candidate should clearly distinguish this from a scoping rule, which solves a related but different problem: a scoping rule sets the default record set shown in list views, reports, and global search for a given persona, without an admin having to hand-build a custom list view filter for every user, but a user can still explicitly broaden what they see within the UI by changing a list view filter, whereas a restriction rule is a hard cap that applies everywhere, including the API and reports, and cannot be worked around by the end user. The right choice here is a restriction rule precisely because leadership wants a firm boundary on visibility, not just a friendlier default.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame this for the team is: sharing answers 'who's allowed to see it,' and a restriction rule answers 'what shows up without having to dig for it' — two completely different layers, and mixing them up is the single most common mistake I see admins make here. Since the actual CRUD and sharing model is intentionally wide open for collaboration, I wouldn't touch OWD at all. Instead I'd go build a restriction rule on Lead: Setup > Restriction Rules, new rule, filter on something like Territory equals the user's Territory field, activate it, and then — this part trips people up — assign it through a permission set group, not a profile, because that's the only way restriction rules get applied to users.

I'd also flag the scoping rule alternative to leadership so they understand the trade-off: a scoping rule just changes what's shown by default, but a rep could still widen a list view filter and see everything, whereas a restriction rule is a hard floor that follows the user everywhere — list views, global search, reports, even API access — and they can't click their way around it. Given that leadership specifically said they want reps capped at their own territory, not just nudged toward it, I'd recommend the restriction rule. One gotcha I'd mention up front: restriction rules aren't supported on every object yet, so before I promise this as the fix, I'd double-check Lead is on the supported list for our current release.
questions.example: A restriction rule on Lead with filter 'Territory equals $User.Territory__c' assigned via a permission set group caps what a rep sees everywhere — list views, search, reports — while the Lead OWD stays Public Read/Write for the cross-territory collaboration the business still needs.

Assuming a restriction rule can grant access rather than only narrow what's already visible under sharing
Not verifying restriction rule support for the specific object before committing to the approach

questions.title: Diagnosing Unexpected Account Visibility for a Support Rep
questions.prompt: A support rep reports being able to open an Account record that belongs to a different business unit and, under Private org-wide defaults, should be invisible to them. The record's Sharing Detail related list shows no manual share and no sharing rule referencing the rep's role or groups. Walk through your systematic troubleshooting process to find the real cause.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats this as a layered investigation rather than jumping straight to 'the sharing rule must be wrong,' because the Sharing Detail page the rep already checked only shows rule-based and manual shares — it does not reveal every path to access. The candidate should first confirm the actual OWD on Account rather than assume it, including whether Account inherits any Controlled-by-Parent relationship from another object that might be granting access indirectly. Second, check the rep's role position in the hierarchy against the actual owner's role — a hierarchy relationship that isn't obvious from job titles can still exist. Third, re-check both owner-based and criteria-based sharing rules for a public group the rep was recently added to, since the rep may not realize their own group membership changed. Fourth, and most important, check the rep's assigned permission sets (not just their profile) for an object-level 'View All' on Account, or the system-level 'View All Data' permission — either of these bypasses the sharing model entirely and will never show up as an entry on the Sharing Detail page, which is exactly why it's the most common cause of this specific symptom. Fifth, check for Account Teams or indirect exposure through a related Opportunity or Case team role that implicitly surfaces the parent Account.

The candidate should explicitly call out that a sharing-model review and a permission-level review are two separate checks, and that whichever one is skipped is usually where the real answer was hiding — in this scenario, an overly broad 'View All' granted through a permission set (perhaps one originally built for an integration user and mistakenly cloned onto a human user) is the single most likely explanation precisely because it would produce exactly the symptom described: visible access with nothing showing in Sharing Detail.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I treat this like a detective process, and I don't stop at the obvious spot. The rep already checked the record's Sharing button and found nothing, so my next move isn't to re-check that again — it's to widen the search to places that never show up there at all. I'd pull up the rep's permission set assignments, not just their profile, and specifically look for 'View All' on the Account object or the broader 'View All Data' system permission, because either one silently grants full visibility and simply never generates a sharing entry on the record — that's the classic 'invisible' cause for exactly this kind of ticket. I've genuinely seen this happen before: an admin cloned a permission set that was originally built for an integration user, and 'View All' came along for the ride onto a real human's assignment without anyone noticing for months.

If that comes up empty, I'd widen out further — check if the rep is a member of an Account Team or got pulled into visibility indirectly through a Case or Opportunity team role tied to that Account, and double-check the role hierarchy in case the rep's role sits in a spot in the tree that isn't obvious from their job title. My instinct, honestly, is to run a quick permission set audit across the team any time I find one of these 'View All' surprises, because if one person has it by accident, there's a decent chance others do too — I'd rather fix the pattern than just the one ticket, and I'd push to remove the unnecessary grant rather than try to compensate for it with tighter sharing rules elsewhere.
questions.example: A permission set originally scoped for a middleware integration user includes 'View All' on Account; it gets cloned as a starting point for a new support permission set and the 'View All' checkbox is left checked, silently granting every assignee full Account visibility with nothing appearing on any record's Sharing Detail page.
commonMistakes: Stopping at the record's Sharing Detail page and not checking permission-level overrides at all
Forgetting that Account Teams or related Opportunity/Case team roles can expose an Account indirectly
Checking only the profile's object permissions and ignoring permission sets, which are evaluated together
Assuming OWD itself must be misconfigured before checking for a View All / View All Data grant
Overlooking a sharing rule that targets a public group the rep was only recently added to
keyPoints: Sharing Detail only shows rule-based and manual shares, not every path to access
View All (object-level) and View All Data (system-level) bypass sharing and never appear as a share record
Permission sets must be checked in addition to the profile, since they combine
Account Teams and related object team roles can expose a record indirectly
A full diagnosis separates the sharing-model review from the permission-level review

Describes a systematic, layered troubleshooting sequence

questions.title: Ownership Changes Not Reflecting in Access After a Mass Transfer
questions.prompt: After a mass reassignment of 50,000 Opportunity records to new owners as part of a territory realignment, several regional managers report they still can't see opportunities that should now belong to their teams, even a full day later. Explain what's likely happening and how you would confirm and resolve it.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer leads with the mechanism rather than guessing at a hierarchy misconfiguration: changing ownership on a record doesn't just update a field, it requires Salesforce to re-evaluate implicit role-based access and any owner-based or criteria-based sharing rules that key off the owner, and at a volume of 50,000 records that re-evaluation runs as an asynchronous background process rather than completing instantly. The candidate should know where to confirm this is actually in progress or stalled — Setup > Sharing Settings shows the status of pending recalculation jobs, and the Setup Audit Trail records when sharing recalculations were kicked off and completed. A full day with no resolution points to one of two likely causes: either the recalculation job is still legitimately queued behind other async work at that data volume, or 'Defer Sharing Calculations' was enabled for the bulk load (a common practice to avoid performance strain during a mass update) and nobody explicitly resumed/recalculated sharing afterward, leaving the org in a state where ownership changed but dependent sharing never caught up.

The resolution path follows directly from the diagnosis: if deferred sharing calculations were left suspended, the fix is to explicitly trigger the recalculation (via the declarative 'Recalculate' option tied to the relevant sharing rules, or by resuming deferred sharing through whatever tool performed the bulk load). If criteria-based sharing rules are also in play and some of the changed fields intersect with their criteria, those rules need to be confirmed as recalculated too, not just the ownership-driven hierarchy access. The key insight an interviewer wants to hear is that this is a process/timing issue tied to data volume, not evidence that the role hierarchy itself is broken, and that jumping straight to rebuilding roles or sharing rules before checking recalculation status would be the wrong first move.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first instinct here isn't to touch the role hierarchy at all — it's to go check whether sharing recalculation actually finished. I'd pull up the Setup Audit Trail and look for the sharing recalculation entries tied to yesterday's mass transfer, and I'd also check Sharing Settings for any recalculation job still shown as pending. At 50,000 records, that kind of job can legitimately take a while, but a full day with managers still locked out tells me something didn't complete, and the most common reason I've personally run into is that whoever ran the bulk update had 'Defer Sharing Calculations' turned on to keep the load from bogging down, and then nobody went back and resumed it afterward — so the ownership field changed, but the dependent sharing never actually got recomputed to match.

If that's what I find, the fix is to explicitly kick off the recalculation rather than wait it out — either through the declarative recalculate option on the relevant sharing rules or by going back to whatever tool ran the bulk load and resuming the deferred sharing job properly. I'd also double check whether any criteria-based rules touch fields that changed as part of this realignment, since those need their own recalculation pass too, not just the ownership-driven hierarchy piece. And honestly, once I fix it this time, I'd push to build a checklist for future mass data loads so 'resume sharing calculations' is a mandatory last step, not something that depends on someone remembering.
questions.example: A data team runs a 50,000-record Opportunity ownership update with Defer Sharing Calculations enabled to protect load performance, but the follow-up step to resume/recalculate sharing is skipped — managers see stale access for a day until an admin manually triggers the recalculation.
commonMistakes: Assuming sharing always recalculates instantly regardless of record volume
Not knowing about Defer Sharing Calculations and forgetting it must be explicitly resumed after a bulk load
Jumping to rebuild or audit the role hierarchy before checking recalculation job status
Forgetting criteria-based rules need their own recalculation pass if relevant fields changed, not just owner-based hierarchy access
Not checking the Setup Audit Trail before escalating the issue as a product bug
keyPoints: Mass ownership changes trigger asynchronous sharing recalculation that queues at scale
Deferred sharing calculations must be explicitly resumed after a bulk operation completes
Setup Audit Trail and sharing recalculation status are the first places to check, not the hierarchy structure
Criteria-based rules need separate recalculation if their criteria fields were part of the bulk change
Diagnosis should start with process/timing before assuming a configuration defect

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies sharing recalculation as the likely cause, not hierarchy misconfiguration
Correctly explains Defer Sharing Calculations and the need to resume it
Describes concrete places to confirm status (Audit Trail, Sharing Settings)
Addresses criteria-based rules needing separate recalculation
Clarity and logical diagnostic order

questions.title: A Permission Set Isn't Granting the Field Access It Should
questions.prompt: An admin assigns a permission set that grants Edit access to a custom field, but the affected user still can't edit it — the field renders as read-only on the page layout. Walk through the layered checks you would perform, in order, to find out why.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer works outward from field-level security to the page layout to the field's underlying nature, because each layer can independently cause this exact symptom. First, confirm the permission set assignment actually took — it should show as active in the user's assigned permission sets, and the specific field should show Edit (not just Read) checked on that permission set's field-level security page, since a field-level security grant requires both Read and Edit to be explicitly checked, not just one. Field-level security itself is evaluated as the most permissive combination across the profile and every assigned permission set, so as long as any one of them grants Edit, the user should have it at the FLS layer — if FLS genuinely grants Edit and the field is still locked, the cause lies elsewhere. Second, check the page layout the user actually sees: page layouts have their own independent 'Read-Only' property on a field, and this can force a field to render as read-only even when field-level security says Edit is allowed — this is the most commonly overlooked cause of exactly this symptom, because admins often check FLS, see it's correct, and stop there.

Third, confirm the field's underlying type — formula fields and roll-up summary fields are never user-editable regardless of any permission granted, so if the 'custom field' in question is actually a formula, no permission set can ever make it editable. Fourth, check for validation rules that might be blocking the save in a way that looks like a locked field. Fifth, check for automation — a Flow, Process Builder, or trigger that runs on save and overwrites the field's value — because that can produce a symptom that looks identical to a permissions problem (the user enters a value, saves, and it reverts) even though the field was genuinely editable. A candidate should present this as a deliberate elimination sequence rather than guessing at a single cause.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd work through this layer by layer rather than guessing. First stop: I'd actually open the permission set and verify the field has Edit checked, not just Read, and confirm the permission set assignment is really active on that user — sounds obvious, but I've seen admins swear they assigned it when the assignment never saved. If that's genuinely correct, field-level security itself should be fine, since FLS takes the most permissive answer across the profile and every permission set a user has, so one correct grant is enough.

The next place I go, and honestly the one that catches people most often, is the page layout the user is actually on — page layouts have their own separate 'Read-Only' checkbox on a field, completely independent of FLS, and that can lock a field down even when FLS says Edit is fine. I've personally debugged this exact ticket before and found the answer sitting in the layout, not the permission set, more than once. If the layout checks out, I'd look at whether the field is actually a formula or roll-up summary field under the hood — those are never editable no matter what permission you grant, full stop. And if everything up to that point looks right, I'd check for a Flow or Process Builder running on save, because a field that silently reverts after save looks exactly like a permissions bug to the end user, but it's actually automation quietly overwriting their input — that one's sneaky because nothing in Setup's permission screens will ever point you toward it directly.
questions.example: A permission set correctly grants Edit on a custom 'Discount %' field, but the field still shows locked because the user's assigned page layout has that same field's 'Read-Only' property checked independently of field-level security.
commonMistakes: Assuming field-level security alone controls editability and missing the page layout's independent Read-Only property
Not verifying the permission set assignment actually saved and is active before troubleshooting further
Forgetting formula and roll-up summary fields are never editable regardless of any permission granted
Overlooking automation (Flow, Process Builder, Apex triggers) that silently reverts a value after save, mimicking a permissions issue
Checking only the profile's field-level security and ignoring that permission sets are evaluated together with it
keyPoints: FLS edit access is the most permissive combination across profile and all assigned permission sets
Page layout's Read-Only property can independently override FLS and force a field read-only
Formula and roll-up summary fields are never user-editable regardless of permissions
Automation can mimic a permissions problem by overwriting a value after save
A full diagnosis checks FLS, page layout, field type, and automation in a deliberate sequence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly checks permission set assignment and FLS Edit setting first
Correctly identifies page layout Read-Only property as a likely independent cause
Correctly notes formula/roll-up fields are never editable regardless of permissions
Considers automation as a cause that mimics a permissions issue
Logical, elimination-style troubleshooting order

questions.title: Designing the Full Sharing Model for a Growing Sales Organization
questions.prompt: A 200-rep sales organization is moving off a flat, fully-public sharing model as it scales into distinct regions and verticals. As the admin leading the redesign, describe the end-to-end sharing architecture you would propose across Accounts, Opportunities, and Leads, including org-wide defaults, the shape of the role hierarchy, and where sharing rules versus teams fit in.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer differentiates the three objects rather than proposing one blanket setting. Accounts often work best at Public Read Only, since broad read visibility supports account research and avoids duplicate records across a 200-rep org, while Opportunities and Leads go to Private, since deal and pipeline data is exactly what the realignment is trying to protect from unrestricted visibility. The role hierarchy should be designed around sharing purpose, not copied literally from the org chart — roles should reflect region and vertical boundaries (for example, 'East Region Manager' and 'West Region Manager' as parallel roles above their respective reps) rather than mirroring every job title, because a hierarchy tied too tightly to job titles requires constant rebuilding as people get promoted or reorganized, while a hierarchy tied to sharing purpose stays stable through personnel changes.

Sharing rules and teams should be assigned to the specific problems each is good at: owner-based or criteria-based sharing rules handle broad, persistent exceptions like a national accounts group needing visibility across every region, or a Deal Desk needing visibility into large deals regardless of owner, while Opportunity Teams handle deal-specific, often temporary collaboration like a sales engineer or a partner-channel rep who needs access to one deal without becoming a permanent member of any public group. The candidate should also address rollout mechanics: because this org has substantial existing data, tightening OWD from Public to Private triggers a real recalculation cost, so the sequence should be to build out the complete replacement model (hierarchy, rules, teams) in a sandbox first, test every persona with Login As, and only then cut over OWD in production during a planned window — cutting over OWD before the replacement grants exist would strand legitimate users without access they currently rely on.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd start this project with discovery, not configuration — sitting down with regional VPs and a few reps from each vertical to actually map who needs to see what today, because at 200 reps there's always more informal reliance on 'I can see everything' than leadership realizes, and I don't want to find that out after I've already tightened access. Once I have that picture, my rough design would be Accounts at Public Read Only so research and duplicate-checking still work broadly, with Opportunities and Leads going Private since protecting deal and pipeline visibility is the actual point of this whole project. For the role hierarchy, I'd build it around region and vertical lines rather than literal titles — I've learned the hard way that a hierarchy mirroring every management title turns into a maintenance headache every time someone gets promoted, whereas one built around sharing purpose barely needs to change.

For the exceptions, I'd lean on criteria-based sharing rules for things that are persistent and group-level, like a national-accounts team needing cross-region visibility, and I'd use Opportunity Teams for anything that's deal-specific and temporary, like a solutions engineer looping in on one deal — I try hard not to let one-off collaboration needs turn into permanent public groups, because that's how sharing models get messy again in two years. On rollout, I'd build the entire new model in a sandbox, run it against copied production data if I can, Login As a rep from each region and vertical to sanity-check what they see, and only then schedule the actual OWD cutover for a low-traffic window, since tightening it on 200 reps' worth of existing data isn't instant — and I'd tell leadership up front that reps will temporarily lose some visibility they're used to, so the comms plan matters as much as the technical plan.
questions.example: A 'National Accounts' criteria-based sharing rule grants a cross-functional team visibility into any Opportunity above a size threshold regardless of region, while a one-off Opportunity Team adds a specific sales engineer to a single large deal without making them a permanent member of any broader sharing group.
commonMistakes: Modeling the role hierarchy as an exact copy of the literal org chart instead of a sharing-purpose structure
Using sharing rules for one-off deal collaboration instead of Opportunity Teams, creating sprawl over time
Tightening OWD to Private before the replacement sharing rules and teams exist, stranding legitimate users
Underestimating the sharing recalculation time and business disruption of changing OWD on a large existing data set
Skipping sandbox testing and persona validation before a production cutover
keyPoints: OWD choice is deliberately differentiated across Accounts, Opportunities, and Leads rather than uniform
Role hierarchy should reflect sharing purpose (region/vertical) rather than literal job titles
Sharing rules handle persistent group/criteria-based exceptions; teams handle deal-specific collaboration
Recalculation cost and rollout sequencing must be planned for an org with substantial existing data
Discovery with stakeholders before configuration prevents stranding users who rely on current broad access

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Differentiates OWD choices across the three objects with sound reasoning
Designs a role hierarchy around sharing purpose rather than literal org chart
Correctly allocates sharing rules vs. teams to the right use cases
Addresses rollout sequencing, recalculation cost, and testing
Clarity and completeness of the overall architecture

questions.title: Designing Case Visibility for a Multi-Tier Support Organization
questions.prompt: A support organization has Tier 1, Tier 2, and an escalations team, plus a requirement that customers' own support contacts, accessing an Experience Cloud site, can see only their own company's cases. Describe the sharing architecture you would design across org-wide defaults, queues, case teams, and guest/community access to meet both the internal and external requirements.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer separates the internal and external visibility problems clearly, because they're solved with different mechanisms. Internally, Case OWD should be Private, with queues (a Tier 1 queue and an Escalations queue, for example) handling routing through assignment rules rather than relying on individual ownership for every new case — agents work cases from the queue and either keep the queue as the effective owner or claim the case as their own, depending on the team's workflow preference. Cross-tier collaboration should use predefined Case Team roles rather than reassigning ownership every time a Tier 2 specialist or an escalation manager needs to get involved — team roles let multiple people work the same case with differentiated access levels (one role might get Read/Write, another Read Only) without disturbing who actually owns the record or triggering reassignment-driven automation.

Externally, the requirement that a contact sees only their own company's cases cannot be met by broadening the internal sharing model — it requires Experience Cloud-specific mechanisms: either a sharing set that scopes access based on a matching field between the User (via Contact) and the Case's Account, or an explicit Experience Cloud sharing rule targeting the appropriate community user group, both scoped tightly to the contact's own Account. The candidate should flag guest user security as a distinct and serious concern if any part of the site is accessible without login: guest users should never be included in broad sharing rules, their profile's object permissions should be explicitly minimized and reviewed (Salesforce has restricted what guest sharing rules can do precisely because of past over-exposure incidents), and any case visibility for anonymous visitors should go through a narrowly scoped mechanism, never a broad Public-level grant.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd treat this as two separate design problems wearing the same case record. Internally, Private OWD plus a Tier 1 queue and an Escalations queue for routing — new cases land in a queue via assignment rules rather than getting auto-owned by an individual, and agents pick them up from there. When Tier 2 or an escalation manager needs to get involved without taking over the case, I'd use predefined Case Team roles instead of reassigning ownership back and forth — that way a Tier 2 specialist can get Read/Write and an escalation manager can get a different access level, all without the case bouncing between owners and triggering notification rules every time someone touches it.

The external piece is where I'd be the most careful, honestly, because this is where I've seen real exposure risk in past projects. 'Customers only see their own company's cases' isn't something I'd try to solve with a normal sharing rule — Experience Cloud sharing sets, scoped so a contact's access maps to their own Account, are the right tool, and I'd test that scoping thoroughly before launch, logging in as a test contact from company A and confirming they can't see company B's cases. And if any part of this site is accessible without login, I get genuinely paranoid about the guest user profile — I'd explicitly strip down its object permissions, make sure no sharing rule accidentally includes the guest user group, and double check against Salesforce's own guest-user security changes, because I've read about orgs that got burned leaving a guest sharing rule in place that was originally fine until the data behind it grew sensitive.
questions.example: A sharing set maps a community User's Contact.AccountId to the matching Account field on Case, so a logged-in customer contact from Acme Corp sees only Acme's cases, while a Case Team role gives a Tier 2 specialist Read/Write on an internal escalation without changing who owns the record.
commonMistakes: Reassigning case ownership on every tier hand-off instead of using case teams for collaboration
Trying to solve external customer visibility with an internal-style sharing rule instead of an Experience Cloud sharing set
Leaving the guest user profile with broad object permissions after launching a community
Not testing external visibility by logging in as a contact from a different account to confirm isolation
Assuming a single OWD setting can serve both internal tiered support and external customer-scoped visibility
keyPoints: Queues plus assignment rules drive internal routing without relying on individual ownership
Case teams allow cross-tier collaboration with differentiated access without transferring ownership
External customer visibility requires Experience Cloud sharing sets scoped to the contact's own Account
Guest user security requires explicit profile lockdown given Salesforce's restrictions on guest sharing rules
Internal and external visibility are solved with distinct mechanisms, not a single universal rule

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs internal queue/case team architecture
Correctly identifies Experience Cloud sharing sets for external, Account-scoped visibility
Addresses guest user security explicitly and specifically
Separates internal vs. external mechanisms clearly rather than conflating them

questions.title: Choosing Between Restriction Rules and Rebuilding the Sharing Model
questions.prompt: Your organization's classic sharing model — a single org-wide default plus a few dozen sharing rules accumulated over years — has become hard to maintain, and users complain about seeing too many records in list views even though the underlying access is largely intentional for reporting purposes. Leadership asks whether you should overhaul the sharing model or adopt restriction rules instead. How do you decide, and what do you recommend?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer establishes the deciding question before recommending a tool: is the underlying record access itself too broad (a genuine security or compliance problem), or is access intentional and correct but overwhelming to work with day to day (a UX/volume problem)? Restriction rules only ever filter what's surfaced in list views, search, and reports — they never grant or revoke actual record access — so if the real finding is that access is too broad, a restriction rule would paper over the symptom while leaving the underlying exposure completely intact, and the sharing model itself (OWD and the accumulated rules) genuinely needs review and tightening. If, on the other hand, the access is intentional and needed for reporting or cross-functional visibility but is simply too much for day-to-day users to wade through, restriction rules are the right tool precisely because they don't touch the sharing model, don't trigger a sharing recalculation, and can be scoped and rolled out per persona through permission set groups relatively quickly and with low risk of breaking something that currently works.

The candidate should recommend doing the access audit first, before picking either tool, since the audit itself will reveal which situation this actually is — and a pragmatic answer is often a hybrid: use a restriction rule to solve the immediate day-to-day complaint quickly and with low risk, while running a separate, properly resourced workstream to review whether any of the dozens of accumulated sharing rules represent real over-exposure that needs to be fixed at the source. The candidate should also flag the practical constraint that restriction rules aren't supported on every object, which can influence which complaint can even be solved this way.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first question is always the same: is this actually a 'people can see too much' problem, or a 'people can see the right amount but it's annoying to find what they need' problem — because those get solved completely differently, and I wouldn't commit to either fix until I know which one this is. I'd do a quick audit first — pull the existing sharing rules, talk to a few of the people who set them up originally if they're still around, and figure out whether the broad access is actually intentional (needed for reporting, cross-team visibility, whatever) or whether it's just accumulated cruft nobody's reviewed in years.

If it turns out access really is too broad from a risk standpoint, I'd tell leadership plainly that a restriction rule is the wrong tool — it only filters what's shown, it doesn't actually reduce access, so relying on it there would just hide a real problem instead of fixing it, and the sharing model itself needs an honest rebuild. But if the audit shows the access is legitimately needed and the complaint is really about volume and list view clutter, I'd push for restriction rules as the fast, low-risk fix — they don't trigger a recalculation, they roll out through permission set groups so I can pilot with one team first, and they're much easier to reverse than ripping apart years of sharing rules. Realistically, I'd probably recommend doing both in parallel: ship the restriction rule fast to make people's day-to-day better now, and run the slower, more careful review of the actual sharing rules as its own project, since that one deserves more time and testing than the urgent complaint can wait for.
questions.example: An access audit finds that 35 of the 40 accumulated sharing rules are genuinely needed for cross-functional reporting, but reps are overwhelmed by volume in their daily list views — a restriction rule scoped to each rep's territory fixes the day-to-day complaint immediately, while a separate review targets the 5 rules that turned out to be stale and over-broad.
commonMistakes: Treating a restriction rule as a security fix when the real finding is that access is too broad
Committing to a full sharing model overhaul when the complaint is really about volume, not access
Not auditing existing sharing rules before recommending either tool
Assuming restriction/scoping rule changes trigger the same costly recalculation as OWD or sharing rule changes
Failing to confirm restriction rule support for the specific object before proposing it as the fix
keyPoints: Restriction rules narrow what's displayed; they never reduce actual record access
A genuine over-exposure problem requires changing OWD/sharing rules, not a filtering tool
An access audit should precede the tool choice, since it determines which problem this actually is
Restriction rules are lower-risk and faster to deploy/reverse than a sharing model rebuild
A hybrid approach often fits: quick restriction-rule relief now, deeper sharing review in parallel

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the deciding question (access vs. volume problem)
Correctly explains restriction rules never reduce actual access
Recommends an audit before committing to a tool
