questions.title: Untangling an Over-Shared Legacy Org Before a Compliance Review
questions.prompt: You inherit an org where Accounts are Public Read/Write org-wide, there are roughly 40 overlapping sharing rules nobody can fully explain the original purpose of, and a compliance review is coming up that requires provable least-privilege access. Describe your architectural approach to redesigning this safely without breaking the business before the review.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer resists the urge to start deleting or tightening things immediately and instead opens with a full audit phase: inventorying every active sharing rule, manual share, team, and any permission set carrying View All or Modify All on Account, and cross-referencing that inventory against actual usage — reports on record access patterns, interviews with the teams who rely on specific rules, and tools like Salesforce Optimizer to surface unused or redundant rules. From that audit, the candidate should define a target-state least-privilege model per persona, then sequence the change carefully: because the current OWD is Public Read/Write, the correct order is to build out the replacement sharing rules, teams, and any needed manual shares first, validate them thoroughly in a sandbox against real usage patterns, and only tighten OWD to Private once the replacement grants are proven to cover every legitimate need — tightening OWD before the replacement exists would strand people from access they currently depend on and likely trigger an immediate business disruption.

The candidate should also address cleanup discipline: the audit will likely reveal that several of the 40 rules are redundant, overlapping, or address a need that no longer exists, and the right move is to consolidate and retire those rather than simply layering a cleaner model on top of the old mess, since leaving stale rules in place defeats the purpose of a least-privilege redesign and recreates the exact documentation problem for the next admin. Given the data volume implied by an org-wide Public Read/Write Account setting, the candidate should flag planning the OWD cutover for a low-traffic window given the sharing recalculation cost, rolling out in phases by business unit rather than all at once, and producing documentation of the final model and rationale as the actual evidence the compliance review will need.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd treat this almost like a project with a compliance deadline as leverage, because getting buy-in to tighten a model like this is usually a hard political conversation, and 'we have a compliance review' gives me real cover to finally do it right. Step one for me is discovery — I'd run workshops with whoever's still around from each business unit, pull actual access and usage data, and go through every one of those 40 rules asking 'who relies on this and why,' because some of them are going to turn out to be dead weight nobody remembers creating.

From there I'd design the target least-privilege model and build it entirely in a sandbox first — new role hierarchy if needed, new sharing rules, teams for anything deal- or case-specific — and I would not touch the live OWD setting until that replacement model is tested against real usage patterns and I'm confident nobody legitimate loses access on day one. My rollout would be phased by business unit rather than a big-bang cutover, with a rollback plan documented before I start, because tightening Public Read/Write to Private on an org with real data volume isn't instant and isn't something I want to be debugging live in front of a compliance deadline. And I'd make a point of actually retiring the redundant rules I find during the audit instead of just adding my cleaner model on top of the old 40 — otherwise I've just created version two of the same documentation problem for whoever inherits this after me, and I'd leave behind a written rationale for every rule that survives, specifically so that record exists for the compliance reviewers and the next admin alike.
questions.example: An audit of the 40 legacy sharing rules finds that 12 overlap with each other targeting the same public group, 8 reference a public group that was deleted months ago and are now silently inert, and only 20 map to a genuine, still-active business need — the redesign consolidates those 20 into a cleaner target model before OWD is ever touched.
commonMistakes: Tightening OWD to Private before the replacement sharing rules and teams exist, stranding legitimate access
Adding yet more sharing rules on top of the existing 40 instead of auditing and consolidating them
Skipping sandbox testing against real usage patterns before a production cutover
Treating the compliance deadline as a reason to rush the change without a rollback plan
Failing to document the rationale for each surviving rule, repeating the original problem for the next admin
keyPoints: Audit existing sharing rules, teams, and View All grants against actual usage before designing anything new
Sequence the change so the replacement least-privilege model exists before OWD is tightened
Consolidate and retire redundant rules rather than layering new ones onto the old mess
Test in sandbox and roll out in phases with a rollback plan given the data volume involved
Document the final model and rationale as the actual compliance evidence, not just the configuration itself

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Leads with a thorough audit phase before proposing changes
Correctly sequences building the replacement model before tightening OWD
Addresses consolidating/retiring redundant rules, not just adding new ones
Includes sandbox testing, phased rollout, and rollback planning
Addresses documentation as compliance evidence

questions.title: Owning an Incident Where a Sharing Rule Briefly Exposed Records
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you made or caught a sharing-rule misconfiguration that briefly gave a role or group access to records they shouldn't have seen. Walk me through what happened, how you discovered and contained it, and what you changed afterward so it couldn't happen again.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer gives a specific, concrete account rather than a hypothetical, and covers four distinct elements in sequence. First, a precise description of what actually went wrong — for example, a criteria-based sharing rule intended to scope access by a current regional picklist value instead matched on a stale or incorrectly entered value, which caused it to grant a broader public group read access to records that should have stayed within a narrower team. Second, how it was discovered — ideally through a proactive mechanism like a routine access review or monitoring, though a user report is also a legitimate and honest discovery path, and the candidate should be candid about which one it actually was. Third, the containment steps taken immediately: deactivating or correcting the rule, and critically, assessing whether any exposed data was actually viewed, exported, or acted on during the exposure window, not just assuming no harm occurred because the fix happened quickly.

Fourth, and the part that most distinguishes a senior answer, is the root cause analysis and the durable fix: identifying why the criteria was wrong in the first place (a stale picklist value, no sandbox validation before the rule went to production, no peer review step), and describing a systemic change that followed — such as requiring sandbox testing and a second-person review for any sharing rule change before it's deployed to production, or adding a periodic access review that would have caught this sooner. The candidate should also address transparency: a strong answer describes proactively informing a manager or security stakeholder about the exposure rather than quietly patching it and saying nothing, since compliance and trust both depend on that disclosure happening.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'll give you the real version of this. I'd built a criteria-based sharing rule meant to extend Read access to a regional operations group, scoped to a specific territory value on the Account record. The rule worked exactly as intended when I tested it — the problem was that a batch of older accounts still had a legacy version of that territory picklist value that I hadn't accounted for, and because my criteria matched more loosely than I'd realized, those legacy-value accounts got swept into the broader grant too, which meant a wider group than intended could see them. I found this during a routine access review about two weeks later, not immediately, which is honestly the part that still bothers me most about it.

The second I saw it, I deactivated the rule, pulled a list of exactly which records had been affected and for how long, and went straight to my manager and our security lead with the specifics rather than quietly fixing it and moving on — I'd rather be the one who reports it than have someone else find it later and ask why I didn't say anything. After that, I rebuilt the rule with tighter, explicitly tested criteria in sandbox against a copy of production data that included those legacy values, and I pushed for a change afterward that we actually adopted team-wide: no sharing rule change goes to production without a second admin reviewing the criteria logic first. That process change is honestly the thing I'm proudest of out of that whole incident, because it's prevented at least one similar mistake since.
commonMistakes: Describing a vague hypothetical instead of a specific, concrete real incident
Focusing only on the technical fix and skipping how the exposure was communicated to stakeholders
Omitting root cause analysis and only describing the quick patch
Not describing a durable, systemic change that prevents recurrence
Downplaying the severity instead of being candid about what was actually exposed and for how long
keyPoints: A specific, concrete description of what the misconfiguration actually was
An honest account of how the exposure was discovered and the timeline involved
Root cause analysis that distinguishes the symptom from the underlying cause
Transparent, proactive communication with stakeholders rather than a quiet fix
A durable process change that prevents recurrence, not just a one-time patch

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives a specific, concrete, credible incident
Clearly describes discovery and containment steps
Includes genuine root cause analysis
Demonstrates transparent stakeholder communication
Describes a durable systemic fix, not just a one-time patch

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Request to Loosen Org-Wide Defaults for Convenience
questions.prompt: Describe a situation where a stakeholder — a sales director, a VP, or similar — asked you to widen org-wide defaults or add a very broad sharing rule purely for convenience, and you believed it would create unnecessary risk. How did you handle the conversation, and what was the outcome?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by showing the candidate took the request seriously rather than reacting defensively — naming the real business pain point behind it, such as reps being frustrated they can't cover a colleague's accounts during PTO, or a manager wanting faster visibility without waiting on IT. From there, the candidate should explain why broadly loosening org-wide defaults is a disproportionate response to that specific pain point: it typically exposes more than the stated need requires (compensation-sensitive terms, competitive deal information, data a compliance policy specifically restricts), and it is hard to walk back once people get used to the wider access, since removing visibility later reads as a punitive change even when it's a correction.

The most important element of a senior-level answer is proposing a narrower alternative that actually solves the underlying need rather than simply saying no — for example, Opportunity Teams or a time-bound manual share for PTO coverage, or a tightly scoped criteria-based sharing rule instead of a blanket Public Read/Write change. The candidate should frame the pushback in terms of business risk the stakeholder actually cares about (what happens if a competitor's buyer sees our pricing terms, what a compliance review would say about this change) rather than an abstract security principle, and should describe following up after implementing the alternative to confirm it genuinely solved the stakeholder's problem, since an alternative that doesn't actually land just reopens the same pressure to loosen access later.
questions.professionalAnswer:
This actually happened almost exactly as you're describing it. A sales director came to me and said, 'just make Opportunities Public Read/Write, my team keeps complaining they can't see each other's deals.' My first move wasn't to say no — it was to ask what was actually driving the complaint, and it turned out the real issue was PTO coverage: reps wanted someone to be able to step in on a deal when a colleague was out, not blanket visibility into every deal in the org all the time.

Once I understood that, I went back with a specific alternative instead of a flat refusal — I proposed using Opportunity Teams for planned coverage situations, plus a public group and a scoped sharing rule for a 'backup coverage' pool the director could assign reps into temporarily. I actually built a quick demo of it in sandbox before pitching it, because I find stakeholders respond a lot better to seeing something work than to hearing me explain why their original idea was risky. The director agreed to try it, and a few weeks later told me it solved the actual problem better than the blanket access would have, since reps weren't drowning in every colleague's pipeline, just the specific deals they needed. Honestly, that director became one of my strongest advocates for keeping things scoped tightly after that, which taught me that pushback lands a lot better when it comes with a working alternative attached rather than just a risk warning.
commonMistakes: Saying no to the request without offering a working alternative that solves the actual business need
Framing the pushback purely in technical/security language instead of business risk the stakeholder cares about
Not following up to confirm the alternative actually satisfied the underlying need
Caving to pressure and implementing the broad change without raising the risk at all
Failing to document the decision and rationale for future reference
keyPoints: Identify and name the real underlying business need behind the request
Explain the risk in terms the stakeholder cares about, not abstract security language
Propose a narrower, targeted alternative rather than a flat refusal
Validate afterward that the alternative actually solved the stakeholder's problem
Document the decision so the rationale survives staff turnover

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies the real underlying business need behind the request
Explains risk in stakeholder-relevant terms, not abstract jargon
Proposes a concrete, narrower alternative rather than a flat no
Describes following up to confirm the alternative worked
Clear, credible narrative

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Admin Through a Role Hierarchy Access Issue
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you mentored a junior admin who was stuck debugging why a manager couldn't see a subordinate's records despite what looked like a correct role hierarchy. What did you teach them about how to approach it, and how did you make sure they could handle a similar case on their own next time?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer emphasizes teaching a transferable method over simply supplying the fix, since that distinction is what mentoring actually means in this context. The candidate should describe resisting the urge to just open Setup and solve it in front of the junior admin, instead walking them through a repeatable diagnostic sequence: first, verify the org-wide default and whether the object actually grants access via role hierarchy at all (checking whether Grant Access Using Hierarchies is unchecked, in the case of a custom object), second, verify the manager's role is genuinely positioned above the subordinate's role in the actual role hierarchy tree rather than assuming it based on job titles or the org chart, since Salesforce's hierarchy relationship depends on how roles were actually built, and third, check for less obvious causes like a restriction rule hiding the record from view even though underlying sharing is intact.

The mentoring-specific elements an interviewer wants to hear are: having the junior admin use Salesforce's own tools directly (the Roles setup page's hierarchy diagram, the record's Sharing Detail page) to see the real structure for themselves rather than being told the answer, having them document the resolution afterward so the next person facing a similar ticket has a reference, and ideally a follow-up moment where the mentee applied the same method independently on a later, similar case — that follow-up is what confirms the mentoring actually transferred the skill rather than just resolving one ticket.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I remember this one pretty specifically. A junior admin on my team was stuck on a ticket where a 'manager' supposedly couldn't see a rep's records, and on paper it looked like the role hierarchy should have covered it. Instead of just logging in and fixing it myself, I sat with them and said, 'let's not trust the org chart, let's go look at the actual role tree in Setup,' and we pulled up the Roles hierarchy diagram together — and it turned out the so-called manager's role was actually a parallel role next to the rep's, not above it, despite what the job titles implied. That's a classic trap, and I wanted them to see it for themselves rather than just hear me say 'check the role hierarchy,' because seeing the mismatch visually is what actually sticks.

After we fixed it, I had them write up what happened in our team wiki — what the ticket looked like on the surface, what the actual cause was, and the steps to check it — specifically so the next junior admin hitting something similar has a reference instead of starting from scratch. The part I'm genuinely proud of is that a few months later, a very similar ticket came in, and that same admin solved it on their own, and told me afterward they went straight to the role hierarchy diagram first instead of assuming the org chart was accurate — which told me the lesson actually transferred, not just the one fix.
commonMistakes: Just fixing the issue for the junior admin instead of teaching a transferable diagnostic approach
Not describing a specific, concrete technical detail from the actual case
Skipping how the mentee's ability to apply the lesson independently was later confirmed
Focusing only on the technical fix and omitting the mentoring/knowledge-transfer angle
Failing to mention documentation or a lasting artifact that helps the next person
keyPoints: Taught a repeatable diagnostic sequence rather than just supplying the answer
Used Salesforce's own role hierarchy visualization to verify the real reporting structure, not assumptions
Checked for less obvious causes beyond the first assumption that the hierarchy must be broken
Had the mentee document the resolution for future reuse
Confirmed the mentoring worked by the mentee later solving a similar case independently

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes teaching a repeatable method rather than just fixing the issue
Gives a specific, concrete technical detail from the case
Describes having the mentee document the resolution
Confirms transfer of skill via a later independent success
Clear, credible mentoring narrative

questions.title: Sizing Batches for a 2 Million Record Bulk Load
questions.prompt: Your team needs to load 2 million Opportunity records into a newly migrated org using the Bulk API. The first attempt at a batch size of 10,000 records in parallel mode caused widespread row lock failures and the job had to be aborted. Walk through how you'd diagnose why parallel mode caused this, and what combination of batch size, processing mode, and sequencing you'd choose to get this load through reliably.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer starts by naming the actual mechanism: when records in different parallel batches share a parent record -- in this case, multiple Opportunities rolling up to the same Account -- inserting or updating them concurrently causes SQL-style row lock escalation up to that shared Account, and two batches racing to touch the same Account at the same time will cause one of them to fail with UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW. At 10,000 records per batch in parallel mode, the odds that two batches both contain Opportunities for the same Account are high, especially if the source data wasn't sorted or grouped beforehand, so widespread lock failures are the expected outcome, not a fluke.

The candidate should describe a concrete remediation path: first, re-run a smaller sample in serial mode to confirm the load itself is clean and the failures really are concurrency-related rather than a data or mapping problem. Then address the root cause directly -- sort or group the load file by Account Id (or the relevant External ID) before chunking it into batches, so records for the same parent land in the same batch rather than being split across concurrent ones. From there, batch size should be tuned down from the 10,000 maximum if the object has heavy automation (triggers, flows, validation rules) running on insert, since each batch holds its locks for the duration of that automation and longer-running automation widens the contention window.

A complete answer also covers monitoring and fallback: use Bulk API job and batch status to identify which specific batches failed and why, rather than treating a job-level "completed" or "aborted" status as the whole story, and have a plan to re-run only the failed batches once the data is resequenced rather than reloading everything from scratch. The candidate should be explicit that parallel mode isn't unsafe in general -- it's unsafe for this specific data shape without pre-sorting, and the fix is sequencing and batch design, not simply switching everything to serial and accepting a much longer load window.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I've hit this exact failure mode before on an Opportunity load, and the first thing I'd do is stop guessing and actually pull the batch-level error detail from the Bulk API job rather than just looking at the overall job status. On a prior migration, I found that almost all of the lock failures traced back to a handful of large Accounts that had hundreds of Opportunities each, and because the source extract wasn't sorted by Account, those records were scattered randomly across different parallel batches that then fought over the same parent row.

Once I know that's the pattern, my fix isn't to just flip everything to serial mode and eat the slower runtime for all 2 million records -- that's the safe-but-lazy answer. Instead, I'd pre-sort the load file by Account Id so records for the same Account cluster together and get chunked into the same batch, which removes most of the cross-batch contention on its own. I'd also pull back the batch size from the max of 10,000 to something like 2,000-5,000 for the first pass, specifically because I'd want to check what automation runs on Opportunity insert -- if there's a heavy flow or trigger chain doing rollups or validation, smaller batches with shorter-held locks are going to be more forgiving than giant ones.

Finally, I'd treat this as a staged rollout rather than a single all-or-nothing job: run it in serial mode on a meaningful sample first to confirm the sort fixed the contention, then step back up to a moderate degree of parallelism once I've seen clean batches come through, watching the job monitor the whole way rather than walking away from an overnight run. I've learned the hard way that a job showing 'Completed' doesn't mean every record inside it succeeded -- you have to check the batch results.
questions.example: A real-world version of this: an org with 50 Accounts each holding 2,000+ Opportunities will almost guarantee lock collisions in parallel mode unless the load file is pre-sorted by Account Id, because unsorted chunking all but ensures multiple batches touch the same Account concurrently.
commonMistakes: Assuming parallel mode is always faster and therefore always the right default, without checking for shared-parent lock contention
Not sorting or grouping the load file by parent record (Account) before chunking it into batches
Defaulting to the maximum batch size of 10,000 regardless of how much automation runs on insert for that object
Treating a job status of 'Completed' as proof every record succeeded, instead of checking batch-level and row-level results
Switching straight to full serial mode as the fix instead of diagnosing and resolving the actual contention pattern
keyPoints: Row locks escalate to the shared parent record, so concurrent batches touching the same Account collide in parallel mode
Sorting or grouping the load file by parent Id before chunking removes most cross-batch contention
Batch size should be tuned down when heavy triggers, flows, or validation rules extend how long each batch holds its locks
Bulk API job status at the job level can mask partial batch or row-level failures
A staged approach (sample in serial, then controlled parallelism) validates the fix before committing to the full volume

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses lock escalation to shared parent as the root cause
Proposes a concrete sequencing/sorting fix, not just 'use serial mode'
Addresses batch size tuning relative to automation complexity
Covers job/batch monitoring and partial-failure awareness
Communicates a staged, verifiable rollout plan

questions.title: Preventing Duplicate Parent Chains During an External ID Upsert
questions.prompt: You're loading a multi-object hierarchy -- Accounts, Contacts, and Opportunities -- from a legacy system into Salesforce using External ID fields for upsert matching. Midway through testing, you discover that several Contacts are being attached to newly created duplicate Accounts instead of matching the existing ones, even though every record in the source file has an External ID value populated. Explain what's most likely causing this and how you'd redesign the load sequence and field mapping to prevent it.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats this as a mapping or sequencing defect rather than a mysterious bug, since upsert against a populated External ID should match reliably if the field and the load are configured correctly. The most likely causes, in rough order of frequency: the Account External ID field isn't actually marked as both External ID and Unique (or Unique is missing, which allows duplicate values to exist and breaks deterministic matching); the Contacts were loaded in a batch or job that ran before the corresponding Account upsert had fully committed, so the lookup had nothing to match against yet and fell back to creating a new Account via an implicit upsert on the relationship field; or the CSV header mapping for the relationship itself is wrong -- for a lookup-by-External-ID, the header needs to reference the relationship path to the External ID field (for example Account:ExternalId__c in Data Loader's relationship syntax), and a malformed or missing header silently falls through to standard Account matching or outright insert behavior.

The candidate should also flag data-quality causes: inconsistent formatting of the External ID value between source systems (case differences if the field isn't case-sensitive-safe, leading/trailing whitespace, or different ID formats from two source systems that were merged), and legacy duplicate Accounts in the source system itself that genuinely have different External ID values pointing to what a human would consider the same company.

The fix is to redesign the load as a strict two-phase sequence: first upsert Accounts alone and confirm every row succeeded with no errors before moving on, second upsert Contacts with the relationship field correctly mapped to the Account's External ID path, and run that second phase only after verifying phase one. The candidate should also mention verifying field configuration (External ID + Unique checked) and running a small reconciliation query afterward -- counting distinct External ID values against distinct Account Ids created -- to catch any residual duplicates before scaling up to the full volume.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd check isn't the data at all -- it's the field definition. I've seen this exact symptom before where someone populates an External ID field correctly in every row, but the field itself was never checked as Unique when it was created, so Salesforce has no way to guarantee one Account per External ID value, and upsert ends up creating new records instead of reliably finding the existing one. That's a thirty-second check in Setup that would have ruled out a whole category of causes before I went digging into the data itself.

Assuming the field is configured correctly, my next suspicion would be sequencing. In my experience, this kind of 'Contacts attaching to brand-new duplicate Accounts' problem shows up constantly when someone runs the Contact load in the same session as the Account load, or kicks it off before confirming the Account batch actually finished committing -- the Contact upsert tries to match against an External ID that technically doesn't exist in the org yet from the system's point of view, even though it's sitting right there in the Account CSV that was 'already run.' I'd want to see the two loads run as genuinely separate, sequential steps, with a hard verification step in between -- actually pulling a report of newly created Accounts and spot-checking their External ID values -- before I'd trust moving on to Contacts.

If both of those check out, I'd go look at the CSV header syntax for the relationship field itself, because getting the dot/colon notation wrong for a lookup-by-External-ID is an easy mistake that fails silently rather than throwing an obvious error -- it just falls back to normal behavior. And honestly, I'd also ask the business side whether the legacy system itself might just have real duplicate Accounts with different IDs, because sometimes the 'bug' is actually accurate data quality from the source.
questions.example: For instance, if the Account External ID field was created without the Unique checkbox, two Account records could legitimately carry the same External ID value in Salesforce, and the Contact upsert's match against that field becomes ambiguous or unreliable rather than deterministic.
commonMistakes: Assuming a populated External ID value is sufficient without verifying the field is marked both External ID and Unique
Running parent and child object loads in the same pass instead of as strictly sequential, verified phases
Getting the CSV relationship-header syntax for a lookup-by-External-ID wrong and not noticing because it fails silently into a different behavior
Overlooking formatting inconsistencies (case, whitespace, ID format) between two merged source systems feeding the same External ID field
Not running a reconciliation check (distinct External ID count vs. distinct Account count) before scaling the fix to the full data volume
keyPoints: External ID fields must be marked Unique, not just External ID, for upsert matching to be deterministic
Parent object loads must fully complete and be verified before dependent child object loads run
Relationship-field CSV headers for lookup-by-External-ID have specific syntax that fails silently when wrong
Formatting inconsistencies (case, whitespace) between merged source systems can break otherwise-correct matching
A post-load reconciliation check catches residual duplicate chains before they propagate to later phases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies field configuration (Unique) as a likely root cause
Diagnoses sequencing/commit-timing between parent and child loads
Addresses CSV relationship-field mapping syntax correctly
Covers data-quality/formatting causes from merged source systems
Proposes a verifiable two-phase load redesign with reconciliation
